Chapter 12. Generating Functions: Packing a Whole Table of Coefficients into One Expression

Difficulty ★★★ (Advanced)

Proofs for this chapter: Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 12 (Proofs 12-1 to 12-7)

So far, a table of coefficients has been a row of numbers laid out in a line. This time we pack that row into a single polynomial. Take 1, 10, 45, …, 10, 1 as coefficients and write 1 + 10x + 45x² + … + x¹⁰, and this is exactly (1+x)¹⁰. An expression that packs a sequence in as the coefficients of a polynomial (or of a power series that goes on forever) is called a generating function. You can read x not so much as a variable to plug values into, but as a “placeholder that remembers the slot number.”

This tool is less about teaching a new calculation than about showing that facts proved separately in earlier chapters come from the same principle. We will write the coefficient of x^k as [x^k]. For example, x³⁵ = C(5,3) = 10.

A map of this chapter

  • The three Bonuses of Chapter 2 and the addition rule of Chapter 3 are re-proved in one line each in 12-1 and 12-2.

  • The dice-sum distribution table of Chapter 8 becomes polynomial multiplication in 12-3.

  • The Fibonacci and Catalan numbers of Chapter 10 are connected to recurrences and generating functions in 12-4.

  • The mean and variance of Chapter 4 and the Poisson limit of Chapter 7 come out together in 12-5.

  • The central limit theorem of Chapter 8 meets the e of Chapter 10 in 12-6.

12-1. Multiplying is joining cases together

Write one coin as 1 + x. The 1 is tails (0 points) and the x is heads (1 point). Two coins give (1+x)(1+x) = 1 + 2x + x², and the coefficients 1, 2, 1 are the numbers of ways to get 0, 1, or 2 heads. The exponent is the total score (xᵃ·xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ) and the coefficient is the number of cases, so multiplying polynomials amounts to joining the cases of two boxes and counting by total. The general rule is this: the coefficient of x^k in a product is the sum of the products of coefficients over all pairs whose total is k.

[x^{k}]\bigl(A(x)\,B(x)\bigr) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i\,b_{k-i}

[xᵏ] ( A(x)·B(x) ) = ∑ᵢ₌₀ᵏ aᵢ · bₖ₋ᵢ

The addition rule of Chapter 3, seen again

Seeing (1+x)ⁿ as (1+x)·(1+x)ⁿ⁻¹: if the newly multiplied coin lands tails (×1), the row above is left as it is; if it lands heads (×x), the row above is shifted over by one slot. Combining the two cases, each coefficient becomes the sum of two neighboring slots.

[x^{k}](1+x)^{n} = [x^{k}](1+x)^{n-1} + [x^{k-1}](1+x)^{n-1} \;\Longrightarrow\; \binom{n}{k}=\binom{n-1}{k}+\binom{n-1}{k-1}

[xᵏ](1+x)ⁿ = [xᵏ](1+x)ⁿ⁻¹ + [xᵏ⁻¹](1+x)ⁿ⁻¹   ⟹   C(n,k) = C(n−1,k) + C(n−1,k−1)

Symmetry in one line, too: since (1+x)ⁿ = xⁿ(1 + 1/x)ⁿ, replacing x with 1/x and multiplying by xⁿ gives the same expression. This means the coefficients read the same backward, that is, C(n,k) = C(n,n−k).

12-2. Plugging values into x to revisit the Bonuses of Chapter 2

Since (1+x)ⁿ is a single expression, we can do expression-level things to it, such as plugging in values for x or differentiating. The three “Bonuses” that we counted with such effort in Chapter 2 all come out in a single line.

| What we do | Result | Which story from Chapter 2 |

| Plug in x = 1 | 2ⁿ = ∑C(n,k) | Method A, the total is 2ⁿ |

| Plug in x = −1 | 0 = ∑(−1)ᵏC(n,k) | Bonus 1, even-sized and odd-sized groups are equal in number |

| Differentiate, then plug in x = 1 | ∑k·C(n,k) = n·2ⁿ⁻¹ | Bonus 2, the mean is n/2 |

| Multiply it by itself | the xⁿ coefficient of (1+x)ⁿ(1+x)ⁿ = (1+x)²ⁿ | Bonus 3, the sum of squares |

Differentiating (Bonus 2)

Differentiating (1+x)ⁿ, the left side becomes ∑k·C(n,k)·xᵏ⁻¹ as each term’s exponent drops down to become a coefficient, and the right side is n(1+x)ⁿ⁻¹. Then plug in x=1.

\sum_{k=0}^{n} k\binom{n}{k} = n\,2^{\,n-1}

∑ₖ₌₀ⁿ k·C(n,k) = n·2ⁿ⁻¹

For n=10 this is 10×512 = 5120, and 5120 ÷ 1024 = 5 is the mean. What we counted in Chapter 2 by “choosing one representative” we have now obtained with a single differentiation.

Multiplying by itself (Bonus 3) and its generalization

We count the xⁿ coefficient of (1+x)ⁿ·(1+x)ⁿ = (1+x)²ⁿ in two ways. The right side gives C(2n,n), and the left side, by the product rule of 12-1, gives ∑C(n,k)·C(n,n−k). Thanks to the symmetry C(n,n−k) = C(n,k), this is the sum of squares of the coefficients, and for n=10 it is 184756 = C(20,10). If we give the two factors different degrees, a more general identity appears.

\sum_{k}\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{r-k} = \binom{m+n}{r}

∑ₖ C(m,k)·C(n,r−k) = C(m+n,r)

This comes from comparing the xʳ coefficients of (1+x)ᵐ·(1+x)ⁿ = (1+x)ᵐ⁺ⁿ, and it is called the Vandermonde identity. Read as choosing groups: “the number of ways to choose r people in total from a team of m and a team of n equals the sum, over all k, of the cases choosing k from the first team and r−k from the second.” For m=3, n=4, r=3 we get 1·4 + 3·6 + 3·4 + 1·1 = 35 = C(7,3).

12-3. Dice: a “coin” with six faces

One die is x + x² + x³ + x⁴ + x⁵ + x⁶. The case where face s comes up is marked by a single xˢ. The distribution of the sum of two dice thrown is the square of this expression.

(x+x^2+\cdots+x^6)^2 = x^2+2x^3+3x^4+4x^5+5x^6+6x^7+5x^8+4x^9+3x^{10}+2x^{11}+x^{12}

(x + x² + ··· + x⁶)² = x² + 2x³ + 3x⁴ + 4x⁵ + 5x⁶ + 6x⁷ + 5x⁸ + 4x⁹ + 3x¹⁰ + 2x¹¹ + x¹²

The coefficient 6 is the coefficient of x⁷, so it means there are 6 ways to get a sum of 7. The distribution table that we built in Chapter 8 by “adding up six neighboring slots” is the same as multiplying this expression by (x+…+x⁶) once more. The number of ways 27 for three dice to sum to 10 is the coefficient of x¹⁰ in the cube.

Sicherman dice: other dice made by factoring

Since these are polynomials, we can also factor them. The expression for one die factors as follows.

x+x^2+\cdots+x^6 = x\,(1+x)\,(1+x+x^2)\,(1-x+x^2)

x + x² + ··· + x⁶ = x · (1+x) · (1+x+x²) · (1−x+x²)

When squared, each of these factors appears twice. If we divide these factors differently from ordinary dice and hand them out to the two dice, we get a different pair of dice with the same distribution of sums (Let ‘em roll, Sicherman Dice).

A(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x^2) = x+2x^2+2x^3+x^4,
B(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x^2)(1-x+x^2)^2 = x+x^3+x^4+x^5+x^6+x^8

A(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x²) = x + 2x² + 2x³ + x⁴            → faces 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4
B(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x²)(1−x+x²)² = x + x³ + x⁴ + x⁵ + x⁶ + x⁸   → faces 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8

If you throw the die with faces (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4) and the die with faces (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8), the probabilities of the sums 2 to 12 are identical to those of two ordinary dice at every value. For example, the ways to get a sum of 9 with ordinary dice are the 4 ways 3+6, 4+5, 5+4, 6+3, and with this pair they are the 4 ways 1+8, 3+6, 3+6 (A has two 3s), 4+5. It is known that, for six-faced dice with positive integer faces, apart from the ordinary dice this one pair is the only one; it is said to have been found by George Sicherman in the 1970s and introduced by Martin Gardner in 1978.

Distribution of the sum of two dice (each █ ≈ 1%) — the ordinary pair and the Sicherman pair are exactly the same

Sum= 2  1/36 =  2.8%  ███
Sum= 3  2/36 =  5.6%  ██████
Sum= 4  3/36 =  8.3%  ████████
Sum= 5  4/36 = 11.1%  ███████████
Sum= 6  5/36 = 13.9%  ██████████████
Sum= 7  6/36 = 16.7%  █████████████████
Sum= 8  5/36 = 13.9%  ██████████████
Sum= 9  4/36 = 11.1%  ███████████
Sum=10  3/36 =  8.3%  ████████

Sum=12  1/36 =  2.8%  ███

Both pairs produce all 11 of these bars identically. The curious part is that the faces differ and yet the distribution of the sum is the same.

12-4. A recurrence in one expression: Fibonacci, Catalan, and making change

Fibonacci

Let F(x) = F₁x + F₂x² + F₃x³ + … (F₁ = F₂ = 1). The recurrence Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ holds coefficient by coefficient for n ≥ 3, so in F(x) − xF(x) − x²F(x) only a single x remains. So (1 − x − x²)F(x) = x, that is, F(x) = x/(1−x−x²). The Fibonacci numbers we obtained in Chapter 10 as “sums along shallow diagonals” come out of the same expression. Here 1/(1−x−x²) = F(x)/x, so the xⁿ coefficient of this expression is Fₙ₊₁. Plugging u = x(1+x) into 1/(1−u) = 1 + u + u² + … gives the following.

\frac{1}{1-x-x^{2}} = \frac{1}{1-x(1+x)} = \sum_{m\ge 0} x^{m}(1+x)^{m} \;\Longrightarrow\; F_{n+1} = \sum_{k}\binom{n-k}{k}

1/(1−x−x²) = 1/(1−x(1+x)) = ∑ₘ₌₀^∞ xᵐ(1+x)ᵐ   ⟹   Fₙ₊₁ = ∑ₖ C(n−k,k)

The coefficient of xⁿ in xᵐ(1+x)ᵐ is C(m, n−m), and rewriting with k = n−m gives C(n−k, k). This is exactly the sum that reads Pascal’s triangle along shallow diagonals. For n=5, C(5,0) + C(4,1) + C(3,2) = 1 + 4 + 3 = 8 = F₆.

Catalan numbers

A correctly matched parenthesis string is either empty (1 way) or splits uniquely into the form “( A ) B”. This is because if you find the closing parenthesis paired with the first opening parenthesis, the inside A and the outside B each become correctly matched strings. If A has k pairs and B has n−k pairs, the whole has n+1 pairs, so the following recurrence comes out.

C₍ₙ₊₁₎ = C₀Cₙ + C₁Cₙ₋₁ + … + CₙC₀

For example, C₃ = C₀C₂ + C₁C₁ + C₂C₀ = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, the same as the 5 ways in Chapter 10. This recurrence is summarized in a single line for the generating function of the Catalan numbers, Cat(x) = C₀ + C₁x + C₂x² + ….

\mathrm{Cat}(x) = 1 + x\,\mathrm{Cat}(x)^{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Cat}(x) = \frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}

Cat(x) = 1 + x·Cat(x)²   ⟹   Cat(x) = (1 − √(1−4x)) / (2x)

It is known that expanding the closed form on the right gives Cₙ = C(2n,n)/(n+1) from Chapter 10 (we omit the derivation here).

Counting ways to make change

A 1-won coin can be written as 1 + x + x² + … (any number of them may be used) = 1/(1−x), a 2-won coin as 1/(1−x²), and a 5-won coin as 1/(1−x⁵). The number of ways to make 10 won with the three coins is the coefficient of x¹⁰ in the product of these three expressions.

\frac{1}{(1-x)(1-x^{2})(1-x^{5})} \;\Longrightarrow\; [x^{10}] = 10

1 / ((1−x)(1−x²)(1−x⁵))   ⟹   [x¹⁰] = 10

We can also count by hand. Using two 5-won coins gives 1 way (5+5); using one gives 3 ways (making the remaining 5 won from 1-won and 2-won coins, with 0, 1, or 2 two-won coins); and using no 5-won coin gives 6 ways (making 10 won from 1-won and 2-won coins, with 0 to 5 two-won coins). 1 + 3 + 6 = 10. The number of ways to make 1000 won with the Korean coins 10 won, 50 won, 100 won, and 500 won is 158.

12-5. Generating functions for probability: mean, variance, and the Poisson limit all at once

When we use generating functions for probability, we put “the probability that X = k” as the coefficient of xᵏ. This is called the probability generating function, and G(x) = ∑P(X=k)xᵏ = E[xˣ] (BME summary sheet). One toss of a fair coin is (1+x)/2, the binomial distribution is (1−p+px)ⁿ (which comes out immediately by the binomial theorem), and the Poisson distribution is e^(λ(x−1)). There are three rules we need.

  • A sum of independent variables is a product: if X and Y are independent, the probability generating function of X+Y is G_X(x)·G_Y(x). This is the product rule of 12-1 carried over to probability.

  • Mean: E[X] = G′(1)

  • Variance: Var(X) = G″(1) + G′(1) − G′(1)²

Mean and variance of the binomial distribution (Chapter 4)

Differentiating G(x) = (1−p+px)ⁿ gives G′(x) = np(1−p+px)ⁿ⁻¹, so G′(1) = np. Differentiating once more gives G″(1) = n(n−1)p². So the variance is n(n−1)p² + np − n²p² = np − np² = np(1−p). For n=10, p=1/2, G″(1) = 22.5 and 22.5 + 5 − 25 = 2.5, the same as the variance in Chapter 4.

The Poisson limit of Chapter 7 in one line

Setting p = λ/n, the generating function of the binomial distribution is (1 + λ(x−1)/n)ⁿ, and as n → ∞, plugging a = λ(x−1) into the limit (1+a/n)ⁿ → eᵃ from Chapter 10 gives the following (Leicester lecture notes).

\Bigl(1+\frac{\lambda(x-1)}{n}\Bigr)^{n} \;\longrightarrow\; e^{\lambda(x-1)}

(1 + λ(x−1)/n)ⁿ → e^(λ(x−1))

The generating function of the Poisson distribution, ∑e^(−λ)λᵏxᵏ/k! = e^(−λ)·e^(λx), is also exactly this expression. There is a theorem that if generating functions go to the same value, the distributions also go to the same distribution, and the result of Chapter 7 follows (here we have shown only the outline). More comes out of the same expression.

  • Why the mean and variance are equal: from G(x) = e^(λ(x−1)), G′(1) = λ and G″(1) = λ², so the variance is λ² + λ − λ² = λ.

  • Sums are Poisson too: the product of two independent Poisson generating functions, e^(λ₁(x−1))·e^(λ₂(x−1)) = e^((λ₁+λ₂)(x−1)), is again Poisson. If two departments have daily average errors of 2 and 3, the total is Poisson with mean 5.

  • Sums of binomials are binomial: since (1−p+px)ᵐ·(1−p+px)ⁿ = (1−p+px)ᵐ⁺ⁿ, adding two binomial distributions with the same p gives a binomial distribution.

12-6. One step further: the road from the central limit theorem to e

If we rewrite the coin as heads +1 and tails −1, the generating function for one toss is (x + 1/x)/2. Plugging in x = e^(it) gives (e^(it) + e^(−it))/2 = cos t. A generating function like this, with the imaginary i plugged in, is called a characteristic function. This coin has mean 0 and variance 1, so the characteristic function of the sum of n tosses divided by √n (standardization) is cos(t/√n) to the n-th power. Since cos s ≈ 1 − s²/2, we have cos(t/√n) ≈ 1 − t²/(2n), and plugging a = −t²/2 into (1+a/n)ⁿ → eᵃ from Chapter 10 gives the following.

\cos^{n}\!\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sqrt n}\Bigr) \approx \Bigl(1-\frac{t^{2}}{2n}\Bigr)^{n} \;\longrightarrow\; e^{-t^{2}/2}

cosⁿ(t/√n) ≈ (1 − t²/(2n))ⁿ → e^(−t²/2)

e^(−t²/2) is the characteristic function of the standard normal distribution. Let’s see how quickly the values approach it at t=1.

| | cos(1/√n)ⁿ | (1 − 1/(2n))ⁿ |

| n=10 | 0.6014 | 0.5987 |

| n=100 | 0.6060 | 0.6058 |

| n=1000 | 0.6065 | 0.6065 |

| Limit | e^(−1/2) = 0.6065 | 0.6065 |

The fact from Chapters 6 and 8 that coin sums head toward a bell shape stands on the same limit as (1+1/n)ⁿ → e from Chapter 10. A rigorous proof needs a separate theorem saying “if characteristic functions converge, the distributions converge too,” and here we have shown only the outline.

12-7. Summary at a glance

| Problem | Generating function | How to read it |

| n coins | (1+x)ⁿ | [xᵏ] = number of ways to get k heads |

| Sum of n dice | (x+…+x⁶)ⁿ | [xˢ] = number of ways to get sum s |

| Making change | 1/((1−x)(1−x²)(1−x⁵)) | [x¹⁰] = number of ways to make 10 won |

| Fibonacci | x/(1−x−x²) | [xⁿ] = Fₙ |

| Catalan | Cat(x) = 1 + x·Cat(x)² | [xⁿ] = Cₙ |

| Binomial distribution | (1−p+px)ⁿ | G′(1) = np, sums of independent variables are products |

| Poisson distribution | e^(λ(x−1)) | mean = variance = λ, sums are Poisson too |

  • Exercise 3: 6 ways. 5+2, 5+1+1, 2+2+2+1, 2+2+1+1+1, 2+1+1+1+1+1, and seven 1s.

Chapter 13. How Fast Do the Coefficients Grow: Stirling’s Formula and Entropy

Difficulty ★★★ (Advanced)

Proofs for this chapter: Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 13 (Proofs 13-1 to 13-6)

How big is C(100,50)? Using the factorial formula as it stands, we would have to compute 100!, but the value is about 1.0089×10²⁹. This chapter deals with how to estimate the size of such huge coefficients, and with what the estimates mean. This chapter also confirms where the value 1/√(2πσ²), which we said in Chapter 6 is the peak of the bell, comes from.

13-1. Stirling’s formula: approximating factorials

For large n, n! can be approximated as follows. This is Stirling’s formula, which we only introduced by name in Chapter 6.

n! \approx \sqrt{2\pi n}\,\Bigl(\frac{n}{e}\Bigr)^{n}

n! ≈ √(2πn) · (n/e)ⁿ

It fits astonishingly well even for small n.

| n | n! | Stirling approximation | Relative error | For reference: 1/(12n) |

| 5 | 120 | 118.02 | -1.65% | 1.67% |

| 10 | 3628800 | 3,598,696 | -0.83% | 0.83% |

| 20 | 2.433e+18 | 2.423e+18 | -0.42% | 0.42% |

| 100 | 9.333e+157 | 9.325e+157 | -0.08% | 0.08% |

The last column shows that the relative error shrinks at roughly 1/(12n). This agrees with the known results on the error of Stirling’s formula (Klappenecker notes).

13-2. The middle coefficient: 4ⁿ/√(πn)

Let’s plug Stirling’s formula into C(2n,n) = (2n)!/(n!)². The numerator is √(4πn)(2n/e)²ⁿ and the denominator is [√(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ]² = 2πn(n/e)²ⁿ, and when (n/e)²ⁿ cancels, the following remains.

\binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{(n!)^{2}} \approx \frac{\sqrt{4\pi n}\,(2n/e)^{2n}}{2\pi n\,(n/e)^{2n}} = \frac{4^{n}}{\sqrt{\pi n}}

C(2n,n) = (2n)! / (n!)² ≈ √(4πn)·(2n/e)²ⁿ / (2πn·(n/e)²ⁿ) = 4ⁿ / √(πn)

Let’s see how well it fits.

P(\text{exactly } n:n) = \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^{n}} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi n}}

P(exactly n:n) = C(2n,n) / 4ⁿ ≈ 1/√(πn)

This is the same story as Chapter 8’s “the difference in counts actually widens,” seen from the opposite direction.

13-3. General k: the binary entropy appears

Even when k is not in the middle, we can approximate in the same way. Plugging Stirling’s formula into the three places n!, k!, (n−k)!, parts like (n/e)ⁿ cancel and nⁿ / (kᵏ(n−k)ⁿ⁻ᵏ) remains, and this value is the 2^(nH(q)) below (Galvin lecture).

\binom{n}{k} \approx \frac{2^{\,nH(q)}}{\sqrt{2\pi n\,q(1-q)}}, \qquad q=\frac{k}{n}, \qquad H(q) = -q\log_2 q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)

C(n,k) ≈ 2^(nH(q)) / √(2πn·q(1−q)),    q = k/n,    H(q) = −q·log₂q − (1−q)·log₂(1−q)

H(q) is the binary entropy, a measure, in units of bits, of the “uncertainty” in a single toss of a coin whose probability of heads is q. The values are as follows.

13-4. What it means: almost all cases lie in the middle

H(q) is at most 1, and equals 1 only at q=1/2. Of all 2ⁿ cases, the cases where the proportion of heads is q number about 2^(nH(q)), so when q is not 1/2 they are exponentially few compared with the whole. For example, at n=100 the case of exactly 30 heads has C(100,30) / 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 2.3×10⁻⁵, that is, about once in 43,000 times. This is the combinatorial reason behind what the law of large numbers in Chapter 8 said, that “the proportion gathers at 1/2.” The number of cases where the proportion strays from 1/2 loses its share of the whole exponentially fast as n grows.

Information and compression

The same expression is used in information theory too. Among 0/1 strings of length 100, those with exactly ten 1s number C(100,10) = 1.7310×10¹³, and since log₂ 1.7310×10¹³ ≈ 43.98, about 44 bits suffice to number each of these strings. That is less than half of the original 100 bits. It is close to the value nH(0.1) = 46.9 in the formula above (the 2.9-bit difference is the correction from the √ part). The fact that a random string in which only 10% of the symbols are 1 can be compressed to about H(0.1) = 0.47 bits per bit means the same thing as Shannon’s source coding theorem, which speaks of the limit of compression.

13-5. The probability of straying shrinks exponentially

For the probability that, in n tosses of a fair coin, the proportion of heads is at least q (q > 1/2), using the fact that the number of cases with proportion at least q is at most 2^(nH(q)) (Galvin lecture), the following upper bound comes out.

P(X \ge qn) \le 2^{-n\,(1-H(q))} \qquad (q\ge \tfrac12,\ p=\tfrac12)

P(X ≥ qn) ≤ 2^(−n(1−H(q)))    (q ≥ ½, fair coin)

For example, for n=100, q=0.6 we have 1−H(0.6) ≈ 0.029, so the upper bound is 2^(−2.9) ≈ 13.4%, and the exact probability is P(X≥60) ≈ 2.84%. Being an upper bound, it is looser than the truth, but the shape of shrinking exponentially is the same. A similar result is Hoeffding’s inequality.

P\bigl(\,|X/n-\tfrac12|\ge\varepsilon\bigr) \le 2\,e^{-2n\varepsilon^{2}}

P( |X/n − ½| ≥ ε ) ≤ 2·e^(−2nε²)

The problem in Chapter 8 of “the proportion of heads is 45 to 55%” is the case ε=0.05, and as the sample grows, the probability of straying shrinks as follows.

| | Exact probability | Hoeffding bound 2e^(−2nε²) |

| n=100 | 36.8% | 121% (exceeds 1, meaningless) |

| n=400 | 5.1% | 27.1% |

| n=1000 | 0.173% | 1.35% |

| n=2000 | 0.000846% | 0.00908% |

The exact probabilities in the table count even the cases where the proportion is exactly 45% or 55% as “straying,” so they are larger than the outside probability of Chapter 8 (27% at n=100) (Proof 13-5). At n=100 the bound exceeds 1 and is useless (the exact value is about 36.8%), and at n=1000 the exact value drops to 0.17%. This is the reason Chapter 8 said that with 1000 tosses the probability that the proportion falls within 45 to 55% is close to 99.9%.

Probability of straying 5 percentage points or more from 1/2 (bar = −log₁₀(probability) ≈ number of digits, each █ ≈ 0.25)

n= 100 exact  36.8%      ██
       bound  121%       (exceeds 1, meaningless)
n= 400 exact   5.1%      █████
       bound  27.1%      ▒▒
n=1000 exact   0.173%    ███████████
       bound   1.35%     ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒
n=2000 exact   0.000846% ████████████████████
       bound   0.00908%  ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒

Bars getting longer as n grows means the probability shrinks exponentially. The Hoeffding bound (▒) is loose, but it lengthens in the same direction.

13-6. Summary at a glance

| What we want to know | Approximation | Result of this chapter |

| n! | √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ | relative error about 1/(12n) |

| Middle coefficient C(2n,n) | 4ⁿ/√(πn) | relative error about 1/(8n) |

| General coefficient C(n,k) | 2^(nH(q)) / √(2πnq(1−q)) | connected to the peak of the bell in Chapter 6 |

| Probability of exactly n:n | 1/√(πn) | shrinks like 1/√n as we toss more |

| Probability of the proportion straying | 2^(−n(1−H(q))), 2e^(−2nε²) | shrinks exponentially |

Checking in code

from math import comb, log2, sqrt, pi

n = 100
for k in (10, 30, 50):
    q = k / n
    H = -q * log2(q) - (1 - q) * log2(1 - q)
    approx = 2 ** (n * H) / sqrt(2 * pi * n * q * (1 - q))
    print(k, comb(n, k), f"{approx:.4g}", f"{(approx / comb(n, k) - 1) * 100:+.2f}%")

Try it yourself

  1. Approximate C(20,10) with the Stirling approximation. 4¹⁰/√(10π) ≈ 187079, and the exact value is 184756.

  2. Among 0/1 strings of length 1000, those with exactly two hundred 1s can be numbered with roughly how many bits?

  3. In the code above, change n to 20, 100, and 1000 and check how the relative error shrinks.

Something to think about: Even though the probability of exactly n:n in 2n tosses shrinks like 1/√(πn), the law of large numbers in Chapter 8 says the proportion gathers at 1/2. Why do these two statements not contradict each other?

Answers

  • Exercise 1: The relative error is (187079 − 184756)/184756 ≈ +1.26%, in line with the 1/(8n) = 1.25% estimate of 13-2.

  • Exercise 2: log₂ C(1000,200) ≈ 716.9 bits. This is nH(0.2) = 721.9 minus the correction of about 5.0 bits from the √ part. 1000 bits shrink to about 717 bits.

  • Exercise 3: Each time n grows tenfold, the relative error shrinks to about one tenth.

  • Something to think about: “Exactly half and half” is a single slot, while a range of proportions (for example 45 to 55%) combines a great many slots, a number proportional to √n. The probability of a single slot shrinks like 1/√n, but the probability of the whole range, whose width is proportional to √n, approaches 1.

Closing: A One-Sentence Summary and Questions to Think About

Starting from a single table of coefficients, the idea of “counting every case without leaving any out” became probability, passed through the bell shape, and reached the margin of error in opinion polls. At the end, we saw that the same table can also be read not as probability but as shapes and rules. Next, in Chapter 11 we widened the table into three directions and met the pyramid and the multinomial distribution; in Chapter 12 we packed the whole table into a single polynomial and re-proved the results of the earlier chapters one line at a time; and in Chapter 13 we read, through entropy, how fast the coefficients grow for large n.

Answers to the four opening questions

  1. Why the sum is 2^n: Because counting the same set of cases all at once or splitting it by type and counting each gives the same result.

  2. Why the middle is high: Because more paths lead to the middle cell than to the edges, and as n grows the shape approaches the normal distribution.

  3. Where we meet it: In places like the margin of error in opinion polls, tests of coins and drug effects, and the number of occurrences of rare events. But we must also remember that the margin of error or the p-value does not capture every real-world error.

  4. Reading the same table as shapes and rules: Along the diagonals we find triangular numbers and Fibonacci numbers; adding conditions on the paths gives Catalan numbers; coloring only the odd entries gives the Sierpiński triangle; and the product of a row gives e. Coefficients, probability, limits, and fractals all live together in one table.

One-line summaries of Chapters 11–13

  • Chapter 11: With three choices, the coefficient becomes n!/(a!b!c!), the table becomes a pyramid, and the probability becomes the multinomial distribution.

  • Chapter 12: Pack the table of coefficients into a single polynomial, and the sum, mean, sum of squares, dice distributions, Fibonacci numbers, Catalan numbers, and the Poisson limit all reduce to “multiplying” and “plugging a value into x.”

  • Chapter 13: By Stirling’s formula, C(n,k) takes the form 2^(nH(k/n)), and this is why the probability that the proportion strays from 1/2 shrinks exponentially.

Three questions to think about

  • When you toss a coin 100 times, what is the probability of getting exactly 50 heads? The answer is about 8%. The normal approximation, 1/(5√(2π)) ≈ 0.080, gives a similar value.

  • If you quadruple the sample size of a poll, how much does the margin of error shrink? The answer is by half.

  • If heads has come up 5 times in a row, has the probability of tails on the next toss gone up? The answer is no; it is still 1/2.

Part 2. Proofs

This part proves each claim of Part 1. “Proofs Chapter n” corresponds to Chapter n of the main text, and the proofs are numbered “Proof n-m.” Wherever it says “main text Chapter n,” it refers to a chapter of Part 1. The proofs mainly use the five tools from Chapter 0 (the product rule, the sum rule, double counting, induction, and the distributive law). If the going gets hard, you can still follow the flow by reading only the “Intuition” paragraphs and the “Checking with numbers” paragraphs first.

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 0. Warm-up: Notation and the Toolbox

0-1. Notation

  • n! = n×(n−1)×…×2×1 : the number of ways to line up n things in a row. We define 0! = 1. The number of ways to line up nothing is exactly 1 way, the “do nothing” way, and we must set it this way so that n! = n×(n−1)! also holds at n=1 (1! = 1×0!).

  • C(n,k) : the number of ways to choose k out of n, without regard to order. This is the binomial coefficient of the main text.

  • Σ : the summation symbol. Σ_{k=0}^{n} a_k means a_0 + a_1 + … + a_n.

  • X ~ B(n,p) : the number of successes when a trial with success probability p is done independently n times. We write q = 1−p.

  • E[X] : the mean (expected value), Var(X) : the variance, σ : the standard deviation (the square root of the variance).

0-2. The Toolbox

Nearly every proof in this book is built from five tools.

  • T1 Product rule: If there are several stages and the choice at each stage does not affect the others, the total number of cases is the product of the numbers of cases at each stage. (3 pairs of trousers × 4 tops = 12 outfits)

  • T2 Sum rule (partition): If you split the whole into pieces with no overlap and no gaps, the total is the sum of the sizes of the pieces.

  • T3 Double counting: Count the same set in two different ways and set the two expressions equal. This is the tool used most often in this book.

  • T4 Mathematical induction: If the first case is true, and you show that “true at n implies true at n+1,” then it is true for every n. It is like dominoes: if the first one falls, they all fall to the end.

  • T5 Distributive law: (a+b)(c+d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. When you expand parentheses, you pick one term from each pair of parentheses, multiply them, and add up all such products.

Proof 0-1. C(n,k) = n! / ( k! (n−k)! )

Intuition: Choices where order matters are easy to count. To erase the order, just divide by the number of times each same group was counted repeatedly.

Proof

  1. Pick k people with order taken into account. The first is 1 person out of n (n ways), the second is 1 out of the remaining n−1, …, and the k-th has n−k+1 ways. By the product rule (T1), there are n×(n−1)×…×(n−k+1) = n!/(n−k)! ways.

  2. If the k people chosen are the same, results that differ only in order are the same “group.” There are k! ways to line up the same group, so in the count from step 1, each group was counted exactly k! times.

  3. Therefore (the number of ordered choices) = C(n,k) × k!, that is, C(n,k) = n! / ( (n−k)! k! ). ∎

Checking with numbers: Choosing 3 out of 10 people with order gives 10×9×8 = 720 ways, and each group was counted 3! = 6 times, so 720÷6 = 120. This matches the 120 in the main text.

Boundary conventions: If k=0, then C(n,0) = n!/(0! n!) = 1 (there is 1 way to choose no one), and if k=n, then C(n,n) = 1. We also agree that C(n,k) = 0 if k<0 or k>n. We introduce this convention so that the addition rule of Chapter 3 works smoothly all the way to the boundary.

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 1. What You See When You Line Up the Coefficients

Chapter 1 of the main text is centered on “listing,” but the three observations (the sum is a power of 2, left-right symmetry, and the middle is the largest) and two hand expansions are what this chapter proves. We also attach the proof of the binomial theorem itself here, because it is the root of every chapter.

Proof 1-1. Hand expansion of (x+y)^2

Proof: (x+y)^2 = (x+y)(x+y). By the distributive law (T5), we pick one term from the first parentheses and one from the second, multiply them, and add everything up.

(x+y)(x+y) = x·x + x·y + y·x + y·y

Multiplication gives the same result when the order is swapped, so y·x = x·y. Hence we get x² + 2xy + y². The coefficients are 1, 2, 1. ∎

The important point here is that the middle coefficient 2 means “there are two ways to get xy (x·y or y·x).” A coefficient is the result of counting.

Proof 1-2. Hand expansion of (x+y)^3

Proof: There are three pairs of parentheses, so the number of ways to pick x or y from each is 2×2×2 = 8 (T1), and 8 products appear in the expansion. We group these 8 by how many y’s they contain.

  • 0 y’s: xxx → 1 way → x³

  • 1 y: xxy, xyx, yxx → 3 ways → 3x²y

  • 2 y’s: xyy, yxy, yyx → 3 ways → 3xy²

  • 3 y’s: yyy → 1 way → y³

Adding up, we get x³ + 3x²y + 3xy² + y³, with coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1. The total count is 1+3+3+1 = 8 = 2³, which matches exactly the 8 ways we counted at the start. ∎

Proof 1-3. The binomial theorem: (x+y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^k

This theorem is the root of the whole main text. We give two proofs.

Proof A (direct counting)

  1. (x+y)^n is the expression obtained by multiplying (x+y) by itself n times. If we repeat the distributive law (T5) n times, the expansion is the sum of all products formed by “picking one x or y from each of the n pairs of parentheses.” There are 2^n ways to choose, and these correspond one-to-one with the 2^n strings of x’s and y’s of length n. (For example, when n=3, a string like xyx.)

  2. If a string has exactly k y’s, its product is x^{n−k} y^k. Thanks to the commutative law of multiplication, the order of the letters does not affect the result.

  3. The number of strings with exactly k y’s is the number of ways to choose the k positions for y among n positions, C(n,k).

  4. Therefore the term x^{n−k} y^k appears C(n,k) times, and adding everything up gives Σ C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^k. ∎

Proof B (induction, T4)

  • Base case: For n=0, (x+y)^0 = 1 = C(0,0) x^0 y^0. True.

  • Inductive step: Assuming it is true for n, (x+y)^{n+1} = (x+y) × Σ_k C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^k. The part multiplied by x is Σ_k C(n,k) x^{n+1−k} y^k, and the part multiplied by y is Σ_k C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^{k+1}; in the second sum, if we rename k+1 as the new k, it becomes Σ_k C(n,k−1) x^{n+1−k} y^k.

  • Collecting like terms x^{n+1−k} y^k, the coefficient is C(n,k) + C(n,k−1), and by the addition rule of Chapter 3 (Proof 3-1) this is C(n+1,k). Therefore the same form holds at n+1 as well. ∎

Proof A tells you “why,” and Proof B tells you that “Pascal’s triangle and the binomial theorem are the same story.”

Proof 1-4. The 11 coefficients of the 10th power

By the binomial theorem and Proof 0-1, C(10,k) = 10!/(k!(10−k)!). Cancelling makes the calculation easy.

  • C(10,0) = 1, C(10,1) = 10

  • C(10,2) = 10×9 / 2 = 45

  • C(10,3) = 10×9×8 / 6 = 120

  • C(10,4) = 10×9×8×7 / 24 = 5040/24 = 210

  • C(10,5) = 10×9×8×7×6 / 120 = 30240/120 = 252

  • C(10,6)~C(10,10) are 210, 120, 45, 10, 1 by symmetry (Proof 1-6)

The coefficients 1, 10, 45, 120, 210, 252, 210, 120, 45, 10, 1 in the main text’s table come out exactly. ∎

Proof 1-5. The sum is 2^n

The two proofs in Chapter 2 (Proofs 2-1 and 2-2) are the main body. Here we double-check the table in Chapter 1 of the main text. The 10th power: 1+10+45+120+210+252+210+120+45+10+1 = (1+10+45+120+210)×2 + 252 = 386×2 + 252 = 772 + 252 = 1024 = 2^10 ✓.

Proof 1-6. Left-right symmetry: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k)

Algebraic proof: C(n,n−k) = n!/((n−k)! (n−(n−k))!) = n!/((n−k)! k!) = C(n,k). The two factorials in the denominator simply swap places.

Combinatorial proof (complement): Choosing k people out of n as “those who go” is the same act as choosing the other n−k people as “those who don’t go.” Taking the complement is a one-to-one correspondence between “choosing k people” and “choosing n−k people,” so the counts are equal. ∎

The main text’s statement that “choosing 3 out of 10 is the same as choosing 7” is exactly C(10,3) = C(10,7) = 120.

Proof 1-7. The middle is the largest (it rises and then falls)

Claim: C(n,k) increases as k goes from 0 to the middle, and decreases after passing the middle. For n=10, the maximum is at k=5.

Intuition: If we compute the ratio of two neighboring coefficients, whether that ratio is greater or less than 1 determines whether the sequence is rising or falling.

Proof

  1. Compute the ratio of neighboring coefficients.

C(n,k+1) / C(n,k) = [ n!/((k+1)!(n−k−1)!) ] × [ k!(n−k)!/n! ] = (n−k)/(k+1)

We expanded (k+1)! = (k+1)·k! and (n−k)! = (n−k)·(n−k−1)! and cancelled.

  1. This ratio being greater than 1 is the same statement as n−k > k+1, that is, k < (n−1)/2. Therefore while k < (n−1)/2 the coefficients increase, and when k > (n−1)/2 they decrease. If k = (n−1)/2 (when n is odd), the ratio is exactly 1, so the two coefficients are equal, and those two share the maximum.

  2. For n=10, (n−1)/2 = 4.5, so going from k=0,1,2,3,4 to the next coefficient it increases (up through k=4→5), and from k=5 on it decreases. The maximum is uniquely C(10,5). ∎

Checking with numbers (climbing one cell at a time using the ratio (10−k)/(k+1))

  • 1 → 10 : ×10/1

  • 10 → 45 : ×9/2 = ×4.5

  • 45 → 120 : ×8/3

  • 120 → 210 : ×7/4

  • 210 → 252 : ×6/5

  • 252 → 210 : ×5/6 (the first time it drops below 1)

We will use this ratio formula again in Chapter 5 (why the middle of the Galton board is high) and Chapter 10 (Catalan numbers).

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 2. Why the Sum Is 2^n: Counting the Same Thing in Two Ways

Proof 2-1. Method A: Plug x=1, y=1 into the binomial theorem

Claim: Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k) = 2^n.

Proof

  1. The binomial theorem (Proof 1-3) is an “identity” that holds for any numbers x and y. So we may plug in x=1, y=1.

  2. Left side: (1+1)^n = 2^n.

  3. Right side: Σ C(n,k) 1^{n−k} 1^k = Σ C(n,k) (every power of 1 is 1).

  4. Since both sides are equal, 2^n = Σ C(n,k). ∎

Why is this allowed?: Because the binomial theorem is a declaration that “this expression holds no matter which x and y you take.” Just swap in numbers and the property comes for free. Plugging in y=−1 in Proof 2-4 below uses the same trick.

Proof 2-2. Method B: Counting by groups (double counting, T3)

Proof

  1. Counting the whole at once: Each of 10 people chooses one of “goes / doesn’t go.” Each person’s choice is independent of the others, so by the product rule (T1) there are 2×2×…×2 = 2^10 = 1024 ways.

  2. Counting by splitting into types: Classify the same 1024 ways by “the number of people who go, k” (k=0,1,…,10). Each outcome belongs to exactly one k, so the classification has no overlap and no gaps (the sum rule, T2). The number of outcomes in which k people go is the number of ways to choose the k people who go out of 10, C(10,k).

  3. Since we counted the same set in two ways, 1024 = Σ_{k=0}^{10} C(10,k). In general, 2^n = Σ C(n,k). ∎

Full check for n=3: Writing out all 8 ways, the sets of “people who go” are ∅, {A}, {B}, {C}, {A,B}, {A,C}, {B,C}, {A,B,C}. By size there are 1, 3, 3, 1 of them, totaling 8. This is the same as the coefficients of (x+y)^3 (Proof 1-2).

The two proofs are really one: “Choosing x or y from each pair of parentheses” in Proof A and “choosing goes/doesn’t go for each person” in Proof B have the same structure. Translate parentheses = person, choosing y = goes, choosing x = doesn’t go, and the sentences carry over almost verbatim.

Proof 2-3. Why a coefficient is “the number of ways to choose”

This part of Chapter 2 in the main text says the same thing as Proof A of Proof 1-3. In one line: there are C(n,k) strings that choose y k times, and each string adds one copy of x^{n−k}y^k.

Proof 2-4. Bonus: The alternating sum is 0, and the even and odd counts are each 2^{n−1}

Claim: If n ≥ 1, then C(n,0) − C(n,1) + C(n,2) − … + (−1)^n C(n,n) = 0. Hence the number of groups of even size equals the number of groups of odd size, and each is 2^{n−1}.

Algebraic proof

  1. Plugging x=1, y=−1 into the binomial theorem, the left side is (1−1)^n = 0^n = 0 (n ≥ 1).

  2. The right side is Σ C(n,k) 1^{n−k} (−1)^k = Σ (−1)^k C(n,k). Therefore (sum over even k) − (sum over odd k) = 0.

  3. (Even sum) + (odd sum) = 2^n (Proof 2-1), and the two are equal, so each is 2^n / 2 = 2^{n−1}. ∎

Combinatorial proof (one-to-one correspondence, the more beautiful method)

  1. Fix one particular person A among the 10.

  2. For every “set of people who go,” apply the transformation that “flips A’s status”: if A is in, remove A; if A is not in, add A.

  3. This transformation changes the size of the set by exactly 1. Even sizes go to odd sizes and odd sizes go to even sizes. Also, applying the same transformation twice returns to the original, so this transformation is a one-to-one correspondence between the sets of even size and the sets of odd size.

  4. Since there is a one-to-one correspondence, the two kinds have the same count, and since the total is 2^10, each is 512. ∎

(If n=0, there is only one group (∅), so it would be 1 vs 0 and the claim fails, which is why the condition n ≥ 1 is needed. In the combinatorial proof, this is because the person A must exist.)

Checking with numbers (n=10)

  • Even k: 1 + 45 + 210 + 210 + 45 + 1 = 512

  • Odd k: 10 + 120 + 252 + 120 + 10 = 512 ✓

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 3. Pascal’s Triangle: Making Coefficients Without Expanding

Proof 3-1. The addition rule: C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k)

Intuition: When forming a group, if you split into cases by “whether the last person A is included or not,” the problem shrinks by one step.

Combinatorial proof (T2 partition + T3)

  1. Consider all the ways to choose k people out of n (C(n,k) ways). Single out one person, A.

  2. Every group either includes A or does not include A, exactly one of the two. There is no overlap and no gap, so we can use the sum rule (T2).

  3. Groups that include A: A is already in, so we just need to choose k−1 more from the remaining n−1 people. C(n−1,k−1) ways.

  4. Groups that exclude A: We choose all k people from the remaining n−1. C(n−1,k) ways.

  5. Therefore C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k). ∎

Algebraic proof (using formulas alone)

Bring the two terms to the common denominator k!(n−k)!. Multiplying the numerator and denominator of (n−1)!/((k−1)!(n−k)!) by k, and the numerator and denominator of (n−1)!/(k!(n−k−1)!) by (n−k), we get

C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k) = (n−1)!·k / (k!(n−k)!) + (n−1)!·(n−k) / (k!(n−k)!)

= (n−1)!·[ k + (n−k) ] / (k!(n−k)!) = (n−1)!·n / (k!(n−k)!) = n! / (k!(n−k)!) = C(n,k) ∎

(This is the calculation for k between 1 and n−1. When k=0 or k=n, thanks to the convention C(n,−1) = C(n,n+1) = 0 from 0-1, both sides hold as 1 = 1 + 0.)

Checking with numbers (5 people, choose 2): The people are A, B, C, D, E, and we single out A.

  • A included: AB, AC, AD, AE → 4 ways = C(4,1)

  • A excluded: BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE → 6 ways = C(4,2)

  • The sum 10 = C(5,2) ✓. This is the main text’s “the 10 in row 5 is the sum of the 4 and 6 in row 4.”

Proof 3-2. The triangle rule really produces C(n,k) (induction, T4)

Claim: If we put 1 in the top row and build each row by the rule “each number = upper left + upper right (0 where there is no entry),” then the k-th number in the n-th row is C(n,k).

Proof

  • Base case: Row 0 is 1 = C(0,0).

  • Induction: Assume row n−1 is C(n−1,0), C(n−1,1), …. By the rule, the k-th number in row n is (the (k−1)-th of row n−1) + (the k-th of row n−1) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k), and by Proof 3-1 this is C(n,k). At the two ends, one parent is missing (treated as 0), so it is 1 + 0 = 1 = C(n,0) = C(n,n). ∎

So the triangle is less a “table of coefficients” than a “coefficient factory.” The fact that Proof B of the binomial theorem (Proof 1-3) used this rule is the same story.

Proof 3-3. Each row sum doubles (a third proof that the sum is 2^n)

Proof (from the structure of the triangle)

  1. Each number in row n−1 is added to exactly two places in row n (directly below-left and directly below-right), once each.

  2. Every number in row n is made only from such “additions” (each end receives from only one side and the other is 0).

  3. Therefore (the sum of row n) = 2 × (the sum of row n−1).

In formulas: Σ_k C(n,k) = Σ_k [ C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k) ] = Σ_j C(n−1,j) + Σ_k C(n−1,k) = 2 Σ C(n−1,k). (In the second line we renamed j = k−1, and the 0’s at the boundary do not affect the sum.)

Since the sum of row 0 is 1, the sum of row n is 2^n. ∎

Checking with numbers: The row sums 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … double exactly each time. Row 8 of Chapter 3 in the main text: 1+8+28+56+70+56+28+8+1 = 256 = 2^8 ✓.

Proof 3-4. Left-right symmetry

Proof 1-6 has already proved it using the formula and the complement. We can also confirm it from the triangle rule. If the upper row is left-right symmetric, the k-th number of the lower row (upper left + upper right) and the k-th number from the end are made from the same two parents with just their positions swapped, so they get the same sum. Since row 0 is symmetric, by induction every row is symmetric. ∎

Proof 3-5. The edges are 1, and their inner neighbors equal the row number n

  • C(n,0) = n!/(0! n!) = 1, C(n,n) = 1.

  • C(n,1) = n!/(1!(n−1)!) = n.

  • In terms of meaning: there is 1 way to choose no one (the empty set), and n ways to choose exactly one person (pointing at each person in turn). ∎

Proof 3-6. Making the coefficients of the 10th power by hand

Adding neighbors in row 9, 1, 9, 36, 84, 126, 126, 84, 36, 9, 1, gives row 10.

  • 1 (the end), 1+9 = 10, 9+36 = 45, 36+84 = 120, 84+126 = 210, 126+126 = 252, then symmetry, and the end 1.

With no multiplication or cancelling, using addition alone, the main text’s coefficients 1, 10, 45, 120, 210, 252, 210, 120, 45, 10, 1 come out. This is the method with the least computation.

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 4. Tossing a Coin 10 Times: The Moment Coefficients Become Probabilities

Proof 4-1. P(X=k) = C(10,k) / 2^10

Proof

  1. The result of tossing a coin 10 times is a string of heads/tails of length 10. Each toss is independent, so the probability that one particular string occurs is (1/2)×…×(1/2) = (1/2)^10 = 1/1024. This is the same no matter how many heads there are. Every string has the same probability.

  2. The event “exactly k heads” consists of all strings with k heads in them, and their number is C(10,k), the number of ways to choose the k positions for heads among 10 positions (the same counting as in Proof 1-3 A).

  3. Since there are C(10,k) outcomes of equal probability, P(X=k) = C(10,k) × (1/1024) = C(10,k)/1024. ∎

For a general probability p: The probability of one string is p^k q^{n−k} (k heads, n−k tails), so P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k}. If p=1/2, this becomes 2^{−n}, giving the formula above.

Proof 4-2. The probabilities add up to 1

Plugging x = p, y = q into the binomial theorem gives (p+q)^n = Σ C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k}. Since p + q = 1, the left side is 1^n = 1 and the right side is the sum of the probabilities over all k. That is, the probabilities sum to 1. For the coin, it is 1024/1024 = 1. ∎

(This is why it is called the “binomial distribution”: the fact that the probabilities must sum to 1 is just a single line of the binomial theorem.)

Proof 4-3. Double-checking the numbers of the bar chart

| k | C(10,k) | C(10,k)/1024 | As displayed |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 0, 10 | 1 | 0.0977% | 0.1% |

| 1, 9 | 10 | 0.977% | 1.0% |

| 2, 8 | 45 | 4.395% | 4.4% |

| 3, 7 | 120 | 11.72% | 11.7% |

| 4, 6 | 210 | 20.51% | 20.5% |

| 5 | 252 | 24.61% | 24.6% |

These match the bar lengths in the main text. Zero and ten heads are each 1/1024 ≈ 1/1000, that is, “roughly once in a thousand times.” ∎

Proof 4-4. Interval probabilities and “three times out of four”

  • 4~6 heads: (210 + 252 + 210)/1024 = 672/1024 = 65.625% ≈ 65.6% ✓

  • 3~7 heads: (120 + 672 + 120)/1024 = 912/1024 = 89.06% ≈ 89.1% ✓

  • 2~8 heads: (45 + 912 + 45)/1024 = 1002/1024 = 97.85% ≈ 97.9% ✓

  • The probability of “not exactly half and half”: 1 − 252/1024 = 772/1024 = 75.4% ≈ 3/4, so the phrase “three times out of four” is right.

All of these add up non-overlapping events by the sum rule (T2). ∎

Proof 4-5. The mean E[X] = np

Method 1 (indicator variables and linearity of expectation)

  1. Let I_i be the variable that is 1 if the i-th toss is heads and 0 if tails; then X = I_1 + I_2 + … + I_n.

  2. E[I_i] = 1·p + 0·q = p.

  3. Expectation is linear (”the expectation of a sum = the sum of the expectations”), so E[X] = np. This linearity holds even without independence. ∎

Method 2 (direct summation)

First we prove the identity k·C(n,k) = n·C(n−1,k−1). Counting the chair: We count in two ways the number of ways to form a committee of k people out of n people and choose 1 chair from it. (Left side) First form the committee in C(n,k) ways, then choose the chair from among them in k ways. (Right side) First choose the chair from among the n people (n ways), then choose the remaining k−1 members from the other n−1 people (C(n−1,k−1) ways). Since we counted the same thing, the two are equal.

Now in E[X] = Σ_{k=0}^{n} k C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k}, the k=0 term is 0, so

= Σ_{k=1}^{n} n C(n−1,k−1) p·p^{k−1} q^{(n−1)−(k−1)} = np Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} C(n−1,j) p^j q^{n−1−j} = np (p+q)^{n−1} = np. ∎

Checking with numbers (n=10, p=1/2): Σ k C(10,k) = 0 + 10 + 90 + 360 + 840 + 1260 + 1260 + 840 + 360 + 90 + 10 = 5120, and 5120/1024 = 5 = np ✓. (It also agrees with the general formula Σ k C(n,k) = n 2^{n−1} = 10×512 = 5120.)

Proof 4-6. The variance Var(X) = npq and the standard deviation √2.5

Proof

  1. A single toss: I² = I, so E[I²] = p. Var(I) = E[I²] − (E[I])² = p − p² = p(1−p) = pq.

  2. The variances of mutually independent variables add. The reason: Var(ΣI_i) = Σ Var(I_i) + Σ_{i≠j} E[(I_i−p)(I_j−p)], but if they are independent, E[(I_i−p)(I_j−p)] = E[I_i−p]·E[I_j−p] = 0·0 = 0, so the cross terms vanish.

  3. Therefore Var(X) = n·pq. For n=10, p=1/2, it is 10 × 1/4 = 2.5, and the standard deviation is σ = √2.5 ≈ 1.5811. ∎

Direct check: Computing Σ (k−5)² C(10,k) from k=0 to 10 gives 25·1 + 16·10 + 9·45 + 4·120 + 1·210 + 0·252 + 1·210 + 4·120 + 9·45 + 16·10 + 25·1 = 25 + 160 + 405 + 480 + 210 + 0 + 210 + 480 + 405 + 160 + 25 = 2560, and 2560/1024 = 2.5 ✓. It matches the formula npq exactly.

Proof 4-7. The most common outcome (the mode)

Multiplying the ratio formula of Proof 1-7 by the probabilities gives P(X=k+1)/P(X=k) = [(n−k)/(k+1)]·(p/q). While this ratio is greater than 1, the probability rises. For n=10, p=q=1/2, the ratio is (10−k)/(k+1), so exactly as in Proof 1-7 the maximum is at k=5. For general p, the probability rises while (n−k)p > (k+1)q, that is, k < (n+1)p − 1, so the mode is near the integer part of (n+1)p. ∎

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 5. The Galton Board: The Triangle Becomes a Physical Device

Proof 5-1. The number of paths by which a ball reaches a given slot is C(n,k)

Proof (two ways)

  1. Counting with strings: If there are n rows of pins, the ball chooses “left (L) / right (R)” n times. One path is an L/R string of length n (2^n of them). The paths that reach the k-th slot at the bottom (numbered 0, 1, …, n from the left) are the strings with exactly k R’s, and their number is C(n,k) (Proof 1-3 A).

  2. Counting with the triangle: Let N(i,j) be the number of paths reaching the j-th pin in the i-th row. A ball can come to a pin only from the upper-left pin or the upper-right pin, so N(i,j) = N(i−1,j−1) + N(i−1,j), and an edge pin has only one route, so it is 1. This is the same as the rule of Pascal’s triangle, and by Proof 3-2, N(i,j) = C(i,j). ∎

When we say the ball “computes” its path, this second proof is exactly what we mean. Each pin is doing one addition.

Proof 5-2. The number of slots and the probability of the center slot

  • The number of R’s is 0, 1, …, n, so there are n+1 slots. With 10 rows of pins there are 11 slots, and with 4 rows there are 5 slots.

  • On an ideal board each path has the same probability (1/2)^n (Proof 4-1), so the probability of the k-th slot is C(n,k)/2^n.

  • Center of 10 rows: 252/1024 = 24.6%. Center of 4 rows: C(4,2)/2^4 = 6/16 = 37.5% ✓. ∎

Proof 5-3. Why more balls pile up in the middle

Proof 1-7 is already the answer. Since the ratio of the path counts of neighboring slots is (n−k)/(k+1), near the edges it grows by more than 1, and after passing the middle it shrinks by less than 1. Intuitively, to reach an edge slot the ball must keep turning to the same side, but for the middle slot there are countless strings mixing L and R. With 10 rows, “all R” is 1 way, while “5 R’s and 5 L’s” is 252 ways. ∎

Proof 5-4. The slot position is binomially distributed, so the mean is n/2 and the standard deviation is √n/2

The slot number k = (the number of R’s) follows B(n,1/2), so by Proofs 4-5 and 4-6 the mean is n/2, the variance is n/4, and the standard deviation is √n/2. With 4 rows, the mean is 2 and the standard deviation is 1; with 10 rows, the mean is 5 and the standard deviation is 1.58. As the number of rows increases, the middle becomes the center, and the width slowly widens like √n. This foreshadows the shape in which the normal distribution appears in Chapter 6. ∎

A caution about the real device: A real ball is not perfectly symmetric when it bounces off a pin, and balls can influence one another, so the results only “follow closely” the calculation above. The proofs above are about an ideal board (probability 1/2 at each pin, independent).

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 6. Where the Bell Shape Comes From: The de Moivre–Laplace Theorem

This chapter is the highlight of this book. Here is the map of the proof.

  • 6-1: We prove Stirling’s formula n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)^n for approximating large factorials. (Down to where the constant √(2π) comes from)

  • 6-2: With the same ingredients, we obtain the central binomial coefficient C(2m,m) ≈ 4^m/√(πm).

  • 6-3: Substituting Stirling into the binomial probability, we prove the local theorem (the probability of a single cell is the height of the bell-shaped curve).

  • 6-4~6-5: We show why it fits especially well when p=1/2, and that the area under the curve really is 1.

  • 6-6~6-8: We check the interval probabilities (the formula using Φ), the continuity correction, and the numbers in the main text’s table.

Proof 6-1. Stirling’s formula: n! ~ √(2πn)·(n/e)^n

Claim: Let a_n = n! / ( √n (n/e)^n ); then a_n → √(2π) as n→∞. (~ means that the ratio of the two values converges to 1.)

Intuition: ln n! = ln 1 + ln 2 + … + ln n is a sum near ∫ ln x dx = n ln n − n. A small correction like √n is attached to it. The proof has two stages. (A) The correction converges to a single constant C. (B) That constant is √(2π).

Stage A: a_n converges to a positive limit C

  1. Compute the ratio of two consecutive terms.

a_n / a_{n+1} = [ n! / (√n n^n e^{−n}) ] · [ √(n+1) (n+1)^{n+1} e^{−(n+1)} / (n+1)! ] = ( (n+1)/n )^{n+1/2} / e

We cancelled using (n+1)! = (n+1)·n!, and grouped √(n+1)/√n and (n+1)^{n+1}/((n+1)n^n) = ((n+1)/n)^n.

  1. Taking logs, ln(a_n/a_{n+1}) = (n+½) ln((n+1)/n) − 1. Here, setting t = 1/(2n+1), we have (n+1)/n = (1+t)/(1−t) and n+½ = 1/(2t).

  2. Since ln((1+t)/(1−t)) = 2( t + t³/3 + t⁵/5 + … ),

(n+½) ln((n+1)/n) = (1/(2t)) · 2( t + t³/3 + t⁵/5 + … ) = 1 + t²/3 + t⁴/5 + …

Therefore ln(a_n/a_{n+1}) = t²/3 + t⁴/5 + t⁶/7 + … > 0.

  1. Bounding from above: t²/3 + t⁴/5 + … < (t²/3)(1 + t² + t⁴ + …) = t² / (3(1−t²)). And since t²/(1−t²) = 1/((2n+1)² − 1) = 1/(4n(n+1)),

0 < ln(a_n/a_{n+1}) < 1/(12n(n+1)) = (1/12)( 1/n − 1/(n+1) )

  1. Conclusion (i): since ln(a_n/a_{n+1}) > 0, a_n is decreasing. Conclusion (ii): rearranging the inequality above, ln a_n − 1/(12n) < ln a_{n+1} − 1/(12(n+1)), that is, a_n·e^{−1/(12n)} is increasing. Therefore a_n ≥ a_1 e^{−1/12 + 1/(12n)} > a_1 e^{−1/12} = e^{11/12} > 0 (a_1 = 1/(1·e^{−1}) = e).

  2. A sequence that decreases and is bounded below converges, so a_n → C > 0. Also, from (i) and (ii) above, C ≤ a_n ≤ C·e^{1/(12n)}. This inequality means “the relative error is about 1/(12n).”

Stage B: C = √(2π) (the Wallis product)

  1. Let W_m = ∫0^{π/2} sin^m x dx. By integration by parts, W_m = (m−1)/m · W{m−2} (m ≥ 2). Derivation: integrating ∫ sin^{m−1}x · sin x dx by parts (boundary term 0) gives (m−1)∫ cos²x sin^{m−2}x dx = (m−1)(W_{m−2} − W_m), hence m W_m = (m−1) W_{m−2}. Initial values W_0 = π/2, W_1 = 1.

  2. Solving this recurrence,

W_{2m} = (π/2) · [ (2m−1)(2m−3)…1 ] / [ (2m)(2m−2)…2 ] = (π/2) · C(2m,m)/4^m

W_{2m+1} = [ (2m)(2m−2)…2 ] / [ (2m+1)(2m−1)…3 ] = 4^m / ( (2m+1) C(2m,m) )

(Check with m=1: W_2 = π/4 = (π/2)(2/4) ✓, W_3 = 2/3 = 4/(3·2) ✓.) Here we used (2m−1)!!/(2m)!! = (2m)!/(2^{2m}(m!)²) = C(2m,m)/4^m.

  1. Since 0 ≤ sin x ≤ 1, sin^m x gets smaller as m grows, so W_{2m+1} ≤ W_{2m} ≤ W_{2m−1}. Dividing everything by W_{2m+1}, 1 ≤ W_{2m}/W_{2m+1} ≤ W_{2m−1}/W_{2m+1} = (2m+1)/(2m) → 1. By the squeeze theorem, W_{2m}/W_{2m+1} → 1.

  2. Substituting the formulas from 2, W_{2m}/W_{2m+1} = (π/2)(2m+1) · ( C(2m,m)/4^m )² → 1, that is, ( C(2m,m)/4^m )² ~ 2/(π(2m+1)) ~ 1/(πm). Therefore

C(2m,m) ~ 4^m / √(πm) (the result of the Wallis product)

  1. Now using a_n from Stage A to write C(2m,m) = (2m)!/(m!)², the e’s and exponents cancel, giving

C(2m,m) = [ a_{2m} √(2m) (2m/e)^{2m} ] / [ a_m² · m · (m/e)^{2m} ] = ( a_{2m} / a_m² ) · (√2/√m) · 4^m

As m→∞, a_{2m} → C and a_m² → C², so C(2m,m) ~ (1/C)(√2/√m) 4^m. Comparing with the result of step 4, √2/C = 1/√π, that is, C = √(2π). ∎

Stirling’s formula: n! ~ √(2πn) (n/e)^n.

Checking with numbers: 10! = 3,628,800, and the Stirling value √(20π)(10/e)^10 = 3,598,696 (error 0.83%). This nearly matches the error bound 1/(12n) = 1/120 = 0.83% from step A. For 5! = 120, the Stirling value is 118.02 (error 1.65%, versus 1/60 = 1.67%).

Proof 6-2. The middle binomial coefficient: C(2m,m) ~ 4^m / √(πm)

Step B-4 of Proof 6-1 is already the proof. The probability of getting exactly m heads in 2m coin tosses is C(2m,m)/4^m ~ 1/√(πm).

  • Exactly 50 heads in 100 tosses (m=50): 1/√(50π) = 1/12.533 = 0.0798 ≈ 8% ✓ (the main text’s “Question to think about 1”). The exact value is C(100,50)/2^100 = 0.07959.

  • Exactly 5 heads in 10 tosses (m=5): 1/√(5π) = 0.2523. The exact value is 0.2461. If we use the next term of Stirling’s formula, n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)^n (1 + 1/(12n)) (proof omitted), the correction factor comes out as (1 + 1/(24m)) / (1 + 1/(12m))² ≈ 1 − 1/(8m). For m=5, 0.2523 × (1 − 0.025) = 0.2460 ✓.

Proof 6-3. The local de Moivre–Laplace theorem

Claim: Let X ~ B(n,p), σ² = npq, and k = np + x. If x moves at a scale smaller than n^{2/3} (x = o(n^{2/3})), then

P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k} ≈ ( 1/√(2πnpq) ) · exp( −x² / (2npq) ) = (1/σ) φ(x/σ)

(φ(z) = e^{−z²/2}/√(2π) is the density of the standard normal distribution.)

Proof

  1. Substitute Stirling: Applying 6-1 to n!, k!, and (n−k)!, the exponents of e cancel because k + (n−k) = n, and since n^n = n^k n^{n−k},

C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k} ≈ √( n / (2π k (n−k)) ) · ( np/k )^k · ( nq/(n−k) )^{n−k}

  1. The square root in front: k = np + x, n−k = nq − x, and x/n → 0, so k ≈ np and n−k ≈ nq. Hence √( n/(2π·np·nq) ) = 1/√(2πnpq) (1 + o(1)).

  2. Take the logarithm of the power part: Let u = x/(np) and v = −x/(nq). Then k/(np) = 1+u and (n−k)/(nq) = 1+v. The logarithm of the power part is

E = −k ln(1+u) − (n−k) ln(1+v) = −np (1+u) ln(1+u) − nq (1+v) ln(1+v)

  1. Taylor expansion: Since ln(1+u) = u − u²/2 + u³/3 − …,

(1+u) ln(1+u) = u + u²/2 − u³/6 + …

(Multiplying out gives u − u²/2 + u³/3 + u² − u³/2 + … = u + u²/2 − u³/6 + ….) Therefore

np (1+u) ln(1+u) = x + x²/(2np) − x³/(6n²p²) + …

nq (1+v) ln(1+v) = −x + x²/(2nq) + x³/(6n²q²) + …

  1. Adding the two expressions, x and −x cancel, and (since 1/p + 1/q = 1/(pq))

E = −x²/(2npq) − (x³/(6n²)) (1/q² − 1/p²) − …

  1. If x = o(n^{2/3}), then x³/n² → 0, and the later terms (x⁴/n³ and so on) also → 0. Therefore e^E ≈ exp(−x²/(2npq)).

  2. Multiplying steps 2 and 6 gives the claim. ∎

One observation: At the center (x=0) the exponential part equals 1, so P(X=np) ≈ 1/√(2πnpq). This is the same as the value in 6-2 (with p=1/2 and n=2m, it is 1/√(πm)). That is why the peak of the normal curve is the leading factor of Stirling’s formula.

Proof 6-4. Why does just 10 tosses work so well when p=1/2?

In step 5 of Proof 6-3, the first error term is (x³/(6n²))(1/q² − 1/p²). If p = q = 1/2, then 1/q² − 1/p² = 0, and this term vanishes entirely. A symmetric distribution has no cubic term (the asymmetry term). The remaining error is one order higher, of order x⁴/n³, which is why even 10 coin tosses match to within 0.6 percentage points.

When p is near 0 or 1, things are different. For example, when p is small and x ~ σ = √(npq), the size of the cubic term is roughly x³/(6n²p²) ≈ (np)^{3/2}/(6n²p²) = 1/(6√(np)). For this to be small, np must be large. The warning in Chapter 6 of the main text that “the approximation gets worse when p is close to 0 or 1,” and the warning in Chapter 9 that “there is a problem if np̂ or n(1−p̂) is less than 5,” both come from this single formula. ∎

Proof 6-5. The area under the curve is 1 (the Gaussian integral)

Claim: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^{−z²/2} dz = √(2π). (This is why the total area of φ(z) = e^{−z²/2}/√(2π) is 1.)

Proof: Let I = ∫ e^{−z²/2} dz. Then I² = ∫∫ e^{−(x²+y²)/2} dx dy. Switching to polar coordinates (x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ, area element r dr dθ),

I² = ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{∞} e^{−r²/2} r dr dθ = 2π · [ −e^{−r²/2} ]_0^{∞} = 2π · 1.

Since I > 0, I = √(2π). ∎

(The √(2π) appeared in two separate places, and they match. The √(2π) in the Wallis product came from “the size of the binomial coefficient,” while the √(2π) in the Gaussian integral came from “the area of the curve.” Since the total probability must be 1, the two values have no choice but to agree.)

Proof 6-6. Interval probabilities: the sum becomes the area under the normal curve

Claim: When n is large, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) ≈ Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a), where z = (k − np)/σ. (Φ is the cumulative area of φ.)

Proof (Riemann sum)

  1. By Proof 6-3, P(X=k) ≈ (1/σ) φ(z_k) for each k. Neighboring values of k are spaced 1/σ apart in z (Δz = 1/σ).

  2. Therefore P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = Σ_{k=a}^{b} P(X=k) ≈ Σ φ(z_k) Δz. This is a Riemann sum, a row of rectangles of width Δz placed side by side.

  3. As n→∞, σ = √(npq) → ∞, so Δz = 1/σ → 0, and the Riemann sum converges to the integral ∫_{z_a}^{z_b} φ(z) dz = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a).

  4. For the tail parts far from the ends of the interval, Chebyshev’s inequality (Proof 8-1) shows that the probability is close to 0, so the difference between the sum and the integral is negligible. Also, when z lies in a bounded range, x = zσ ~ √n = o(n^{2/3}), so the condition of 6-3 is satisfied and the approximation error goes to 0 uniformly over that range. ∎ (The rigorous treatment of the tails is omitted.)

Proof 6-7. Continuity correction: why ±0.5?

Look closely at the rectangles from step 2: the bar for k has width 1 and height P(X=k). That is, the bar occupies the interval [k−½, k+½]. The bars from a to b together fill [a−½, b+½], so the area under the curve should also be measured over this interval.

P(a ≤ X ≤ b) ≈ Φ( (b+½−np)/σ ) − Φ( (a−½−np)/σ )

Effect (n=10, p=1/2, σ = 1.5811)

  • P(4≤X≤6): the exact value is 65.6%. With correction: ±1.5/1.5811 = ±0.9487 → 2Φ(0.9487) − 1 = 65.7%. Without correction: ±1/1.5811 = ±0.632 → 47.3%. Without the correction we lose the outer half of each end bar and are off by about 18 percentage points.

  • P(X=5): the exact value is 24.6%. With correction: ±0.5/1.5811 = ±0.3162 → 2Φ(0.3162) − 1 = 24.8%.

  • P(2≤X≤8): the exact value is 97.85%. With correction: ±3.5/1.5811 = ±2.2136 → 97.3%.

The formula Φ((b−np)/σ) − Φ((a−np)/σ) in the main text is the basic form without this correction; adding the correction raises the accuracy a notch. ∎

Proof 6-8. Checking the table in the main text: exact probability vs. height of the normal curve

The height of the normal curve is f(k) = (1/√(2π·2.5)) exp( −(k−5)²/(2·2.5) ) = 0.25231 · exp( −(k−5)²/5 ).

| k | exp value | Normal curve height | Exact probability | Difference |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 5 | 1 | 25.2% | 24.6% | 0.6 pp |

| 4, 6 | e^{−0.2} = 0.8187 | 20.7% | 20.5% | 0.2 pp |

| 3, 7 | e^{−0.8} = 0.4493 | 11.3% | 11.7% | 0.4 pp |

| 2, 8 | e^{−1.8} = 0.1653 | 4.2% | 4.4% | 0.2 pp |

These match the numbers in the main text exactly, and the largest difference is 0.6 pp at k=5. (In the tails, k=0 and 10, the curve gives 0.17% versus the exact 0.098%, a large difference in ratio but a small difference in absolute terms.) ∎

A note on reading the main text’s comparison of “within 1 and 2 standard deviations”: In a discrete distribution the boundaries fall between bars. The range k=4 to 6 is the interval ±1.5 from the mean, which is 0.95 times σ (with correction), and k=2 to 8 is ±3.5, which is 2.21 times σ. So rather than comparing exactly with “±1σ (68.3%)” and “±2σ (95.4%),” it is more accurate to read it this way: measuring the same widths with the normal curve gives 65.7% and 97.3%, which are close to the exact 65.6% and 97.9%.

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 7. The Mathematics of Rare Events: The Poisson Approximation

Proof 7-1. Binomial distribution → Poisson distribution

Claim: Set p = λ/n. As n→∞, for each k, C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k} → e^{−λ} λ^k / k!.

Proof

  1. Split the expression into three pieces as follows.

C(n,k) (λ/n)^k (1−λ/n)^{n−k} = ( λ^k / k! ) · [ n(n−1)…(n−k+1) / n^k ] · (1−λ/n)^n · (1−λ/n)^{−k}

(Here C(n,k) = n(n−1)…(n−k+1)/k!, and the n^k from (λ/n)^k has been moved to the denominator.)

  1. The bracket: n(n−1)…(n−k+1)/n^k = 1·(1−1/n)·(1−2/n)…(1−(k−1)/n). Since k is a fixed constant and there are only k factors, as n→∞ each factor goes to 1, so the whole product goes to 1.

  2. (1−λ/n)^n → e^{−λ}: Taking the logarithm, n ln(1−λ/n) = n( −λ/n − λ²/(2n²) − … ) = −λ − λ²/(2n) − … → −λ. Hence (1−λ/n)^n → e^{−λ}.

  3. (1−λ/n)^{−k}: Since k is fixed and 1−λ/n → 1, this goes to 1.

  4. Multiplying, we get ( λ^k / k! ) · 1 · e^{−λ} · 1 = e^{−λ} λ^k / k!. ∎

Proof 7-2. Properties of the Poisson probabilities: total 1, mean λ, variance λ

  • Total is 1: Since e^λ = Σ λ^k/k! (Taylor series), Σ e^{−λ}λ^k/k! = e^{−λ} e^{λ} = 1.

  • Mean: Σ_{k≥1} k e^{−λ}λ^k/k! = λ e^{−λ} Σ_{k≥1} λ^{k−1}/(k−1)! = λ e^{−λ} e^{λ} = λ.

  • Variance: E[X(X−1)] = Σ_{k≥2} e^{−λ}λ^k/(k−2)! = λ², so E[X²] = λ² + λ and Var = E[X²] − λ² = λ.

This agrees with the binomial distribution’s mean np = λ and variance npq = λ·q → λ (as q→1) (Proofs 4-5 and 4-6). ∎

Proof 7-3. Seeing the resemblance of the two distributions through a recurrence

The ratio of neighboring probabilities in the binomial distribution is P(k+1)/P(k) = [(n−k)/(k+1)]·(p/q) (Proof 4-7), and for the Poisson distribution it is e^{−λ}λ^{k+1}/(k+1)! ÷ e^{−λ}λ^k/k! = λ/(k+1). When n is large and p is small, (n−k)p/q ≈ np = λ, so the two ratios are nearly the same. Starting from the same point (P(0) ≈ e^{−λ}) and proceeding with nearly the same ratios, the values end up the same. ∎

Proof 7-4. Checking the hypothetical example in the main text (n=1000, p=0.002, λ=2)

  • P(0) = 0.998^1000 = exp(1000 ln 0.998) = exp(−2.002003) = e^{−2} · e^{−0.002003} = 0.135335 × 0.99800 = 0.13506. Poisson: e^{−2} = 0.13534.

  • Recurrence (Proof 7-3): P(1) = P(0) × (1000/1) × (0.002/0.998) = 0.13506 × 2.00401 = 0.27067. Poisson: 2e^{−2} = 0.27067.

  • P(2) = P(1) × (999/2) × 0.002004 = 0.27067 × 1.00100 = 0.27094. Poisson: 0.27067.

  • P(3) = P(2) × (998/3) × 0.002004 = 0.27094 × 0.66667 = 0.18063. Poisson: (4/3)e^{−2} = 0.18045.

The difference between the exact values and the approximation is within 0.03 pp for every k, and to the first decimal place the values 13.5 / 27.1 / 27.1 / 18.1 (18.0) agree with the main text. The scale of the error is about np² = 1000 × 0.002² = 0.004, which is consistent in size with Le Cam’s inequality (proof omitted), which says that “even if you add up all the differences between the binomial and Poisson probabilities, the total does not exceed 2np².” ∎

Proof 7-5. The criterion that separates the two approximations

  • The normal approximation works well when the variance npq is large. This is because the size of the error in Proof 6-4 was roughly 1/(6√(np)).

  • The Poisson approximation works well when p is small. This is because what we needed in Proof 7-1 was p = λ/n → 0.

Checking with a counterexample: If we use the Poisson distribution for 10 coin tosses (p=1/2, λ=np=5), P(5) ≈ e^{−5}5^5/5! = 0.0067379 × 3125/120 = 17.5%, which differs greatly from the exact 24.6%. Since p is not small, the premise of the Poisson approximation breaks down. Conversely, in the transaction-error example (np = 2, p = 0.002), the normal approximation is unsuitable (npq ≈ 2 is small, and the distribution is lopsided to one side).

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 8. The Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers

Proof 8-1. Markov’s inequality and Chebyshev’s inequality

Markov’s inequality: If Y ≥ 0 and a > 0, then P(Y ≥ a) ≤ E[Y]/a.

Proof: Since Y ≥ 0, E[Y] ≥ E[ Y · 1{Y ≥ a} ] ≥ E[ a · 1{Y ≥ a} ] = a · P(Y ≥ a). (1{…} is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise.) Divide both sides by a. ∎

Chebyshev’s inequality: For X with mean μ and variance σ², P(|X−μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/ε².

Proof: Apply Markov with Y = (X−μ)² and a = ε², giving P((X−μ)² ≥ ε²) ≤ E[(X−μ)²]/ε² = σ²/ε². The event (X−μ)² ≥ ε² is the same as |X−μ| ≥ ε. ∎

Proof 8-2. The law of large numbers

Claim: If X_1, …, X_n are independent with mean μ and (finite) variance σ², then for the sample mean X̄_n and any ε > 0, P(|X̄_n − μ| ≥ ε) → 0.

Proof

  1. E[X̄_n] = (1/n) Σ E[X_i] = μ.

  2. By independence, variances add, so Var(X̄_n) = (1/n²) · nσ² = σ²/n.

  3. By Chebyshev (Proof 8-1), P(|X̄_n − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ² / (nε²) → 0 (n→∞). ∎

Numbers for coins (σ² = 1/4, ε = 0.05): Chebyshev’s upper bound is 1/(4n·0.0025) = 100/n.

| n | Chebyshev upper bound | Actual probability that the proportion falls outside 0.45 to 0.55 |

| --- | --- | --- |

| 100 | 1 (useless) | about 36.8% |

| 1000 | 0.1 | about 0.17% |

| 10000 | 0.01 | essentially 0 |

(The last column of the table is P(|X/n − 1/2| ≥ 0.05) including the boundary. As in the discussion of boundaries in Proof 13-5, the cases where the proportion is exactly 45% or 55% are also counted as “deviating.” Excluding the boundary, n=100 gives about 27%.)

Chebyshev is a coarse tool that guarantees only that the probability “must go to 0.” What tells us its speed and shape precisely is the central limit theorem that follows. This contrast is the distinction made in the main text: the law of large numbers says “where,” and the central limit theorem says “in what shape.”

Proof 8-3. The central limit theorem (the coin case to the end, the general case as an outline)

Tool: the moment generating function (mgf) M_Z(t) = E[e^{tZ}]

  • (a) For independent variables, the mgf of a sum is the product: E[e^{t(A+B)}] = E[e^{tA}e^{tB}] = E[e^{tA}] E[e^{tB}] (by independence the expectation splits into a product).

  • (b) Constant multiples: M_{cZ}(t) = M_Z(ct).

  • (c) The mgf of the standard normal: ∫ e^{tz} φ(z) dz = ∫ e^{tz − z²/2}/√(2π) dz. Completing the square in the exponent gives tz − z²/2 = −(z−t)²/2 + t²/2, so this equals e^{t²/2} ∫ φ(z−t) dz = e^{t²/2} (the area of a shifted normal density is 1, Proof 6-5).

  • (d) The mgf convergence theorem: if the mgf converges, at every t near 0, to the mgf of some distribution, then the distributions converge too. (Lévy’s continuity theorem, proof omitted.)

Proof for the coin case

  1. Let heads be +1 and tails be −1, and call these ξ_i (each with probability 1/2). The sum is S_n = Σ ξ_i and the number of heads is X = (S_n + n)/2. The standardized value is Z_n = (X − n/2)/(√n/2) = S_n/√n.

  2. The mgf of a single ξ: M_ξ(s) = (e^s + e^{−s})/2 = cosh s = 1 + s²/2 + s⁴/24 + …

  3. By (a) and (b), M_{Z_n}(t) = [ cosh(t/√n) ]^n.

  4. Taking the logarithm gives n ln( 1 + t²/(2n) + t⁴/(24n²) + … ), and since ln(1+w) = w − w²/2 + …,

n · ( t²/(2n) + O(1/n²) ) = t²/2 + O(1/n) → t²/2.

  1. Therefore M_{Z_n}(t) → e^{t²/2}. This is the mgf of the standard normal from (c), so by (d) the distribution of Z_n converges to the standard normal distribution. ∎

Checking with numbers (n=10, t=1): cosh(1/√10)^10 = cosh(0.3162)^10 = 1.0504^10 = e^{0.4919} = 1.635. The limit value is e^{1/2} = 1.649. With just 10 coin tosses we are already within 0.8%.

The general case (outline): Suppose the X_i are independent with the same distribution, mean μ, and variance σ². Then Y_i = (X_i − μ)/σ has mean 0 and variance 1. If the mgf exists, the Taylor expansion gives M_Y(s) = 1 + 0·s + s²/2 + o(s²). The mgf of the standardized sum Z_n = (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) = (1/√n) Σ Y_i is [ M_Y(t/√n) ]^n = [ 1 + t²/(2n) + o(1/n) ]^n → e^{t²/2}. The computation is exactly the same as for coins, and we finish with (d). For distributions without an mgf, the same argument is made with the expectation of e^{itY} (the characteristic function) (proof omitted). This is the statement in the main text, Z_n = (S_n − nμ)/√(nσ²) → N(0,1). ∎

Relation to Chapter 6: The proof in Chapter 6 “substituted Stirling directly into the binomial probabilities,” while this proof reaches the same conclusion with “a general tool that works for every distribution (the mgf).” That is why the de Moivre–Laplace theorem is the first instance of the central limit theorem.

Proof 8-4. The probability that the proportion of heads falls within 45 to 55%: checking the table

  • Standard deviation of the proportion: Var(X/n) = Var(X)/n² = npq/n² = pq/n, so the standard deviation is √(1/(4n)) = 0.5/√n. For n=10: 0.1581; n=100: 0.05; n=1000: 0.0158 (the main text’s 15.8 pp, 5.0 pp, 1.6 pp).

  • n=10: A proportion of 45 to 55% means a head count between 4.5 and 5.5, that is, exactly 5. The probability is 252/1024 = 24.6%.

  • n=100: The head count is 45 to 55 (mean 50, σ=5). With the continuity correction (Proof 6-7): z = 5.5/5 = 1.1, 2Φ(1.1) − 1 = 2(0.8643) − 1 = 0.7286 ≈ 73%. (The exact sum is 72.87%.) Without the correction, z=1 gives 68.3%, which is off by 4.6 pp.

  • n=1000: The head count is 450 to 550 (σ = √250 = 15.81). z = 50.5/15.81 = 3.194, 2Φ(3.194) − 1 = 0.9986 ≈ 99.9%. (The exact sum is 99.86%.) ∎

Proof 8-5. The gambler’s fallacy

Claim: Even after 5 heads in a row, the probability that the next toss is tails is still 1/2.

Proof: Let H_i be the event that the i-th toss is heads. Since the tosses are independent, P(H_1 ∩ … ∩ H_6) = (1/2)^6 and P(H_1 ∩ … ∩ H_5) = (1/2)^5. By the definition of conditional probability,

P(H_6 | H_1 ∩ … ∩ H_5) = (1/2)^6 / (1/2)^5 = 1/2.

So the probability that the next toss is heads, and the probability that it is tails, are both 1/2. That the past cannot influence the future is exactly what “independence” means. ∎

Then what makes the proportion gather around 1/2 (dilution)?: Suppose the first 5 tosses were all heads, and we toss a fair coin m more times. The expected proportion of heads is (5 + m/2)/(5 + m), and its difference from 1/2 is

(5 + m/2)/(5 + m) − 1/2 = (10 + m − 5 − m) / (2(5+m)) = 2.5/(5+m) → 0.

  • m = 95 (100 tosses in total): 52.5%

  • m = 995 (1000 tosses in total): 50.25%

It is not that tails “make up for” the heads; the initial lopsidedness is buried under the new tosses and gradually becomes smaller. ∎

Proof 8-6. The deviation in counts grows, while the deviation in proportions shrinks

The standard deviation of the number of heads is √(npq) = √n/2 (Proof 4-6): 5 for n=100, 15.81 for n=1000, and 50 for n=10000. It grows by a factor of √n as n grows. The proportion is the count divided by n, so its standard deviation shrinks to (√n/2)/n = 0.5/√n. The numerator is √n and the denominator is n, and the denominator grows faster. ∎

Proof 8-7. Two conditions: sampling without replacement and the 10% rule, and finite variance

Variance when sampling without replacement (finite population correction)

  1. From a population of size N (values v_1, …, v_N, population variance σ²), draw n values without replacement and call them X_1, …, X_n. Each X_i has the same distribution and variance σ². By symmetry, the covariance of any two distinct i, j is the same value c.

  2. If we draw all N, the sum is always fixed at the population total, so the variance is 0. From Var(X_1 + … + X_N) = Nσ² + N(N−1)c = 0, we get c = −σ²/(N−1).

  3. Then the variance of the sum of n values is nσ² + n(n−1)c = nσ² [ 1 − (n−1)/(N−1) ] = nσ² (N−n)/(N−1).

  4. Dividing to get the mean, Var(X̄) = (σ²/n) · (N−n)/(N−1). The sampling-with-replacement value (σ²/n) is multiplied by the “finite population correction factor” (N−n)/(N−1) ≈ 1 − n/N. ∎

The meaning of the 10% rule: If n is 10% of N, the factor is about 0.9, which is √0.9 = 0.95 times in terms of standard deviation, so assuming independence overestimates it by about 5%. If n is 10% or less, the effect is small, within 5%, so it is fine to assume independence. That is the rule in the main text.

Why the variance must be finite (a counterexample): The standard Cauchy distribution has no mean and no variance, and its characteristic function is e^{−|t|}. The characteristic function of the mean of n of them is [ e^{−|t|/n} ]^n = e^{−|t|}, so no matter how many values we average, the distribution does not narrow at all. Neither the law of large numbers nor the central limit theorem works. ∎

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 9. Coming Down to Everyday Life: Opinion Polls, Confidence Intervals, and the Binomial Test

Proof 9-1. Deriving the Wald confidence interval

  1. The sample proportion p̂ = X/n has mean p and standard deviation √(pq/n) (divide the X of Proofs 4-5 and 4-6 by n).

  2. By the central limit theorem (Proof 8-3), (p̂ − p)/√(pq/n) follows the standard normal distribution.

  3. For the standard normal, P(−1.96 ≤ Z ≤ 1.96) = 0.95 (1.96 is the value of z for which Φ(z) = 0.975; the table value is 1.95996). Hence, with probability about 95%, |p̂ − p| ≤ 1.96 √(pq/n).

  4. Since we do not know the true p, we replace the p under the square root with the observed value p̂ (this is allowed when n is large, because p̂ → p by the law of large numbers). This gives p̂ ± 1.96 √( p̂(1−p̂)/n ). ∎

Proof 9-2. The margin-of-error table and “four times the sample, half the error”

p(1−p) ≤ 1/4: Since p(1−p) = 1/4 − (p − 1/2)², the maximum 1/4 occurs at p = 1/2. So for any p, the margin of error is at most 1.96 × √(1/(4n)) = 0.98/√n. This is why the error is largest when the approval rating is near 50%.

| Sample n | 0.98/√n | Value in the main text |

| --- | --- | --- |

| 100 | 0.0980 | ±9.8 pp |

| 400 | 0.0490 | ±4.9 pp |

| 1000 | 0.0310 | ±3.1 pp |

| 2500 | 0.0196 | ±2.0 pp |

| 10000 | 0.0098 | ±1.0 pp |

Four times the sample, half the error: 0.98/√(4n) = (1/2) · 0.98/√n, because the error is inversely proportional to √n. Required sample size: To get an error of ±3 pp, n = (0.98/0.03)² = 1067.1, that is, 1068 people. This is why you get “±3 pp with around 1000 people.” ∎

(Actual polls may report errors that differ somewhat from this simple formula because of response rates, weighting adjustments, and so on. The calculation above assumes simple random sampling.)

Proof 9-3. The correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval

The two endpoints of the interval, p̂ ± 1.96√(…), are random variables that vary from sample to sample, while the true p is a fixed constant. Step 3 of Proof 9-1 is the statement “the probability that the interval covers p is 95%.” That probability refers to the interval “before the sample is drawn.” Once we actually compute the interval and get numbers (for example, 0.52 to 0.58), p is either inside it or not, one or the other. So the correct interpretation is not “there is a 95% probability that the true value lies in this interval,” but “if we keep building intervals by the same procedure, about 95% of them will cover the true value.” This is the same story as the normal approximation of Chapter 6, but what it refers to is the “procedure,” not a “value.” ∎

Proof 9-4. Deriving and computing the Wilson interval

Idea: Wald put p̂ under the square root, but Wilson leaves p as it is under the square root and solves the inequality for p.

  1. Condition: |p̂ − p| ≤ z √(p(1−p)/n). Squaring both sides, (p̂ − p)² ≤ (z²/n) p(1−p).

  2. Expand: p̂² − 2p̂p + p² ≤ (z²/n)p − (z²/n)p², and rearranging, (1 + z²/n) p² − (2p̂ + z²/n) p + p̂² ≤ 0.

  3. This is a quadratic inequality in p, so the solution lies between the two roots. The discriminant is (2p̂ + z²/n)² − 4(1 + z²/n)p̂² = 4p̂(1−p̂)z²/n + z⁴/n² = 4z² [ p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²) ].

  4. Using the quadratic formula,

p = [ (p̂ + z²/(2n)) ± z √( p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²) ) ] / (1 + z²/n) ∎

Numbers (65/100, z = 1.96): z² = 3.8416. Center = (0.65 + 0.019208)/1.038416 = 0.64443. Half-width = 1.96 × √(0.002275 + 0.000096)/1.038416 = 1.96 × 0.048693/1.038416 = 0.09191. The interval is 0.5525 to 0.7364. This matches the main text’s 0.553 to 0.736 ✓. Wald gives 0.65 ± 1.96×0.0477 = 0.5565 to 0.7435, which is shifted slightly upward.

Proof 9-5. Why Wald breaks down for small samples, and Clopper–Pearson

Wald’s weakness (zero successes): With n=10 and 0 successes, p̂ = 0, and the interval 0 ± 1.96√(0·1/10) is the single point {0}. If the true p is not 0, this interval is certainly wrong. The probability of such a result is (1−p)^n, and for p = 0.1 it is 0.9^10 = 0.349. So in this setting the probability that the Wald interval covers the true value is at most 1 − 0.349 = 65%, falling far short of the nominal 95%. This is the simplest evidence for the main text’s statement that “when the sample is small or the proportion is extreme, Wald’s coverage falls below the nominal level.”

Clopper–Pearson (the exact interval): When the observed value is x successes, the lower limit p_L is the p that satisfies P(X ≥ x | p_L) = 0.025, and the upper limit p_U is the p that satisfies P(X ≤ x | p_U) = 0.025. Because it uses the tail probabilities of the binomial distribution itself, coverage of at least 95% is guaranteed without the normal approximation (since it inverts the binomial test, it is conservative, that is, slightly wide).
