Comparison (0/10): Clopper–Pearson upper limit: (1−p_U)^10 = 0.025 → p_U = 1 − 0.025^{0.1} = 0.3085. Wilson upper limit: center = (z²/2n)/(1 + z²/n) = 0.19208/1.38416 = 0.1388, and the half-width is the same, so the upper limit is 0.2775. Wald: upper limit 0. What the two intervals say is that the conclusion “0/10, so the defect rate is 0%” is wrong, and the rate could be as high as about 30% (the “rule of 3/n”: 3/10 = 0.30).

65/100 (the case in the main text): Clopper–Pearson 0.548 to 0.743, Wilson 0.553 to 0.736, Wald 0.557 to 0.743 (recalculated values). With a sample of 100 and a proportion of 0.65, the three intervals nearly overlap. ∎

Proof 9-6. The p-value of the binomial test: 10 coin tosses

Definition: Assuming the coin is fair, the p-value is the probability of getting a result as extreme as, or more extreme than, the one observed (in both directions). When p=1/2 the distribution is symmetric, so for x heads (x > 5), the p-value = P(|X − 5| ≥ x − 5) = 2·P(X ≥ x).

| Number of heads x | Extreme results (both sides) | Calculation | p-value (two-sided) |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 6 | everything except exactly 5 | 1 − 252/1024 = 772/1024 | 75.4% |

| 7 | X ≤ 3 or X ≥ 7 | 2 × (120+45+10+1)/1024 = 352/1024 | 34.4% |

| 8 | X ≤ 2 or X ≥ 8 | 2 × (45+10+1)/1024 = 112/1024 | 10.9% |

| 9 | X ≤ 1 or X ≥ 9 | 2 × (10+1)/1024 = 22/1024 | 2.1% |

| 10 | X = 0 or X = 10 | 2 × 1/1024 = 2/1024 | 0.2% |

“Extreme results” means all results whose distance from the mean 5 is at least |x − 5|. Since the distribution is symmetric around the mean, we can compute one tail P(X ≥ x) and double it. For example, with 8 heads, P(X ≥ 8) = (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 = 56/1024, and doubling gives 112/1024.

With a 5% criterion, up to 8 heads is “something that could happen by chance” (10.9%), and from 9 heads on it is “strange” (2.1%). ∎

The p-value 0.0035 in the painkiller example (65/100): The exact binomial calculation gives 0.0035. With the normal approximation and continuity correction, z = (64.5 − 50)/5 = 2.9 and 2(1 − Φ(2.9)) = 0.0037, which is nearly the same. Without the correction, z = 3 and the value is 0.0027, slightly different.

The p-value is not “the probability that the coin is fair” (checking with Bayes): Let us set up a hypothetical situation. Suppose 99% of coins are fair and 1% are faulty coins that come up heads 90% of the time. If we toss one 10 times and get exactly 9 heads,

  • From a fair coin: P(9 heads) = 10/1024 = 0.00977

  • From a faulty coin: P(9 heads) = 10 × 0.9^9 × 0.1 = 0.3874

  • Probability of being faulty = (0.01 × 0.3874) / (0.01 × 0.3874 + 0.99 × 0.00977) = 0.003874/0.013542 = 28.6%

The two-sided p-value is 2.1%, which by the “5% criterion” is a strange result, yet the probability that this coin is faulty is only about 29%. This confirms with numbers the main text’s caution: the p-value is “the probability of getting this result assuming the coin is fair,” while “the probability that it is fair” must be computed separately, together with a prior belief. (The proportions 1% and 90% in this example are assumptions chosen for illustration.) ∎

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 10. Treasure Hunt in the Triangle: Rereading the Same Coefficient Table by Shape and Rule

Proof 10-1. The hockey stick identity

Claim: Σ_{j=0}^{k} C(n+j, j) = C(n+k+1, k). (The sum going down a diagonal from the edge equals the value of the one cell at the bend.)

Proof 1 (induction, T4)

  • Base case k=0: the left side is C(n,0) = 1 and the right side is C(n+1,0) = 1.

  • Inductive step: assuming it holds for k, add C(n+k+1, k+1) to both sides. The right side becomes C(n+k+1,k) + C(n+k+1,k+1), which by Pascal’s addition rule (Proof 3-1) is C(n+k+2, k+1) = C(n+(k+1)+1, k+1). So it holds for k+1 as well. ∎

Proof 2 (combinatorial: split by the largest number)

  1. By symmetry (Proof 1-6), C(n+j,j) = C(n+j,n). So the sum is Σ_{m=n}^{n+k} C(m,n).

  2. The number of ways to choose n+1 items out of n+k+1 items numbered 1, 2, …, n+k+1 is C(n+k+1, n+1) = C(n+k+1, k).

  3. Sort these choices by “the largest number chosen,” m+1 (m = n, …, n+k). If the largest number is m+1, the remaining n items are chosen from 1 to m, in C(m,n) ways. The classes do not overlap and nothing is missed (T2), so the sums agree. ∎

Checking with numbers: For n=3, k=3, C(3,0) + C(4,1) + C(5,2) + C(6,3) = 1 + 4 + 10 + 20 = 35 = C(7,3) ✓. This is the main text’s “1+4+10+20 = 35.” The shape is a hockey stick because as we come down the diagonal (the handle), the answer appears one cell over (the blade).

Proof 10-2. The sum along a shallow diagonal is a Fibonacci number

Claim: Let s_n = Σ_j C(n−j, j) (j = 0, 1, … as long as n−j ≥ j). Then s_n = F_{n+1}. (F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n.)

Proof

  1. Initial values: s_0 = C(0,0) = 1, s_1 = C(1,0) = 1.

  2. By Pascal’s rule, C(n−j, j) = C(n−1−j, j) + C(n−1−j, j−1).

  3. Summing over j, the first sum is Σ_j C(n−1−j, j) = s_{n−1}. For the second sum, renaming i = j−1, we get Σ_i C(n−2−i, i) = s_{n−2}.

  4. Therefore s_n = s_{n−1} + s_{n−2}, and since the initial values 1, 1 are the same as Fibonacci’s, s_n = F_{n+1}. ∎

Checking with numbers: s_0..s_6 = 1, 1, 2 (= 1+1), 3 (= 1+2), 5 (= 1+3+1), 8 (= 1+4+3), 13 (= 1+5+6+1). The last is the main text’s “1+5+6+1 = 13 = F(7).”

Interpretation (tiling): Let t_n be the number of ways to cover a strip of length n with 1-cell tiles and 2-cell tiles. If the last tile is a 1-cell tile there are t_{n−1} ways, and if it is a 2-cell tile there are t_{n−2} ways, so the recurrence is the same. If there are j 2-cell tiles, the total number of tiles is n−j, and the number of ways to choose the positions of the 2-cell ones is C(n−j, j), so t_n = s_n as well. The shallow diagonal is the shape of this tile counting.

Proof 10-3. Triangular numbers and tetrahedral numbers

  • The first diagonal C(n,1) = n: 1, 2, 3, 4, … (Proof 3-5).

  • The second diagonal (triangular numbers): C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2 = 1 + 2 + … + (n−1). This is because, by the hockey stick (Proof 10-1), Σ_{m=1}^{n−1} C(m,1) = C(n,2). The values are C(2,2), C(3,2), C(4,2), C(5,2) = 1, 3, 6, 10. In meaning, it is the number of line segments joining two of n points.

  • The third diagonal (tetrahedral numbers): By the hockey stick, C(m,3) = Σ_{j=2}^{m−1} C(j,2), that is, a running total of triangular numbers. 1, 1+3 = 4, 4+6 = 10, 10+10 = 20. When balls are stacked into a tetrahedron, each layer is in the shape of a triangular number, so the total count is a running total of triangular numbers; it is the same story. ∎

Proof 10-4. The Sierpiński triangle: the rule for odd cells

Claim: C(n,k) is odd ⟺ every position where k has a 1 in binary also has a 1 in the binary form of n. Therefore the number of odd entries in row n is 2^r (r = the number of 1s in the binary form of n).

Proof (look at the polynomial modulo 2)

  1. (A+B)² ≡ A² + B² (mod 2): Expanding gives A² + 2AB + B², and the middle term is even.

  2. (1+x)^{2^m} ≡ 1 + x^{2^m} (mod 2): Induction. The case m=0 is trivial. Under the hypothesis, (1+x)^{2^{m+1}} = ( (1+x)^{2^m} )² ≡ (1 + x^{2^m})² ≡ 1 + x^{2^{m+1}}.

  3. Let n = 2^{m_1} + 2^{m_2} + … + 2^{m_r} (distinct m_i, the binary representation). Then

(1+x)^n = ∏{i=1}^{r} (1+x)^{2^{m_i}} ≡ ∏{i=1}^{r} (1 + x^{2^{m_i}}) (mod 2)

  1. When we expand this product, the x^k term arises from every case of “choosing some of the 2^{m_i} and adding them to make k.” Since the binary representation is unique, different subsets give different k, so the terms do not overlap, and each coefficient is 1.

  2. Therefore the remainder of C(n,k) is 1 (odd) ⟺ k is a sum of some of the binary 1-positions of n ⟺ the binary 1-positions of k form a subset of the binary 1-positions of n. There are 2^r subsets. ∎

Checking with coefficients from the main text

  • Row 8 (8 = 1000₂, r=1): 2 odd entries, only the 1s at both ends. The main text’s row 8 is 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1 ✓.

  • Row 7 (111₂, r=3): 8 odd entries, that is, all of them are odd. 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1 ✓.

  • Row 10 (1010₂, r=2): 4 odd entries, at k = 0, 2, 8, 10. C(10,0) = 1, C(10,2) = 45, C(10,8) = 45, C(10,10) = 1. Among the 11 coefficients of this book’s protagonist (x+y)^10, only 1, 45, 45, 1 are odd, and 10, 120, 210, 252 are all even ✓.

Why it is a fractal: If n = 2^m + r (0 ≤ r < 2^m), then the cases where k is a subset of n are (i) k < 2^m and k ⊆ r, or (ii) k = 2^m + k′ and k′ ⊆ r. In other words, the odd pattern of row n is the pattern of row r repeated twice, left and right. This is the self-similarity of the Sierpiński triangle, where small triangles recur inside a large triangle. ∎

Proof 10-5. Catalan numbers: C(2n,n)/(n+1) = C(2n,n) − C(2n,n+1)

Proof (formula): From the ratio formula in Proof 1-7, with k = n we get C(2n,n+1)/C(2n,n) = (2n−n)/(n+1) = n/(n+1). Therefore

C(2n,n) − C(2n,n+1) = C(2n,n) · (1 − n/(n+1)) = C(2n,n)/(n+1). ∎

Since it is written as a difference of integers, this also proves at the same time that C(2n,n)/(n+1) is always an integer. For n=3, C(6,3) = 20, C(6,4) = 15, and 20 − 15 = 5 = 20/4 ✓ (the main text’s “C(6,3)=20 → 20/4 = 5”).

Why is this number the “number of valid parenthesis arrangements”? (the reflection argument)

  1. The number of ways to line up n opening parentheses ( and n closing parentheses ) is C(2n,n). Of these, the “valid” ones are the arrangements in which, at no point when reading from the front, are there more ) than (. The 5 for n=3 are ((())), (()()), (())(), ()(()), ()()().

  2. An invalid arrangement has a first point where there is exactly one more ) than (. Swap every ( and ) after that point.

  3. The swapped arrangement has n−1 opening parentheses ( and n+1 closing parentheses ) in total (up to the first point there are k ( and k+1 ), and the remaining n−k ( and n−k−1 ) are reversed by the swap).

  4. Conversely, an arrangement with n−1 ( and n+1 ) ends with 2 more ) than (, and since it moves one step at a time, there must be a first point where there is one more ). Swapping everything after it again returns us to the original invalid arrangement. So this is a one-to-one correspondence.

  5. The number of invalid arrangements = C(2n,n+1). The number of valid arrangements = C(2n,n) − C(2n,n+1) = C(2n,n)/(n+1). For n=3, 20 − 15 = 5 ✓. ∎

Proof 10-6. The product of all the numbers in a row: the limit of the ratio is e

Claim: Let S(n) = ∏_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k). Then S(n−1)·S(n+1) / S(n)² = (1 + 1/n)^n → e.

Proof

  1. Ratio between neighboring rows: For 0 ≤ k ≤ n−1, C(n,k) / C(n−1,k) = [ n!/(k!(n−k)!) ] · [ k!(n−1−k)!/(n−1)! ] = n/(n−k).

  2. Therefore S(n) = C(n,n) · ∏_{k=0}^{n−1} C(n−1,k) · n/(n−k) = S(n−1) · n^n / [ n(n−1)…1 ] = S(n−1) · n^n / n!.

  3. Hence S(n)/S(n−1) = n^n/n!. Replacing n with n+1, S(n+1)/S(n) = (n+1)^{n+1}/(n+1)!.

  4. Dividing the two expressions,

S(n+1)S(n−1) / S(n)² = [ (n+1)^{n+1}/(n+1)! ] · [ n!/n^n ] = (n+1)^{n+1} / ((n+1) n^n) = (n+1)^n/n^n = (1 + 1/n)^n.

  1. The logarithm of (1 + 1/n)^n is n ln(1 + 1/n) = n(1/n − 1/(2n²) + …) = 1 − 1/(2n) + … → 1, so the limit is e. ∎

Checking with numbers: S(0..5) = 1, 1, 2, 9, 96, 2500 (for example, S(5) = 1·5·10·10·5·1 = 2500). S(5)/S(4) = 2500/96 = 26.04 = 5^5/5! = 3125/120 ✓. For n=4: S(3)S(5)/S(4)² = 9·2500/9216 = 2.4414 = (5/4)^4 = 625/256 ✓. Toward the limit, (1+1/10)^10 = 2.594, (1+1/100)^100 = 2.705, and (1+1/1000)^1000 = 2.717 approach e = 2.71828….

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 11. Splitting Three Ways: The Multinomial Theorem and Pascal’s Pyramid

The proofs in this chapter need no new tools. We widen Proof 1-3 A’s “pick one from each parenthesis” to three branches, and we reuse Proof 0-1’s “to erase the order, divide by the number of repeats” as it stands. The map is as follows.

  • 11-1: The multinomial theorem (why the coefficient n!/(a!b!c!) appears) and the hand expansion in the main text

  • 11-2: The number of letter arrangements. The second meaning of the same coefficient

  • 11-3: Properties of the pyramid (number of terms, sum 3^n, edges, addition rule)

  • 11-4: Sum, mean, variance, and covariance of the multinomial distribution, and checking the two examples in the main text

  • 11-5: How the chi-square statistic becomes z² with two branches, and the calculation for the dice test

  • 11-6: The exercises and “Things to think about” in the main text

Proof 11-1. The multinomial theorem: (x+y+z)^n = Σ n!/(a! b! c!) x^a y^b z^c

Intuition: In the binomial theorem we picked x or y from each parenthesis. Now we pick one of x, y, z. The coefficient is how many times the same term appears.

Proof

  1. (x+y+z)^n has n parentheses. Applying the distributive law (T5) repeatedly, the expansion is the sum of all products formed by “picking one of x, y, z from each of the n parentheses.” There are 3^n ways to pick, and they correspond one-to-one with the 3^n x/y/z strings of length n.

  2. Since multiplication is commutative, every string with a x’s, b y’s, and c z’s gives the same term x^a y^b z^c (with a+b+c = n).

  3. We count such strings. There are C(n,a) ways to choose the a positions for x among the n positions (the first step of T1), and then C(n−a,b) ways to choose the b positions for y among the remaining n−a positions. The remaining c positions are determined: they are z.

  4. Multiplying gives:

C(n,a) · C(n−a,b) = n!/(a!(n−a)!) · (n−a)!/(b!(n−a−b)!) = n!/(a! b! c!)

(What cancels is (n−a)!, and n−a−b = c.)

  1. Summing over all (a,b,c), we get (x+y+z)^n = Σ_{a+b+c=n} n!/(a! b! c!) x^a y^b z^c. ∎

Checking the hand expansion in the main text (n=3)

  • x³, y³, z³: 3!/(3!0!0!) = 1 (3 terms)

  • Terms of the form x²y: 3!/(2!1!0!) = 3 (6 terms: x²y, x²z, xy², y²z, xz², yz²)

  • xyz: 3!/(1!1!1!) = 6 (1 term)

  • Sum: 3×1 + 6×3 + 1×6 = 27 = 3³ ✓

The meaning of the coefficient 6: The strings that produce xyz are the six strings xyz, xzy, yxz, yzx, zxy, zyx. There are 3 ways to choose the position of x (C(3,1)), then 2 ways to choose the position of y among the remaining two positions (C(2,1)), and the rest is determined to be z, so 3×2 = 6. The main text’s explanation “3×2×1 = 6” is exactly this product.

Four or more branches: Repeating the same argument, the coefficient in (x₁+…+x_m)^n is n!/(a₁!a₂!…a_m!). The binomial theorem (Proof 1-3) is the case m = 2. (In this book we use only up to m = 3.)

Proof 11-2. n!/(a! b! c!) is the number of letter arrangements

Intuition: Exactly the same as Proof 0-1. Treat all letters as distinct and line them up, then divide out the repeats caused by swapping identical letters among themselves.

Proof

  1. Let N be the number of ways to arrange a x’s, b y’s, and c z’s in a row (with a+b+c = n).

  2. Number the identical letters to make them distinct (x₁…x_a, y₁…y_b, z₁…z_c). Now all n letters are distinct, so there are n! ways to line them up.

  3. Now erase the numbers again. For any one arrangement (for example xyxzy), the lines that take that shape once numbers are attached number a! b! c!: the product (the multiplication principle, T1) of a! ways to assign numbers among the x’s, b! among the y’s, and c! among the z’s. Every arrangement has been counted exactly a! b! c! times.

  4. Therefore n! = N × a! b! c!, that is, N = n!/(a! b! c!). ∎

(This is the same number as the result of the “choosing positions” count in step 3 of Proof 11-1, because we counted the same strings.)

Checking the examples in the main text

  • BANANA (B 1, A 3, N 2): 6!/(1!·3!·2!) = 720/12 = 60

  • MISSISSIPPI (M 1, I 4, S 4, P 2): 11!/(1!·4!·4!·2!) = 39916800/1152 = 34650

  • BOOKKEEPER (B 1, O 2, K 2, E 3, P 1, R 1): 10!/(2!·2!·3!) = 3628800/24 = 151200

Relation to binomial coefficients: With two kinds of letters, n!/(a! b!) = C(n,a). The arrangements of 10 letters with 3 y’s and 7 x’s number C(10,3) = 120, the same as the 120 in Proof 0-1.

Proof 11-3. Properties of Pascal’s pyramid

Notation: M(a,b,c) = n!/(a! b! c!) (with a+b+c = n). The pyramid is these numbers placed on layer n.

(1) The number of terms is C(n+2,2) = (n+1)(n+2)/2

The number of terms x^a y^b z^c is the number of non-negative integer triples (a,b,c) with a+b+c = n. This equals the number of ways to lay out n stars (★) and 2 bars (|) in a row. The two bars act as dividers, so the number of stars in the first section is a, in the second is b, and in the third is c. We just choose the 2 positions for the bars among n+2 positions, giving C(n+2,2). For n=3 it is C(5,2) = 10, and for n=4 it is 15 ✓. ∎

(2) The sum is 3^n

Substituting x = y = z = 1 in Proof 11-1, the left side is 3^n and the right side is the sum of all the M’s. Alternatively, there are 3^n strings in total (step 1 of 11-1), and each string is added to exactly one coefficient exactly once. Layer 2: 9, layer 3: 27, layer 4: 81 ✓. ∎

(3) One edge is Pascal’s triangle

If z = 0, only the terms with c = 0 remain, and M(a,b,0) = n!/(a! b! 0!) = C(n,a). The bottom row of layer 4 (c = 0) is C(4,0..4) = 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. This says the same thing as: setting z = 0 in (x+y+z)^n gives (x+y)^n. ∎

(4) Addition rule: M(a,b,c) = M(a−1,b,c) + M(a,b−1,c) + M(a,b,c−1)

(Values outside the range of a, b, c are taken to be 0 by convention. If a−1 < 0, then M = 0.)

Combinatorial proof: Split the strings of length n with a x’s, b y’s, and c z’s according to the last letter. If the last letter is x, the first n−1 letters form a string with a−1 x’s, b y’s, and c z’s, and there are M(a−1,b,c) of them. The cases where the last letter is y or z are the same. The three cases do not overlap and leave nothing out (T2), so the sum is M(a,b,c). ∎

Algebraic proof: Writing the coefficients on layer n, (n−1)!/((a−1)! b! c!) = n!/(a! b! c!) · (a/n); similarly the second and third terms are that value multiplied by (b/n) and (c/n) respectively. Adding them gives n!/(a! b! c!) · (a+b+c)/n = n!/(a! b! c!) ✓. ∎

Checking values in the main text: On layer 3, xyz (6) = on layer 2, xy (2) + xz (2) + yz (2) = 6 ✓. On layer 3, x²y (3) = M(1,1,0) + M(2,0,0) + M(2,1,−1) = 2 + 1 + 0 = 3 ✓ (the out-of-range term is 0). On layer 4, x²yz (12) = on layer 3, xyz (6) + x²z (3) + x²y (3) = 12 ✓. The whole of layer 4: 1, 4, 4, 6, 12, 6, 4, 12, 12, 4, 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, with sum 81, which agrees with the layer-4 triangle in the main text.

Proof 11-4. The multinomial distribution

Claim: In n independent trials, if each trial results in one of A, B, C with probabilities p_A, p_B, p_C (summing to 1), then the probability that A occurs a times, B occurs b times, and C occurs c times is P(a,b,c) = n!/(a! b! c!) p_A^a p_B^b p_C^c.

Proof (same method as Proof 4-1)

  1. The outcome is an A/B/C string, and since the trials are independent, the probability of a particular string is the product of the probabilities of its letters. For any string with a A’s, b B’s, and c C’s, this is p_A^a p_B^b p_C^c.

  2. The number of such strings is n!/(a! b! c!) from Proof 11-2.

  3. There are that many outcomes of equal probability, so multiplying gives the claim. ∎

The probabilities sum to 1: Substituting (x,y,z) = (p_A, p_B, p_C) in Proof 11-1, (p_A+p_B+p_C)^n = 1^n = 1 equals the sum of all the P(a,b,c) on the right (the three-branch version of Proof 4-2). With two branches this is the binomial distribution of Proof 4-1. ∎

Mean, variance, covariance

  1. Let I_A^{(i)} be the variable that is “1 if trial i gives A, 0 otherwise.” The count of A, N_A = Σ I_A^{(i)}, is B(n, p_A), so its mean is n p_A and its variance is n p_A(1−p_A) (Proofs 4-5, 4-6).

  2. In a single trial, A and B do not occur together, so I_A · I_B = 0, and the covariance for one trial is E[I_A I_B] − E[I_A]E[I_B] = 0 − p_A p_B = −p_A p_B.

  3. Different trials are independent, so their covariance is 0, and summing over n trials gives Cov(N_A, N_B) = −n p_A p_B. ∎

Check: Since N_A + N_B = n − N_C, we must have Var(N_A+N_B) = Var(N_C) = n p_C(1−p_C). Computing the left side with the values above: n p_A(1−p_A) + n p_B(1−p_B) − 2n p_A p_B = n[(p_A+p_B) − (p_A+p_B)²] = n(p_A+p_B)(1−p_A−p_B) = n(1−p_C) p_C, which agrees. ✓ In 12 rolls of a die, the count of one particular face has mean 12×(1/6) = 2 and variance 12×(1/6)(5/6) = 1.667.

Example 1 in the main text: every face exactly twice in 12 rolls of a die

12!/(2!)^6 = 479001600/64 = 7484400, and the probability = 7484400/6^12 = 7484400/2176782336 = 0.003438 ≈ 0.34% ✓. For 6 dice showing each of 1 through 6 once: 6!/6^6 = 720/46656 = 0.01543 ≈ 1.5% ✓. By the same logic, unlike exactly half-and-half in 10 coin flips (24.6%), as the number of branches grows the probability of the “most even outcome” shrinks drastically. This is because the number of possible cases (6^12) grows enormously, while there is only one kind of “most even” arrangement among them.

Example 2 in the main text: Mendel’s 9:3:3:1

n = 16, (a,b,c,d) = (9,3,3,1), with probabilities (9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16) (Proofs 11-1 and 11-2 carry over unchanged to four branches, so we use the same formula). The coefficient is 16!/(9!·3!·3!·1!) = 1601600, and

P = 1601600 × (9/16)^9 × (3/16)^3 × (3/16)^3 × (1/16)^1 = 0.024521 ≈ 2.45% ✓

Proof 11-5. The chi-square statistic

With two branches, χ² = z²

Suppose that in n trials the first branch occurs O₁ times and the second occurs O₂ = n − O₁ times, with expected counts E₁ = np and E₂ = nq. Then O₂ − E₂ = −(O₁ − E₁), so

χ² = (O₁−np)²/(np) + (O₂−nq)²/(nq) = (O₁−np)² (1/(np) + 1/(nq)) = (O₁−np)² · (p+q)/(npq) = (O₁−np)²/(npq) = z². ∎

(npq is the variance from Proof 4-6. Therefore the two-branch chi-square test is the square of the z-test that comes from the normal approximation in Proof 6-6. As the number of branches grows, the normal distribution turns into the chi-square distribution, and the fact that the degrees of freedom become (number of branches − 1), the “number of free branches,” because of the constraint that the total is fixed at n, is part of the same story.)

The theorem that the distribution of χ² converges to the chi-square distribution for general numbers of branches is stated without proof. The 5% critical value 11.07 in the main text is the value from the chi-square table for 5 degrees of freedom (11.0705).

Checking the main text’s calculation: The expected count is 60/6 = 10, and the observed counts are 7, 12, 10, 11, 8, 12, so (−3)²+2²+0²+1²+(−2)²+2² = 9+4+0+1+4+4 = 22, and dividing by 10 gives χ² = 2.2. With 5 degrees of freedom the p-value is 0.8208, so the main text’s conclusion “not inconsistent with a fair die” is correct. (In the same way, for χ² with 5 degrees of freedom to reach 11.07, one face would have to deviate substantially from the expected count. For example, if a 6 came up 22 times, (22−10)²/10 = 14.4 alone would exceed the threshold.)

Proof 11-6. The exercises in the main text

Exercise 1: the coefficient of xyz² in (x+y+z)^4

M(1,1,2) = 4!/(1!·1!·2!) = 24/2 = 12. Building the whole of layer 4 confirms that (a,b,c) = (1,1,2) gives 12. In the layer-4 triangle, the row where the exponent of x is 1 (the fourth row from the top) is 4, 12, 12, 4, and the third from the left is y¹z². ∎

Exercise 2: The calculations in Proof 11-3(4), layer 3: 6 = 2+2+2 and layer 4: 12 = 6+3+3, are the answer (see the checks above).

Exercise 3: BOOKKEEPER: The value from Proof 11-2, 151200 ✓.

Things to think about: with k branches, the number of terms on layer n is C(n+k−1, k−1)

The same stars and bars as in Proof 11-3(1): if we lay out n stars and k−1 bars in a row, the bars make k sections, and the number of stars in each section is the exponent. Among n+k−1 positions we choose the k−1 positions for the bars, giving C(n+k−1, k−1) ways. For k = 3 this is C(n+2,2), and for k = 2 it is C(n+1,1) = n+1, which agrees with the number of terms (n+1) of the binomial. ∎

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 12. Generating Functions: Packing a Whole Table of Coefficients into One Expression

The proofs in this chapter stand on a single rule (12-1): “multiplying polynomials means collecting the pairs whose indices sum to k and adding them up.” Everything else is just this rule renamed wherever it is used. The map is as follows.

  • 12-1: The product rule, the addition rule, symmetry, and the Vandermonde identity

  • 12-2: Plugging values into x and differentiating (the three bonuses of Chapter 2)

  • 12-3: The sum of dice, factorization, and the “Sicherman” dice

  • 12-4: Fibonacci, Catalan, and making change

  • 12-5: Probability generating functions (mean, variance, the Poisson limit)

  • 12-6: The road by which the central limit theorem leads to e^(−t²/2) (characteristic functions)

(We read a power series as “an expression with its coefficients strung together,” and we do not deal with convergence. The series 1/(1−u) = 1+u+u²+… and the series for e^u used in 12-4 and 12-5 are the same as those already used in this book (Proof 7-2).)

Proof 12-1. The product rule and its applications

The product rule: If A(x) = Σ aᵢ xⁱ and B(x) = Σ bⱼ xʲ, then x^k = Σ_{i=0}^{k} aᵢ b_{k−i}.

Proof: By the distributive law (T5), A(x)B(x) is the sum over all pairs (i,j) of aᵢ xⁱ · bⱼ xʲ = aᵢ bⱼ x^{i+j}. The x^k terms among them come from the pairs with i+j = k, so the coefficient is Σ_{i+j=k} aᵢ bⱼ. ∎

The addition rule seen again (Proof 3-1 in one line)

(1+x)^n = (1+x)(1+x)^{n−1}, and in the product rule the only coefficients of (1+x) are a₀ = a₁ = 1, so

x^k^n = a₀ · x^k^{n−1} + a₁ · x^{k−1}^{n−1}

that is, C(n,k) = C(n−1,k) + C(n−1,k−1) ✓ (by the binomial theorem of Proof 1-3, we read x^k^n = C(n,k)). ∎

Symmetry (Proof 1-6 in one line): (1+x)^n = x^n (1 + 1/x)^n. Expanding the right side by the binomial theorem gives x^n Σ C(n,j) x^{−j} = Σ C(n,j) x^{n−j}, and the coefficient C(n,k) of x^k on the left equals the term on the right with n−j = k, namely C(n,n−k). ∎

The Vandermonde identity: Σ_k C(m,k) C(n,r−k) = C(m+n,r)

We find the coefficient of x^r in (1+x)^m (1+x)^n = (1+x)^{m+n} in two ways. The right side gives C(m+n,r) by the binomial theorem, and the left side gives Σ_k C(m,k) C(n,r−k) by the product rule. The two are equal. ∎

The same story combinatorially: Consider choosing r people in total from a team of m people and a team of n people. If we split by the number k of people chosen from the first team (T2), then for each k there are C(m,k) C(n,r−k) ways. Summing gives C(m+n,r), choosing r people from all m+n (the same “double counting” as in Proof 1-3 A).

Checking with numbers: m=3, n=4, r=3: k=0: 1·4 = 4, k=1: 3·6 = 18, k=2: 3·4 = 12, k=3: 1·1 = 1, and the sum is 4+18+12+1 = 35 = C(7,3) ✓.

The special case m = n = r: Σ C(n,k) C(n,n−k) = C(2n,n), and by symmetry (Proof 1-6) C(n,n−k) = C(n,k), so Σ C(n,k)² = C(2n,n). For n=10 this gives 184756 = C(20,10) ✓ (Chapter 2, bonus 3).

| x = 1 | (1+1)^n = 2^n = Σ C(n,k) | Proof 2-1 |

| x = −1 | (1−1)^n = 0 = Σ (−1)^k C(n,k) | Proof 2-4 |

| Differentiate, then x = 1 | Σ k C(n,k) = n 2^{n−1} | Below |

| Sum of squares | Σ C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) | Proof 12-1 |

Differentiation (mean n/2): Differentiate both sides of (1+x)^n = Σ C(n,k) x^k with respect to x. The right side becomes Σ k C(n,k) x^{k−1} term by term, and the left side is n(1+x)^{n−1}. Plugging in x = 1 gives Σ k C(n,k) = n 2^{n−1}. For n=10 this is 10×512 = 5120, and 5120/1024 = 5 ✓. This is the same value obtained by “counting committee chairs” in Proof 4-5, Method 2 (summing both sides of k C(n,k) = n C(n−1,k−1) over all k gives this identity). ∎

(Differentiation is justified because a polynomial may be differentiated term by term. With finitely many terms, there is no problem.)

Proof 12-3. The sum of dice and the Sicherman dice

The sum of dice: One die is written D(x) = x + x² + … + x⁶ (the face s is xˢ). By the product rule (Proof 12-1), the number of ways two dice sum to s is Σ_{i+j=s} 1·1 = (the number of pairs with i+j = s and 1≤i,j≤6) = [xˢ] D(x)². Likewise, the sum of n dice is [xˢ] D(x)^n. Thus the single line of the product rule in Proof 12-1 is the main text’s Chapter 8 “add up the six neighboring cells.” This is because, with the new die’s face j ranging over 1 to 6, [xˢ]D^{n+1} = Σ_{j=1}^{6} [x^{s−j}]D^n.

Check: D² = x² + 2x³ + 3x⁴ + 4x⁵ + 5x⁶ + 6x⁷ + 5x⁸ + 4x⁹ + 3x¹⁰ + 2x¹¹ + x¹², and the coefficient of x¹⁰ in D³ = 27 ✓ (the 27/216 in the main text’s Chapter 8). The sum 7 has coefficient 6, namely the six pairs (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1).

Proof by factorization

  1. The sum of a geometric sequence: x + x² + … + x⁶ = x(1 − x⁶)/(1 − x).

  2. 1 − x⁶ = (1 − x³)(1 + x³), and 1 − x³ = (1 − x)(1 + x + x²), 1 + x³ = (1 + x)(1 − x + x²) (the sum-of-cubes formula).

  3. Therefore D(x) = x · (1 + x + x²) · (1 + x) · (1 − x + x²). ∎

The Sicherman dice: Let A(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x²) and B(x) = x(1+x)(1+x+x²)(1−x+x²)².

  1. Multiplying all the factors, A(x)B(x) = x²(1+x)²(1+x+x²)²(1−x+x²)² = [x(1+x)(1+x+x²)(1−x+x²)]² = D(x)². (This is the factorization in Proof 12-3, squared.)

  2. We find the coefficients. (1+x)(1+x+x²) = 1 + 2x + 2x² + x³, so A = x + 2x² + 2x³ + x⁴. Next, (1−x+x²)² = 1 − 2x + 3x² − 2x³ + x⁴, and computing the coefficients of (1 + 2x + 2x² + x³)(1 − 2x + 3x² − 2x³ + x⁴) by the product rule (Proof 12-1) gives 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, so B = x + x³ + x⁴ + x⁵ + x⁶ + x⁸.

  3. The coefficients of A and B are all non-negative integers and sum to 6 (A(1) = 6, B(1) = 6), so each can be read as a die with 6 faces. The faces are 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 for A and 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 for B.

  4. The number of ways this pair sums to s is [xˢ] A(x)B(x) = [xˢ] D(x)², which equals the number of ways two ordinary dice sum to s, for every s. ∎

Checking with numbers: Counting directly the cases where the sum is 9, we get four: (A,B) = (1,8), (3,6), (3,6), (4,5) (A has two 3’s, so (3,6) occurs twice). This matches the 4 ways (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3) of making 9 with two ordinary dice ✓. All coefficients of A·B and D² agree.

(That this is the only such pair other than the ordinary dice is proved using the uniqueness of factorization, but this book omits the proof.)

Proof 12-4. Turning recurrences into a single expression: Fibonacci, Catalan, and making change

(1) Fibonacci

Let F(x) = F₁x + F₂x² + F₃x³ + … (F₁ = F₂ = 1, Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂). Then

F(x) − xF(x) − x²F(x) = F₁x + (F₂ − F₁)x² + Σ_{n≥3}(Fₙ − Fₙ₋₁ − Fₙ₋₂)xⁿ = x + 0 + 0 = x.

(The x² term: F₂ − F₁ = 0, and the terms for n ≥ 3 are 0 by the recurrence.) Therefore (1 − x − x²) F(x) = x, so F(x) = x/(1−x−x²). ∎

Connection with binomial coefficients: Putting u = x(1+x) into 1/(1−u) = 1 + u + u² + … gives

1/(1−x−x²) = Σ_{m≥0} x^m (1+x)^m. The coefficient of xⁿ in x^m(1+x)^m is the coefficient C(m, n−m) of x^{n−m} in (1+x)^m, so changing to k = n−m, [xⁿ] 1/(1−x−x²) = Σ_k C(n−k, k). Since F(x)/x = 1/(1−x−x²), this coefficient is Fₙ₊₁, so Fₙ₊₁ = Σ_k C(n−k, k) (the same result as Proof 10-2, and this way it comes out directly without a recurrence). For n = 5: C(5,0)+C(4,1)+C(3,2) = 1+4+3 = 8 = F₆ ✓ (for n = 0..7 this gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21). ∎

(2) Catalan numbers

Proof of the recurrence: A correctly matched parenthesis string (with n+1 pairs) can always be written uniquely in the form “( A ) B.” This is because the closing parenthesis that pairs with the first opening parenthesis is determined, and the inside A and the outside B are each correctly matched strings. If A has k pairs, then B has n−k pairs. Conversely, if we choose correct A and B arbitrarily, “( A ) B” is a correct string. Therefore Cₙ₊₁ = Σ_{k=0}^{n} Cₖ Cₙ₋ₖ. C₃ = C₀C₂ + C₁C₁ + C₂C₀ = 2+1+2 = 5 ✓. (This is the same number as the one counted by the reflection argument in Proof 10-5.)

The generating function equation: Let Cat(x) = C₀ + C₁x + C₂x² + …. By the product rule (Proof 12-1), the coefficient of xⁿ in Cat(x)² is Σ Cₖ Cₙ₋ₖ = Cₙ₊₁, so x Cat(x)² = C₁x + C₂x² + … = Cat(x) − 1. That is, Cat(x) = 1 + x Cat(x)². ∎

Solving: Solving x Cat² − Cat + 1 = 0 as a quadratic equation in Cat gives Cat = (1 ± √(1−4x))/(2x). As x → 0, Cat(0) = C₀ = 1 must be finite. If we take “+”, the numerator goes to 2 and diverges as x → 0, so we take “−”. Cat(x) = (1 − √(1−4x))/(2x). ∎

Extracting the coefficients: In the generalized binomial series (1−4x)^{1/2} = Σ C(1/2, m)(−4x)^m, the coefficient of x^m (for m ≥ 1) is

C(1/2, m)(−4)^m = [(1/2)(−1/2)(−3/2)⋯(1/2−m+1)/m!] (−4)^m = −(1·3·5⋯(2m−3)) · 2^m / m!

(The sign (−1)^{m−1} of the numerator and the sign (−1)^m of (−4)^m combine to give −.) And since 1·3·5⋯(2m−3) = (2m−2)!/(2^{m−1}(m−1)!),

= −(2m−2)! · 2^m / (2^{m−1}(m−1)! m!) = −2 (2m−2)!/((m−1)! m!) = −(2/m) C(2m−2, m−1).

Checking small values: m = 1 gives −2, m = 2 gives −2·2/2 = −2, m = 3 gives −(2/3)·6 = −4 ✓ (the same as the values −2, −2, −4 computed directly from C(1/2,m)(−4)^m).

Therefore [x^m]√(1−4x) = −(2/m) C(2m−2,m−1), and the coefficient of x^{m−1} in Cat(x) = (1 − √(1−4x))/(2x) is (1/2) · (2/m) C(2m−2,m−1) = C(2m−2,m−1)/m. Writing m−1 = n, we get Cₙ = C(2n,n)/(n+1), the same as the result of Proof 10-5. For n = 0..7 this gives 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429. ∎

(3) Making change

If we write one kind of coin (for example the 2-unit coin) as “any number may be used,” we get 1 + x² + x⁴ + … = 1/(1−x²), and the 1-unit coin is 1/(1−x), the 5-unit coin 1/(1−x⁵). Multiplying the three expressions, by the product rule (Proof 12-1) the coefficient of x^N is “the number of ways to make N = i+2j+5l with i 1-unit coins, j 2-unit coins, and l 5-unit coins.” This is the multiplication rule used three times, and it is exactly the act of counting the number of ways.

N = 10: With zero 5-unit coins, the ways to make 10 with 1-unit and 2-unit coins number 6 (0 to 5 two-unit coins); with one 5-unit coin, the ways to make the remaining 5 with 1-unit and 2-unit coins number 3 (0 to 2 two-unit coins); with two 5-unit coins, 1 way. The sum is 6+3+1 = 10 ✓. N = 7: With zero 5-unit coins there are 4 ways (0 to 3 two-unit coins), and with one 5-unit coin there are 2 ways (0 to 1 two-unit coins), giving 6, which agrees with the 6 ways in the main text’s exercise. The number of ways to make 1000 with coins of 10, 50, 100, and 500 is 158. ∎

Proof 12-5. Probability generating functions

Definition: When X takes values 0, 1, 2, …, G(x) = Σ P(X=k) xᵏ = E[x^X]. (This sum equals 1 at x = 1, because the coefficients are probabilities.)

Proofs of three rules

  • A sum of independent variables is a product: If X and Y are independent, E[x^{X+Y}] = E[x^X x^Y] = E[x^X] E[x^Y] (the property that for independent variables the expectation splits into a product, as in Proof 8-3 (a)). That is, G_{X+Y} = G_X G_Y. This is also the probabilistic version of the product rule (Proof 12-1).

  • Mean: G′(x) = Σ k P(X=k) x^{k−1}, so G′(1) = Σ k P(X=k) = E[X].

  • Variance: G″(1) = Σ k(k−1) P(X=k) = E[X(X−1)] = E[X²] − E[X], so Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]² = G″(1) + G′(1) − G′(1)². ∎

The binomial distribution

  1. The G for one coin flip (probability p of heads) is q + px (q = 1−p). The sum of n independent flips is a product, so G(x) = (q + px)^n. (Expanding by the binomial theorem gives Σ C(n,k) p^k q^{n−k} x^k, and the coefficients are the probabilities of Proof 4-1 ✓.)

  2. From G′(x) = np(q+px)^{n−1}, G′(1) = np (q+p = 1).

  3. From G″(x) = n(n−1)p²(q+px)^{n−2}, G″(1) = n(n−1)p².

  4. Var = n(n−1)p² + np − n²p² = np − np² = np(1−p) = npq. ∎

For n = 10, p = 1/2, G″(1) = 90/4 = 22.5 and 22.5 + 5 − 25 = 2.5 ✓ (the same as the direct summation 2560/1024 = 2.5 in Proof 4-6).

The Poisson distribution and the limit

  1. The G of the Poisson is Σ e^{−λ}λᵏxᵏ/k! = e^{−λ} Σ (λx)ᵏ/k! = e^{−λ}e^{λx} = e^{λ(x−1)}. (The series for e^u is in Proof 7-2.)

  2. Since G′(x) = λe^{λ(x−1)}, G′(1) = λ and G″(1) = λ². Var = λ² + λ − λ² = λ. (We obtained the same result as Proof 7-2 in two lines.)

  3. The limit: Putting p = λ/n into the binomial distribution, G(x) = (1 − λ/n + (λ/n)x)^n = (1 + λ(x−1)/n)^n. As shown in the B-block of Proof 7-1, n ln(1 + a/n) → a, so (1+a/n)^n → e^a. With a = λ(x−1), the limit is e^{λ(x−1)}, the same as the Poisson’s G. ∎

(The theorem that if the generating functions converge for all x then the distributions converge, that is, the “continuity theorem for probability generating functions,” is stated without proof. In Chapter 7 of the main text, the convergence of the probability for each k was shown directly in Proof 7-1, so this method simply sees the same result again in one line.)

Properties of sums (one line of multiplication)

  • The sum of two independent Poissons: e^{λ₁(x−1)} e^{λ₂(x−1)} = e^{(λ₁+λ₂)(x−1)}. The sum is also Poisson, and the means add (2 cases + 3 cases → 5 cases).

  • The sum of two binomials with the same p: (q+px)^m (q+px)^n = (q+px)^{m+n}. The sum is also binomial. ∎

Proof 12-6. The road by which the central limit theorem leads to e^(−t²/2)

Proof 8-3 used the moment generating function E[e^{tZ}]. This chapter makes the same argument with the characteristic function E[e^{itZ}], which includes the imaginary unit i. The advantage of the characteristic function is that it always exists for every distribution (some distributions have no moment generating function).

Proof (the coin case)

  1. Let ξ be the variable that is +1 for heads and −1 for tails. The characteristic function of ξ is E[e^{itξ}] = (e^{it} + e^{−it})/2 = cos t.

  2. The sum Sₙ of n independent flips, divided by √n, gives Zₙ = Sₙ/√n, whose characteristic function is [cos(t/√n)]^n, for the same reason as “independent means product” in Proof 12-5 (e^{it(A+B)} = e^{itA}e^{itB} and independence).

  3. Since cos s = 1 − s²/2 + s⁴/24 − …, we have ln cos s = ln(1 − u) (with u = s²/2 − s⁴/24 + …) = −u − u²/2 − … = −s²/2 − s⁴/12 − …. (The s⁴ term: +1/24 − 1/8 = −1/12.)

  4. Putting in s = t/√n and multiplying by n, n ln cos(t/√n) = −t²/2 − t⁴/(12n) − … → −t²/2.

  5. Therefore [cos(t/√n)]^n → e^{−t²/2}. This is the characteristic function of the standard normal distribution (the value obtained from the mgf e^{t²/2} of Proof 8-3 (c) by replacing t with it). ∎

The theorem that if characteristic functions converge then the distributions converge (Lévy’s continuity theorem) is used under the same name as in Proof 8-3 (d), and its proof is omitted.

Part 2 (Proofs), Chapter 13. How Fast Do the Coefficients Grow: Stirling’s Formula and Entropy

The proofs in this chapter center on the calculation of substituting Proof 6-1 (Stirling’s formula) into binomial coefficients. The map is as follows.

  • 13-1: Why the error of Stirling’s formula is about 1/(12n)

  • 13-2: The middle coefficient C(2n,n) ≈ 4ⁿ/√(πn) and the probability of exactly n:n

  • 13-3: The general coefficient C(n,k) ≈ 2^{nH(q)}/√(2πnq(1−q)), and why H(q) is at most 1

Proof 13-1. The error of Stirling’s formula: about 1/(12n)

Claim: n! ≥ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ, and n! ≤ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ e^{1/(12n)}.

Proof: In Step A of Proof 6-1, aₙ = n!/(√n (n/e)ⁿ) was a decreasing sequence with limit C, and the inequality C ≤ aₙ ≤ C e^{1/(12n)} held. In Step B, C = √(2π), so immediately √(2π) ≤ n!/(√n(n/e)ⁿ) ≤ √(2π)e^{1/(12n)}. Multiplying both sides by √n(n/e)ⁿ gives the claim. ∎

Reading it as a relative error: Let the approximation be S_n = √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ. Then S_n/n! ∈ [e^{−1/(12n)}, 1], that is, the relative error (S_n − n!)/n! is always negative and at least −(1 − e^{−1/(12n)}). And 1 − e^{−1/(12n)} ≈ 1/(12n).

Proof 13-2. The middle coefficient and the probability of “exactly n:n”

Claim: C(2n,n) ≈ 4ⁿ/√(πn), and the relative error is about 1/(8n).

Proof

  1. Proof 6-1, Step B-4 (the Wallis product) already proved C(2n,n) ~ 4ⁿ/√(πn). The same expression also comes out by substituting into Stirling: (2n)! ≈ √(4πn)(2n/e)^{2n} and (n!)² ≈ 2πn(n/e)^{2n}, so the ratio is √(4πn)/(2πn) · 2^{2n} = 2√(πn)/(2πn) · 4ⁿ = 4ⁿ/√(πn).

  2. The size of the error: Using Stirling’s next term n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ(1 + 1/(12n)) (the same next term as in Proof 6-2, proof omitted), the correction factor multiplying 4ⁿ/√(πn) is (1 + 1/(24n))/(1 + 1/(12n))² ≈ (1 + 1/(24n))(1 − 1/(6n)) ≈ 1 − 1/(8n). Therefore the approximation 4ⁿ/√(πn) is larger than the exact value by about 1/(8n). ∎

Proof 13-3. General coefficients and binary entropy

Claim: With q = k/n and H(q) = −q log₂q − (1−q) log₂(1−q), C(n,k) ≈ 2^{nH(q)}/√(2πn q(1−q)).

Proof

  1. Substitute Stirling’s formula from Proof 6-1 into n!, k!, and (n−k)!.

C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) ≈ [√(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ] / [√(2πk)(k/e)ᵏ · √(2π(n−k))((n−k)/e)^{n−k}]

  1. The exponent of e is k + (n−k) = n, so the e^{−n} in the denominator and the e^{−n} in the numerator cancel. What remains is

√(n/(2πk(n−k))) · nⁿ/(kᵏ (n−k)^{n−k}).

(This is the same expression as step 1 of Proof 6-3, except that p^k q^{n−k} is simply not multiplied in.)

  1. For the square root in front, since k = qn and n−k = (1−q)n, we have k(n−k) = q(1−q)n², and √(n/(2π q(1−q) n²)) = 1/√(2πn q(1−q)).

  2. The latter part is nⁿ/(kᵏ(n−k)^{n−k}) = (n/k)ᵏ (n/(n−k))^{n−k} = q^{−k}(1−q)^{−(n−k)}. Taking the logarithm to base 2 gives −k log₂q − (n−k) log₂(1−q) = n[−q log₂q − (1−q) log₂(1−q)] = nH(q), so this part is 2^{nH(q)}.

  3. Multiplying steps 3 and 4 gives the claim. ∎

Checking q = 1/2: H(1/2) = 1 and √(2πn · 1/4) = √(πn/2), so C(n,n/2) ≈ 2ⁿ/√(πn/2). Substituting 2n for n gives 4ⁿ/√(πn), the same as Proof 13-2. ✓

H(q) ≤ 1, with equality only at q = 1/2: H′(q) = −log₂q − 1/ln2 + log₂(1−q) + 1/ln2 = log₂((1−q)/q). This is positive when q < 1/2 and negative when q > 1/2, so H is maximal at q = 1/2, with H(1/2) = 1. ∎

The size of the error (Stirling’s next term, proof omitted): If we insert the (1 + 1/(12m)) correction into each of n!, k!, and (n−k)!, the amount by which the approximation exceeds the exact value is, in relative terms, about (1/12)(1/k + 1/(n−k) − 1/n). Check: for C(10,3), (1/12)(1/3 + 1/7 − 1/10) = 3.14% (the table’s 3.17%); for C(100,10), 0.84% (0.85%); for C(100,30), 0.31% (0.31%), matching the table. We can see from this expression that the error shrinks in inverse proportion to n.

Proof 13-4. Almost all cases lie in the middle

Comparison with the whole: 2^{nH(q)}/2ⁿ = 2^{−n(1−H(q))}. If q ≠ 1/2, then H(q) < 1 (Proof 13-3), so this ratio goes to 0 exponentially as n grows. That is, the share that the number of cases with ratio q takes of the total 2ⁿ vanishes exponentially.

Numbers (n=100, k=30): C(100,30)/2^{100} = 2.317×10⁻⁵ = 1/43158. This matches the main text’s “about once in 43,000 times.” ✓

The number of bits for compression: Among 0/1 strings of length 100, those with exactly 10 ones number C(100,10) = 17,310,309,456,440, and log₂ C(100,10) = 43.98 bits. From the expression in Proof 13-3, nH(0.1) = 46.90, and the logarithm of the square-root part is log₂√(2π·100·0.1·0.9) = log₂√56.55 = log₂ 7.52 = 2.91, so 46.90 − 2.91 = 43.99, which matches (the main text’s “difference of 2.9 bits”). To label N distinct strings with numbers, log₂ N bits suffice (a number from 0 to N−1 takes ⌈log₂ N⌉ binary digits), so about 44 bits are enough. ∎

(Shannon’s source coding theorem, that a random string whose proportion of ones is 10% can be compressed to H(0.1) ≈ 0.47 bits per bit, is an extension of this calculation to probabilities, and this book omits its proof.)

Proof 13-5. The probability of deviating shrinks exponentially

(1) Combinatorially: the number of cases with ratio at least q is ≤ 2^{nH(q)} (q ≥ 1/2)

  1. If q ≥ 1/2, then q/(1−q) ≥ 1. If k ≥ qn, then (q/(1−q))^k ≥ (q/(1−q))^{qn}.

  2. Therefore q^k(1−q)^{n−k} = (1−q)ⁿ (q/(1−q))^k ≥ (1−q)ⁿ (q/(1−q))^{qn} = q^{qn}(1−q)^{(1−q)n} = 2^{−nH(q)}. (The last equality is the definition of H in Proof 13-3.)

  3. Putting x = q and y = 1−q in the binomial theorem (Proof 1-3), we get 1 = Σ_k C(n,k) q^k (1−q)^{n−k}. Collecting only the terms with k ≥ qn in this sum gives 1 ≥ Σ_{k≥qn} C(n,k) q^k(1−q)^{n−k} ≥ 2^{−nH(q)} Σ_{k≥qn} C(n,k).

  4. Therefore Σ_{k≥qn} C(n,k) ≤ 2^{nH(q)}. For a fair coin each case has probability 2^{−n}, so P(X ≥ qn) ≤ 2^{nH(q)−n} = 2^{−n(1−H(q))}. ∎

Numbers (n=100, q=0.6): 1 − H(0.6) = 0.02905, the upper bound is 2^{−2.905} = 0.1335 = 13.4%, and the exact P(X ≥ 60) = 2.84% ✓. Being an upper bound it is loose, but the shape of exponential decrease is the same.

(2) Hoeffding’s inequality: P(|X/n − 1/2| ≥ ε) ≤ 2e^{−2nε²}

Proof (using Markov’s inequality of Proof 8-1 and the moment generating function tool of 8-3)

  1. X is B(n,1/2), and X−n/2 = Σ(Iᵢ − 1/2). Since Iᵢ − 1/2 is +1/2 with probability 1/2 and −1/2 with probability 1/2, E[e^{λ(Iᵢ−1/2)}] = (e^{λ/2} + e^{−λ/2})/2 = cosh(λ/2).

  2. cosh y ≤ e^{y²/2}: Comparing the two series, cosh y = Σ y^{2k}/(2k)! and e^{y²/2} = Σ y^{2k}/(2^k k!), and since (2k)! ≥ 2^k k!, the cosh side is smaller term by term. Therefore cosh(λ/2) ≤ e^{λ²/8}.

  3. By independence, E[e^{λ(X−n/2)}] = cosh(λ/2)^n ≤ e^{nλ²/8}.

  4. Applying Markov (Proof 8-1) with Y = e^{λ(X−n/2)} and a = e^{λnε}, P(X − n/2 ≥ nε) ≤ e^{−λnε} e^{nλ²/8}.

  5. The λ that makes the exponent −λnε + nλ²/8 smallest is λ = 4ε, and the value is −4nε² + 2nε² = −2nε². Therefore P(X−n/2 ≥ nε) ≤ e^{−2nε²}.

  6. By symmetry the other side is the same, and combining gives P(|X/n − 1/2| ≥ ε) ≤ 2e^{−2nε²}. ∎

Things to think about: why the law of large numbers holds even though the probability of exactly n:n shrinks like 1/√(πn)

  1. “Exactly n:n” is a single cell. That the probability of a single cell goes to 0 like 1/√(πn) was shown in Proof 13-2.

  2. The range where the proportion is within ε of 1/2, that is, where the count is n ± εn (when tossing 2n times in total, the count has mean n and standard deviation √(n/2)), is the union of a number of cells proportional to √n (about 2εn cells). By Proof 6-6 (the interval theorem), the probability of an interval within c·σ of the mean is a constant value regardless of n (for example, about 95% for c=2). This is because the two effects, the interval’s width growing in proportion to √n and the probability of a single cell shrinking in proportion to 1/√n, cancel exactly.

  3. On the other hand, if we fix the range ε of the proportion, the width of the count is εn, which is ε√n times the standard deviation (about √n) and grows without bound as n grows. That is why the probability goes to 1 (Chebyshev in Proof 8-2, the exponential bound in Proof 13-5). There is no contradiction: we have simply viewed “a single cell” and “a range whose width is proportional to √n” as events of different sizes. ∎

A-1. Majority-Vote Ensembles: The Sum of Many Weak Models

1. The problem

Suppose there is a classifier with 60% accuracy. If n mutually independent classifiers solve the same problem and the answer is decided by majority vote, what is the accuracy? (We take n to be odd to avoid ties.)

In Chapter 4 we wrote the probability of k heads in n coin tosses as C(n,k)pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ. If we read “heads” here as “this classifier gets it right,” we get the same expression. The number X of classifiers that get it right follows B(n, p), and for the majority vote to be correct, X must exceed n/2.

P(\text{majority correct}) = P\bigl(X \ge \tfrac{n+1}{2}\bigr) = \sum_{k=(n+1)/2}^{n} \binom{n}{k}\,p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}

P(majority correct) = P(X ≥ (n+1)/2) = ∑ₖ₌₍ₙ₊₁₎/₂ⁿ C(n,k) pᵏ (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ

2. Working it out

With p = 0.6 and n = 3, the majority is correct when at least 2 are right, so 3·0.6²·0.4 + 0.6³ = 0.432 + 0.216 = 0.648. The 60% rose to 64.8%. For other n and other p, the values are as follows.

  • Even if p is only slightly above 1/2, adding models raises the accuracy without limit. Even with p = 0.55, 501 models give 98.8%.

  • If p is below 1/2, it is the reverse. The more 45% classifiers you gather, the worse it gets, and at 501 only 1.2% are correct. Majority voting merely amplifies the direction of the individual models’ bias, whether it is toward being right or toward being wrong.

3. How many are needed

To reach 99% or more, p = 0.6 needs 133 (odd), and p = 0.7 needs 31. When the individual accuracy rises by 10 percentage points, the number needed drops to below a quarter. This number can also be estimated with the normal approximation (Proof A-1, Claim 4).

n \gtrsim \frac{z^{2}\,p(1-p)}{(p-1/2)^{2}}, \qquad z=2.326 \ (\text{wrong-answer probability } 1\%)

n ≳ z² · p(1−p) / (p − ½)²,    z = 2.326 (wrong-answer probability 1%)

  • The standard normal value corresponding to a wrong-answer probability of 1% is z = 2.326, so z² = 5.41.

  • With p = 0.6, 5.41 × 0.24 / 0.01 ≈ 130, and with p = 0.7, 5.41 × 0.21 / 0.04 ≈ 28. The exact values 133 and 31 are a little larger than the estimates because the number must be chosen odd and because the binomial distribution takes only integer values.

  • The number needed is inversely proportional to (p − ½)². If the distance from 1/2 doubles, the number becomes a quarter.

  • As p approaches 1/2, the number explodes. With p = 0.51, 5.41 × 0.2499 / 0.0001 ≈ 13,500 are needed.

4. What Chapters 6 and 13 do

With n = 101 and p = 0.6, the mean is np = 60.6 and the standard deviation is √(npq) = √24.24 ≈ 4.92. For the majority to be correct, X ≥ 51, and using the continuity correction (Chapter 6) the boundary is 50.5. Then z = (50.5 − 60.6)/4.92 ≈ −2.05, and the normal approximation gives about 97.99%. This agrees with the exact value 97.91% to within 0.1 percentage points. The majority-vote problem is a problem of approximating the binomial distribution by a normal distribution, and as the number of models grows, the standard deviation √(npq) grows like √n while the distance n(p − 1/2) between the mean and the threshold grows like n, so the probability of being wrong shrinks rapidly.

The Hoeffding inequality of Chapter 13 gives this rate as an upper bound.

P(\text{majority wrong}) \le e^{-2n\,(p-1/2)^{2}}

P(majority wrong) ≤ e^(−2n(p−½)²)

| p = 0.6 | Exact error rate | Hoeffding bound |

| n = 101 | 2.09% | 13.3% |

| n = 501 | 0.00030% | 0.0045% |

The bound is loose, but the shape “decreases exponentially in the number of models” is the same. To guarantee an error rate of at most 1% with this bound, we need e^(−0.02n) ≤ 0.01, that is, n ≥ 230.3, so 231 models. This is far more than the 133 from the exact calculation, because the bound is crude.

  • This bound holds for every p greater than 1/2 (Proof A-1, Claim 3).

  • The reason the bound is several times larger than the exact value lies not in the exponent but in the coefficient in front. The tail of the normal approximation is e^(−a²/2) / (a√(2π)) with a = √n (p − ½) / √(pq). With p = 0.6, a²/2 = n(p − ½)²/(2pq) = 0.0208n, which is almost the same as Hoeffding’s exponent 2(p − ½)² n = 0.02n. Hoeffding discards the 1/(a√(2π)) in front.

  • At n = 101, a ≈ 2.05, so this coefficient is about 0.19, and 13.3% × 0.19 ≈ 2.5% is close to the exact value 2.09%.

  • In summary, Hoeffding is a simple and safe bound that uses only “how far p is from 1/2.” If you need the exact number, it is better to compute the binomial distribution directly or use the normal approximation.

5. The most important caveat: when independence breaks

The table above is correct only when the classifiers are mutually independent. What was said in Chapters 4 and 5, that “if independence does not hold, the binomial calculation changes,” is decisive here. If they were trained on the same data or have the same structure, they tend to be wrong together on the same problems.

We set up the simplest hypothetical model. For each problem, with probability ρ all models give the same result (together right or together wrong, according to the probability p = 0.6 of being right), and with probability 1−ρ they are solved independently of each other. In this model, the majority-vote accuracy is as follows.

| 0.25 | 60.0% | 66.2% | 76.9% | 88.4% | 90.0% | 90% |

| 0.5 | 60.0% | 64.1% | 71.3% | 79.0% | 80.0% | 80% |

| 0.75 | 60.0% | 62.1% | 65.6% | 69.5% | 70.0% | 70% |

The limit is determined by ρp + (1−ρ) (Proof A-1). However many models there are, the part where they are wrong in common is not erased, and that part becomes the ceiling. That is why, for ensembles, it is said that the degree to which models make different mistakes (diversity) matters more than the number of models.

6. Checking with code

from math import comb

def majority(n, p):
    """Accuracy of a majority vote of n (odd) independent classifiers, each with accuracy p."""
    return sum(comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k) for k in range(n // 2 + 1, n + 1))

for n in (1, 5, 21, 101):
    print(n, f"{majority(n, 0.6) * 100:.2f}%")

# A toy model with a common-mistake rate rho
def with_common(n, p, rho):
    return rho * p + (1 - rho) * majority(n, p)

print(with_common(101, 0.6, 0.5))   # 0.7896...

A-2. Cross-Entropy: A Model’s Loss Is a “Number of Bits”

1. What we bring from Chapter 13

In Chapter 13, among 0/1 strings of length 100, those with exactly 10 ones numbered C(100,10), and labeling them needed only log₂ C(100,10) ≈ 43.98 bits. In terms of binary entropy, this was nH(0.1) = 46.90 bits minus the 2.9-bit correction from the √ part.

H(q) = -q\log_2 q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)

H(q) = −q·log₂q − (1−q)·log₂(1−q)

H(0.1) ≈ 0.469 bits. In this chapter we go one step further. If the true probability that generated the data is p, but the model believes it to be q, how many more bits does it cost?

2. Cross-entropy and KL

If we encode a 1/0 string whose true probability is p with the model q, the average number of bits per symbol is as follows.

\mathrm{CE}(p,q) = -p\log_2 q-(1-p)\log_2(1-q), \qquad
\mathrm{CE}(p,q)=H(p)+D(p\,\|\,q)

CE(p,q) = −p·log₂q − (1−p)·log₂(1−q),    CE(p,q) = H(p) + D(p‖q)

The first is the cross-entropy, and the second, D(p‖q) ≥ 0, is the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL), the “number of bits wasted because the model is wrong.” When the true p = 0.1, the values are as follows.

| Model q | CE (bits) | Waste D = CE − H(0.1) | 2^CE |

| 0.05 | 0.4988 | 0.0298 | 1.41 |

| 0.10 (correct) | 0.4690 | 0 | 1.38 |

| 0.20 | 0.5219 | 0.0529 | 1.44 |

| 0.30 | 0.6368 | 0.1678 | 1.55 |

| 0.50 | 1.0000 | 0.5310 | 2.00 |

The value is smallest when the model is the correct q = 0.1, and grows as the model is more wrong. For a string of length 100 with 10 ones, the total number of bits needed to encode this string with q is 100·CE.

  • q = 0.1: 46.90 bits (the nH(0.1) of Chapter 13)

  • q = 0.2: 52.19 bits

  • q = 0.5: 100.00 bits (if the model has “no information,” it is 1 bit per bit, with no compression at all)

Cross-entropy of model q when the true p=0.1 (one █ ≈ 0.05 bits)

q=0.05  0.499  ██████████
q=0.10  0.469  █████████  ← minimum (correct)
q=0.20  0.522  ██████████
q=0.30  0.637  █████████████
q=0.40  0.795  ████████████████
q=0.50  1.000  ████████████████████

The bar is shortest at the correct q=0.1, and grows longer the farther we move to either side. Bits are wasted in proportion to how wrong the model is.

3. Why “the probability of one particular string” is this value

The probability of one string is a product (Chapter 4). The probability that a particular string with k ones and n−k zeros appears under the model q is qᵏ(1−q)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. The −log₂ of this probability is as follows.

-\log_2\bigl(q^{k}(1-q)^{n-k}\bigr) = n\Bigl(-\tfrac{k}{n}\log_2 q-\bigl(1-\tfrac{k}{n}\bigr)\log_2(1-q)\Bigr) = n\,\mathrm{CE}(k/n,\;q)

−log₂( qᵏ(1−q)ⁿ⁻ᵏ ) = n·( −(k/n)·log₂q − (1−k/n)·log₂(1−q) ) = n·CE(k/n, q)

That is, the cross-entropy is the −log₂ of the probability the model assigned to the entire data string, divided by the number of symbols. If we set k/n = q, qᵏ(1−q)ⁿ⁻ᵏ becomes 2^(−nH(q)), which is the expression already used in step 2 of Proof 13-5(1). It has the same root as the story in Chapter 13 that “the probability of one particular string is 2^(−nH),” and that there are about 2^(nH) such strings, so the total comes to near 1.

4. Maximum likelihood and minimizing cross-entropy are the same thing

When k ones have appeared in the data, the most common way to set the model’s q is to choose the q that makes the above probability qᵏ(1−q)ⁿ⁻ᵏ largest (maximum likelihood). Maximizing a probability is the same as minimizing −log, so by the expression in Section 3, this is the task of choosing the q that minimizes n·CE(k/n, q). Differentiating, from −p/q + (1−p)/(1−q) = 0 we get q = p = k/n (Proof A-2). The proportion counted in the data is itself the optimal model.

The phrase “reduce the model’s loss” unpacks like this. It means adjusting the model so that it gives the data the highest probability, and the value measuring that degree in bits (or in natural-log units) is the loss.

It is the same thing when there are many branches.

  • If class i appeared nᵢ times and the proportion is p̂ᵢ = nᵢ/n, the multi-branch cross-entropy of the model q is CE(p̂, q) = −Σ p̂ᵢ log qᵢ, which equals H(p̂) + D(p̂‖q).

  • Since D ≥ 0 with equality only when q = p̂, if the model can choose any probability vector, the maximum-likelihood answer is q = (nᵢ/n), the counted proportions as they are (Proof A-2, (2) and (6)).

  • Real models have a restricted range of probabilities they can express, so the task becomes choosing the model with the smallest CE within that range.

  • With two branches, this is the same result as the earlier q = k/n.

5. With several branches, and perplexity

Suppose there are 4 symbols and the true probabilities are (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8). The entropy is as follows.

H = 0.5·1 + 0.25·2 + 0.125·3 + 0.125·3 = 1.75 bits

We compare two models.

| Model | Probabilities | CE | KL (waste) | 2^CE |

| True | (0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125) | 1.7500 | 0 | 3.36 |

| Uniform | (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) | 2.0000 | 0.2500 | 4.00 |

| Slightly off | (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) | 1.8007 | 0.0507 | 3.48 |

The last column, 2^CE, is the perplexity. We read it as “how many equally plausible candidates the model, on average, wavers among as if choosing.” The uniform model is in effect choosing among 4 (4.00), and the model that knows the true probabilities shrinks to 3.36. For a die (6 faces), the uniform model’s cross-entropy is log₂6 = 2.585 bits and its perplexity is exactly 6. If the cross-entropy falls by 1 bit, the perplexity is halved (3 bits → 8, 2 bits → 4, 1 bit → 2).

6. Softmax is the probability of a multinomial distribution

In Chapter 11 we wrote the probability for three or more branches as the multinomial distribution. The function by which a classifier produces a score (logit) z for each class and converts it into probabilities is the softmax.

p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}

pᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / ∑ⱼ e^(zⱼ)

These p’s correspond to p_A, p_B, p_C, … of the multinomial distribution in Chapter 11. If class i appeared nᵢ times in the data, the multinomial probability is n!/(n₁!n₂!…) · Πpᵢ^(nᵢ). The leading multinomial coefficient is independent of the model, so choosing the model is the task of making Πpᵢ^(nᵢ) large, that is, making −Σ nᵢ log pᵢ small. This is the multi-branch cross-entropy.

For example, if the logits are (2, 1, 0), the softmax output is (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), and when the correct answer is the first class the loss is −log₂ 0.665 = 0.588 bits (0.408 in natural log). If the correct answer had been the third class, it would be −log₂ 0.090 = 3.47 bits, nearly 6 times larger. It is a property of the log loss that a large penalty is attached to being confident and wrong.

If we put a “temperature” T into the softmax and change it to e^(zᵢ/T), the probabilities change.

| Temperature T | Probabilities (z = 2, 1, 0) |

| 0.5 | (0.867, 0.117, 0.016) |

| 1 | (0.665, 0.245, 0.090) |

| 2 | (0.506, 0.307, 0.186) |

When T is small, the probability concentrates on the first place (the distribution becomes sharp), and when T is large, it flattens. This is the same sense as Chapter 6’s “the larger the variance, the wider the bell spreads.”

Softmax probabilities (logits z = 2, 1, 0 / one █ ≈ 2%)

T=0.5
  1st  86.7%  ███████████████████████████████████████████
  2nd  11.7%  ██████
  3rd   1.6%  █

T=1  
  1st  66.5%  █████████████████████████████████
  2nd  24.5%  ████████████
  3rd   9.0%  ████

T=2  
  1st  50.6%  █████████████████████████
  2nd  30.7%  ███████████████
  3rd  18.6%  █████████

When T is small it concentrates on the first place and becomes sharp, and when T is large it flattens.

p_i(T)=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i}=\frac{p_i(T)-\mathbf 1[i=y]}{T}

pᵢ(T) = e^(zᵢ/T) / ∑ⱼ e^(zⱼ/T),    ∂L/∂zᵢ = ( pᵢ(T) − 1[i=y] ) / T

  • As T → 0, the probability of the class with the largest score goes to 1 and the others go to 0 (argmax, keeping only the maximum). T = 0.5 in the table above is a picture of going one step in that direction.

  • As T → ∞, all probabilities go to 1/K (K is the number of classes) and the distribution becomes uniform. In this case the cross-entropy is log₂K and the perplexity is K (the uniform model in Section 5 above).

  • The gradient is multiplied by 1/T, so for the same error, the smaller T is, the larger the gradient (Proof A-2, (5)).

  • Where and how T ≠ 1 is used in real systems is not covered in this section.

The gradient of the cross-entropy with respect to the logits is surprisingly simple. If the correct class is y, then ∂loss/∂zᵢ = pᵢ − 1[i = y] (Proof A-2). “The probability the model gave, minus the correct answer (1 or 0)” is itself the gradient.

7. Units and cautions

  • Bits and natural-log units: If the base of the logarithm is 2 the unit is bits, and if it is e the unit is natural-log units (nats). 1 bit = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 nat. 2 bits = 1.386 nat, and the perplexity 2² = e^1.386 = 4 is the same. The loss values of many libraries are in natural-log terms, so a conversion is needed when comparing with bit values.

  • Different symbol units cannot be compared: Since it is an average “per symbol,” it is known that the losses of a model split into characters and a model split into words cannot be compared directly. If we measure the total number of bits on the same string, they can be compared.

  • A low loss does not mean usefulness: Cross-entropy measures only “how well it assigns probability to the data.” Whether a response is useful is a separate matter.

8. Connection with compression

This connects in one line with the story of 13-4. The better a model predicts the data (the lower the cross-entropy), the shorter a bit string it can encode the same data with. In the string above, the difference between 0.469 bits per bit (q = 0.1) and 1 bit (q = 0.5) is the difference in compression rate. The saying “good prediction is good compression” is contained in this one table. Shannon’s source coding theorem says that this value is the limit, and this book omits its proof (the same as 13-4).

9. Try it yourself

  1. With true p = 0.2 and model q = 0.4, find CE(p, q) and the waste D in bits. (Use H(0.2) = 0.7219 bits.)

  2. What is the difference in cross-entropy, in bits, between a model with perplexity 8 and one with perplexity 4?

  3. When the logits are (4, 2, 0), the softmax output is (0.867, 0.117, 0.016). Find the loss in bits when the correct answer is the first class and when it is the third.

Things to think about: The cross-entropy of the model q = 0.5 (knowing nothing) is exactly 1 bit whatever the true p is. Why is it independent of p?

A-3. Statistics of Model Evaluation: How to Read “85% Accuracy”

This section transfers all of Chapter 9 to model comparison. If a model gets x of n test questions right, x is binomial (Chapter 4), and the error of the accuracy p̂ = x/n is the margin of error of Chapter 9.

1. One model’s accuracy: the margin of error

When a model gets 85% right, the 95% margin of error (Wald, Chapter 9) is 1.96·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n).

| Number of questions n | Wald ± error | Wilson 95% interval |

| 100 | ±7.0 pp | 76.7% ~ 90.7% |

| 500 | ±3.1 pp | 81.6% ~ 87.9% |

| 1000 | ±2.2 pp | 82.7% ~ 87.1% |

| 5000 | ±1.0 pp | 84.0% ~ 86.0% |

| 10000 | ±0.7 pp | 84.3% ~ 85.7% |

(pp = percentage points.) An 85% on a 100-question test means “anything between 76.7% and 90.7% is possible.” As in Chapter 9, the number of questions must be quadrupled to halve the error (1000 → 5000 is a factor of 5, so the error shrinks by √5 ≈ 2.2 times, from 2.2 to 1.0).

Wilson 95% interval for 85% accuracy (one cell = 0.5 pp, ● = 85%)

n=  100      ├────────────────●──────────┤    76.7~90.7%
n=  500                ├──────●─────┤    81.6~87.9%
n= 1000                  ├────●───┤    82.7~87.1%
n= 5000                     ├─●─┤    84.0~86.0%
n=10000                      ├●┤    84.3~85.7%
        74%                   85%         91%

As the number of questions grows, the interval narrows around 85%. With 100 questions the interval is 14 pp wide, and with 10000 questions it is 1.4 pp.

The Wilson interval in the table is computed by the following expression (Proof A-6).

\frac{\hat p+\dfrac{z^{2}}{2n}\ \pm\ z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}+\dfrac{z^{2}}{4n^{2}}}}{1+\dfrac{z^{2}}{n}}, \qquad z=1.96

( p̂ + z²/(2n) ± z·√( p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²) ) ) / ( 1 + z²/n ),    z = 1.96

  • This expression is obtained by solving for p the inequality “p̂ is within 1.96 standard errors of the true p.” Wald puts the observed value p̂ into the standard error, while Wilson leaves the true p as it is before solving.

  • The center of the interval is not p̂ but the weighted average of p̂ and 1/2, n/(n + z²)·p̂ + z²/(n + z²)·½. When n is small, it is pulled toward 1/2.

  • As n grows, it approaches Wald. At n = 10000 the two intervals agree to the first decimal place (84.3% ~ 85.7%).

  • The interval always lies between 0 and 1, and even if the number correct is 0 or n, the width does not become 0. For a model that got all 20 questions right, the Wald interval is [100%, 100%] but the Wilson interval is [83.9%, 100%]. This is because the lower bound is n/(n + z²) = 20/23.84.

  • The literature assesses that the actual coverage probability of the Wilson interval is close to 95% even for small n or when p̂ is near 0 or 1, and that it is better than Wald (see the references).

2. The score difference between two models: independent comparison

Suppose model A scored 85.0% and model B scored 86.0% on 1000 questions. Could the 1 pp difference be chance? The calculation is exactly that of Chapter 9, Section 4 (A/B testing). If we regard the two scores as independent of each other, the standard error of the difference is 1.57 pp, z = 0.64, and the p-value is 0.53. It is a difference that could easily arise by chance. We compare the following in the same way.

| Scores | Number of questions | Difference | z | p-value |

| 85.0% vs 86.0% | 1000 | 1 pp | 0.64 | 0.525 |

| 85.0% vs 88.0% | 1000 | 3 pp | 1.96 | 0.0496 |

| 85.0% vs 86.0% | 10000 | 1 pp | 2.01 | 0.0446 |

A 3 pp difference sits just inside the 5% line with p-value 0.0496, exactly like the 12% vs 15% example of Chapter 9. To pick out a 1 pp difference, 10 times as many questions are needed.

3. Two models that solved the same problems: the paired comparison

There is an important correction here. If the two models solved the same 1000 questions, the two scores are not independent. This is because both get the easy questions right and both get the hard questions wrong. In such a case we divide the questions into four kinds.

  • Both right, both wrong: these do not create a difference, so we discard them.

  • Only A right (b questions), only B right (c questions): we look only at these discordant questions.

If the two models are equally skilled, then on a discordant question each is equally likely, with probability 1/2, to be the one that gets it right. Therefore, in b + c trials, the number of times c that B wins follows the binomial distribution B(b+c, 1/2) of tossing a fair coin. This is the sign test (binomial test) of Chapter 9, and has the same structure as the p-value table for 10 coin tosses (Chapter 9, Section 3).

We compare hypothetical examples. All are on 1000 questions.

| Discordant (A only, B only) | Score difference | Exact binomial test p-value |

| (40, 50) | 1.0 pp | 0.343 |

| (30, 60) | 3.0 pp | 0.0021 |

| (20, 45) | 2.5 pp | 0.0026 |

| (100, 130) | 3.0 pp | 0.056 |

In the case (30, 60), B is higher by 3.0 pp, and among the 90 discordant questions B won 60. By the normal approximation z = (60 − 45)/√(90/4) = 3.16 (3.06 with the correction), and the exact p-value is 0.0021. In Section 2 above, the same 3 pp difference had p = 0.0496 as an independent comparison, but viewed as a pair it becomes 0.0021, more than 20 times more certain. Conversely, in the last row (100, 130) the difference is the same 3.0 pp, but the discordant questions are numerous at 230, so the p-value is 0.056. Even for the same score difference, the fewer the discordant questions, the more trustworthy the difference.

p-value for the same 3 pp difference: independent vs paired comparison (bar = −log₁₀ p-value, one █ ≈ 0.1)

Independent   p=0.0496 █████████████  (1.3)
Paired        p=0.0021 ███████████████████████████  (2.7)
(1.3 is the 5% line)

The score difference is the same, but the bar lengths differ by more than a factor of two. For two models that solved the same test, comparing them as a pair is far sharper.

The practical conclusion is this. When comparing two models on the same test, instead of just placing the scores side by side, it is far sharper to pair the question-by-question results and compare on the discordant questions.

This test has a name, the McNemar test. When the discordant questions are numerous enough, the following statistic can be used instead of the binomial test (Proof A-3).

\chi^{2}=\frac{(b-c)^{2}}{b+c}, \qquad \chi^{2}_{\text{corrected}}=\frac{(|b-c|-1)^{2}}{b+c}

χ² = (b − c)² / (b + c),    χ²(corrected) = ( |b − c| − 1 )² / (b + c)

  • χ² follows the chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom, and the 5% threshold is χ² > 3.84 (= 1.96²). This is the square of the normal-approximation z of the binomial distribution.

  • For (30, 60), χ² = 900/90 = 10.0 (p = 0.0016), the corrected version is 29²/90 = 9.34 (p = 0.0022), and the exact binomial test gives 0.0021. With 90 discordant questions the three values are nearly the same.

  • When the discordant questions are few (roughly b + c < 25), the chi-square approximation is hard to trust. For (12, 4), the exact p-value is 0.077, but the uncorrected χ² = 4.0 gives p = 0.046, so the conclusions split.

  • Simulations report that the exact binomial test and the corrected version are somewhat conservative, and some of the literature recommends the mid-p test, which subtracts only half the probability of the observed value from the exact p-value. The mid-p for (30, 60) is 0.0015.

  • The information content of this test is not the total number of questions but the number of discordant questions. However many questions there are, if the two models give nearly the same answers, b + c is small and the power is low.

4. If you build many models and pick the best

In Chapter 9, Section 5 we said that “if you test 20 fair coins at the 5% criterion, the probability that at least one is judged a strange coin is 64%.” In model comparison, this appears as follows.

(a) If you run the test k times: When all the models are equally skilled, the probability that at least one comes out as a “significant improvement” in a test at the 5% criterion is 1 − 0.95ᵏ.

| Number of models compared k | 5 | 10 | 20 | 100 |

| Probability that at least one looks significant | 22.6% | 40.1% | 64.2% | 99.4% |

(b) If you pick the best score: This one is more vivid. Build k models whose true accuracy is all the same 80%, test them on the same 1000 questions, and report the highest score. The standard deviation of an individual score is √(0.8·0.2/1000) = 1.26 pp, so the mean of that maximum is inflated as follows (mean of 4000 simulations).

| Number of models k | 1 | 5 | 20 | 100 | 1000 |

| Mean of the reported best score | 80.0% | 81.5% | 82.3% | 83.1% | 84.0% |

Although there is no difference in skill at all, if you build 100 and pick the best, it comes out higher by more than 3 pp on average. This is selection bias, and it has the same structure as the way that repeatedly choosing settings with the same test set ends up over-fitting to that test set. “The best score usually drops when measured again on the same test” is a mathematically expected result.

Inflation of the best score among k equally skilled models (one █ ≈ 0.2 pp, ▒ = upper bound)

k=   1 simulation +0.0pp  ·
       bound      +0.0pp  ·
k=   5 simulation +1.5pp  ████████
       bound      +2.3pp  ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒
k=  20 simulation +2.3pp  ███████████
       bound      +3.1pp  ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒
k= 100 simulation +3.1pp  ████████████████
       bound      +3.8pp  ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒
k=1000 simulation +4.0pp  ████████████████████
       bound      +4.7pp  ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒

Even if we increase the number of models tenfold, the bar only lengthens a little at a time (√ ln k). Even so, merely by choosing among equally skilled models, the inflation keeps accumulating.

(c) What to do: The simplest thing is to make the criterion stricter. When comparing k times, there is a method of lowering each test’s criterion to 5%/k (the Bonferroni correction), which is 0.25% for k = 20. More fundamentally, separate the data used for choosing from the data used for measuring the final score.

(d) An upper bound on the inflation: The mean of the maximum of k standard normal variables has the following upper bound (Proof A-4).

\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_{i\le k} Z_i\bigr]\le\sqrt{2\ln k}

E[ max Zᵢ ] ≤ √(2 ln k)

  • This upper bound holds even if the Zᵢ are not independent of each other. Even if the scores of models using the same test set are correlated with each other, it remains an upper bound as it is.

  • If the standard deviation of an individual score is 1.26 pp, then for k = 5, 20, 100, 1000 the upper bounds are 2.3, 3.1, 3.8, 4.7 pp respectively, and the simulated 1.5, 2.3, 3.1, 4.0 pp above are all below them.

  • The upper bound grows slowly like √(ln k). Even if the models are increased tenfold from 100 to 1000, the upper bound rises only 22%, from 3.8 pp to 4.7 pp. The more candidates are added, the more the inflation keeps growing, but the rate is slow.

5. The number of questions needed

To pick out a 1 pp difference (85% vs 86%) by independent comparison at the 5% significance level with 80% probability, about 19,458 questions per model are needed.

n \approx \frac{(1.96+0.84)^{2}\,\bigl(p_1q_1+p_2q_2\bigr)}{(p_2-p_1)^{2}}

n ≈ (1.96 + 0.84)² · (p₁q₁ + p₂q₂) / (p₂ − p₁)²

0.84 is the value of the normal distribution corresponding to the power of “catching the difference with 80% probability.” If the difference halves, the number of questions needed is 4 times. This is the same √ law as in Chapter 9, where we said that to halve the error, the sample must be 4 times larger. If we compare as a pair, as in item 3 of the previous section, the number of questions needed is reduced from this.

  • This expression solves for n the condition “the difference δ = p₂ − p₁ must be at least (z_α/2 + z_β) times the standard error to be rejected with 80% probability” (Proof A-7).

  • z_α/2 = 1.96 corresponds to the 5% significance level (two-sided), and z_β = 0.84 to the power of 80%. Using the exact values 1.959964 and 0.841621 gives about 19,457.4, which rounds up to 19,458 questions. Using the rounded 2.80 gives 19,435 questions. Either way the conclusion is “about 19,000 questions.”

  • Raising the power to 90% (z_β = 1.2816) makes the number of questions about 1.34 times larger, around 26,000.

  • When comparing as a pair on the same test, the key is the proportion π_d of questions on which the two models answer differently, and the number of questions needed is as follows (Proof A-7).

n \approx \frac{\bigl(z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\pi_d}+z_{\beta}\sqrt{\pi_d-\delta^{2}}\bigr)^{2}}{\delta^{2}}

n ≈ ( zα/2·√π_d + zβ·√(π_d − δ²) )² / δ²

  • With π_d = 9% and δ = 3 pp, about 783 questions suffice for the paired comparison. Under the same conditions (85% vs 88%), the independent comparison needs about 2,033 questions.

  • π_d is not known before the test, so it must be assumed from a pilot test or from the value for a similar model. If the assumption is wrong the result also changes, so read it only as a rough scale.

6. What this calculation cannot capture

The “what numbers do not tell you” of Chapter 9, Section 5 applies as it stands.

  • The assumption that the questions are independent of one another is not fully met. If many questions of a similar type are included, or if questions are derived from the same material, the actual error is larger than in the table above.

  • If the test questions overlap with material the model has seen, the score is inflated. The margin of error cannot capture such bias.

  • If the model’s output is stochastic (it answers the same question differently each time), then even re-measuring the same model changes the score, which is yet another source of fluctuation.

  • “Significant” and “large enough to be useful” are different. A 0.5 pp difference on 10000 questions may be significant, but usefulness is a separate judgment.

7. Checking with code

import numpy as np
from math import comb

# (1) Mean of the best score among k models of equal skill (80%)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for k in (1, 5, 20, 100):
    best = rng.binomial(1000, 0.8, size=(4000, k)).max(axis=1) / 1000
    print(k, f"{best.mean() * 100:.2f}%")

# (2) Paired comparison: exact binomial test (two-sided) on discordant questions b, c
def paired_p(b, c):
    n, k = b + c, min(b, c)
    return min(1.0, 2 * sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(k + 1)) / 2**n)

print(paired_p(30, 60))   # 0.00206
print(paired_p(100, 130)) # 0.0556

A-4. Mini-Batches and the √ Law

When training a neural network, instead of computing the gradient (the direction in which the loss decreases) from the entire dataset, we use the mini-batch gradient, obtained by drawing B items from the data and averaging. This value is an estimate of the true gradient, and it behaves exactly like the sample mean of Chapter 8.

  • If each sample’s gradient has mean μ and variance σ² and the samples are independent, the average of B has mean μ and variance σ²/B (Proof 8-2).

  • Therefore the noise (standard deviation) shrinks to σ/√B. This is the same expression as Chapter 9’s “with 4 times the sample, half the error.”

| Batch size B | 1 | 4 | 16 | 64 | 256 | 1024 |

| Noise size (relative to B=1) | 1 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 0.125 | 0.0625 | 0.031 |

The batch must be enlarged 1024 times for the noise to become 1/32. The computation grows in proportion to B but the noise shrinks only as √B, so the larger the batch, the smaller the gain (diminishing returns). The law of large numbers tells us “where it gathers,” and the central limit theorem tells us that “the shape of the noise is normal.”

This calculation rests on the assumption that the samples are independent of one another. If the samples in a batch are similar to one another (the correlation ρ of A-1), the variance becomes σ²(ρ + (1−ρ)/B), which has a floor (ρσ²), so enlarging the batch no longer reduces it (Proof A-1). When choosing the batch size, other factors such as the learning rate are also entangled, but this section does not deal with them.

Taking correlation ρ = 0.1 as an example, we compute the size of the noise σ·√(ρ + (1−ρ)/B) (Proof A-8).

  • With B = 1 it is 1.000σ, with B = 9 it is 0.447σ, with B = 64 it is 0.338σ, with B = 1024 it is 0.318σ, and as B → ∞ it is √ρ·σ = 0.316σ.

  • If independent, it goes down to 0.125σ at B = 64 and 0.031σ at B = 1024. With correlation there is a floor, so even if B is enlarged 16 times from 64 to 1024, it falls only about 6%, from 0.338σ to 0.318σ.

  • The point where the gain begins to vanish is B* = (1−ρ)/ρ = 9, where the two terms ρ and (1−ρ)/B become equal. Once B exceeds a few multiples of B*, it is already close to the floor.

  • The smaller ρ is, the larger B* becomes, so the √B law holds for longer. With ρ = 0.01, B* = 99.

  • Setting ρ as a single number is a toy model. The correlation between real sample gradients is not determined in this way.
