A-5. Hash Collisions and Bloom Filters: Where the Poisson Goes to Work

1. The birthday problem and hash collisions

When n items are placed at random into a space of m hash values, we look at the probability that a collision occurs, in which some two items fall into the same slot. There are C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2 distinct pairs, and each pair collides with probability 1/m. The number of colliding pairs is “the number of times a rare event happens in many trials,” so the Poisson approximation of Chapter 7 can be used, and the mean is λ = n(n−1)/(2m).

P(\text{no collision}) \approx e^{-\lambda}, \qquad \lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}

P(no collision) ≈ e^(−λ),    λ = n(n−1)/(2m)

In the 365-day birthday problem, with n = 23, λ = 253/365 = 0.693 (= ln 2), and the probability of a collision is 1 − e^(−0.693) = 50.0%. The exact value is 50.7%. The n at which the collision probability reaches half is estimated by √(2m ln 2), which is 22.5 for 365. The Poisson approximation tells us exactly the scale of this √.

n=20   41.1%  █████████████████████
n=23   50.7%  █████████████████████████  ← first exceeds 50%

With 23 people it has already passed half, and with 60 it becomes nearly certain. It is the same shape as hash collisions beginning at the √ scale of the space.

Applying the same expression to hash spaces gives the following.

| Hash size | Number of items | Probability of at least one collision | Number of items for 50% collision probability |

| 32 bits (m = 2³²) | 100,000 | 68.8% | about 77,000 |

| 64 bits (m = 2⁶⁴) | 1 billion | about 2.7% | about 5 billion |

With 32 bits, the probability of a collision is already half at a mere 77,000 items. The key point is that collisions arise at the scale of the square root of the space. With 64 bits, even if a billion are inserted, the collision probability is below 3%.

  • The Poisson approximation is always wrong in one direction. The probability of no collisions is (1 − 1/m)(1 − 2/m)…(1 − (n−1)/m), and since 1 − x ≤ e^(−x), this product is always less than or equal to e^(−λ) (Proof A-9).

P(\text{no collision})=\Bigl(1-\frac1m\Bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac2m\Bigr)\cdots\Bigl(1-\frac{n-1}{m}\Bigr)\le e^{-\lambda}

P(no collision) = (1 − 1/m)(1 − 2/m)…(1 − (n−1)/m) ≤ e^(−λ)

  • Therefore the collision probability is at least 1 − e^(−λ). For 365 days, the exact value 50.73% is larger than the approximation 50.0%.

  • The n at which the collision probability is half is the positive solution of n(n−1) = 2m ln 2, n = ½ + √(¼ + 2m ln 2) ≈ ½ + √(2m ln 2). For 365 it is 0.5 + 22.49 ≈ 23, the same as the actual answer.

  • If the hash space becomes 2^b times larger, the number of items needed grows only 2^(b/2) times. Going from 32 bits to 64 bits, the space becomes 2³² times as large and the number of items 2¹⁶ = 65,536 times (about 77,000 → about 5 billion).

2. Bloom filters: a data structure that designs its probability of being wrong

A Bloom filter is a structure that answers “have we seen this item before?” with little memory. It starts with m bits all 0, and when an item is inserted it changes the bits at k hash positions to 1. When checking, it answers “present” if all k positions are 1. If an item that is not present happens to have all k positions at 1, that is a false positive (it never says an item that is present is absent).

After n items are inserted, the probability that a given bit is still 0 is (1 − 1/m)^(kn), which for large m is e^(−kn/m). This is exactly the limit (1 − λ/N)^N → e^(−λ) proved in Chapter 7. Since the probability that a bit is 1 is 1 − e^(−kn/m), the probability of a false positive is as follows.

P(\text{false positive}) \approx \bigl(1-e^{-kn/m}\bigr)^{k}

P(false positive) ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))ᵏ

We compare the case m = 1000 bits and n = 100 items (that is, 1/10 of an item per bit).

| Number of hashes k | Fraction of bits that are 1 | False positive probability |

| 3 | 25.9% | 1.74% |

| 7 | 50.3% | 0.82% |

| 10 | 63.2% | 1.02% |

If k is too small, there are few positions, so a chance match is easy; if k is too large, the bits fill up with 1’s and it is also wrong. The optimal k is the point where half the bits are 1, k = (m/n)·ln 2 ≈ 0.693·m/n (Proof A-5). At the optimum the false positive probability is 0.6185^(m/n).

| Bits per item m/n | 5 | 8 | 10 | 16 |

| False positive probability at the optimum | 9.05% | 2.14% | 0.82% | 0.046% |

Each time about 5 more bits per item are used, the false positives fall by roughly one order of magnitude. The advantage of this structure is that one can first decide “how wrong is acceptable” and then compute the memory. The table above was computed with the e approximation. The values of (1 − (1 − 1/m)^(kn))^k and the e approximation agreed to within 0.005 pp in all the rows above. However, these expressions all carry the assumption that “the events that each bit is 1 are independent of one another,” so they are not strictly exact values.

  • In reality they are not independent. In a filter where the total number of 1 bits is large, the entanglement is such that other bits are also more likely to be 1. This point was noted by Bose et al. (2008) and refined again by Christensen et al. (2010).

  • The classical expression underestimates the actual value. The probability that all k positions of a queried item are 1 is the expectation E[Xᵏ] of the k-th power of the fraction X of 1 bits, while the classical expression is (E X)ᵏ. Since xᵏ (k ≥ 2) is convex, Jensen’s inequality gives E[Xᵏ] ≥ (E X)ᵏ (Proof A-9).

  • In large filters X is strongly concentrated near its mean, so the difference is small. For m = 1000, n = 100, computing directly while taking into account the distribution of the number of 1 bits gives 1.75%, 0.83%, 1.03% at k = 3, 7, 10, which is higher than the table’s 1.74%, 0.82%, 1.02% by around 0.01 pp (0.3 to 1.4% in relative terms).

  • In small filters the difference is noticeable. For m = 64, n = 8, k = 4, against the classical expression’s 2.40% the directly computed value is 2.54%, about 6% higher. In an extreme example, for m = 8, n = 2, k = 2 they are 15.5% and 17.8%.

  • The Bloom filter tables in this section are all classical-expression values, so for a small filter, or when the exact value is needed, it is safer to compute directly with the code below.

From a target false positive probability ε, the number of bits per item can also be found directly (step 5 of Proof A-5).

\frac{m}{n}=\frac{\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{\ln 2}\approx 1.44\,\log_{2}\frac1\varepsilon, \qquad k_{\text{optimal}}=\log_{2}\frac1\varepsilon

m/n = log₂(1/ε) / ln 2 ≈ 1.44·log₂(1/ε),    optimal k = log₂(1/ε)

  • For ε = 1%, it is 9.59 bits per item and the optimal k is 6.64. For ε = 0.1%, 14.4 bits and k = 9.97. For ε = 10⁻⁶, 28.8 bits and k = 19.9.

  • To reduce false positives to a tenth, 1.44 × log₂10 ≈ 4.8 more bits per item are used. This is the value behind the “one order of magnitude per 5 more bits” above.

Checking with code

import numpy as np
from math import exp

def bloom_fp(m, n, k):
    """False positive probability, taking into account the distribution of the number of 1 bits (throwing kn balls into m cells)."""
    dist = np.zeros(m + 1); dist[0] = 1.0
    idx = np.arange(m + 1)
    for _ in range(n * k):
        new = dist * idx / m                         # lands in a cell that is already 1
        new[1:] += dist[:-1] * (m - idx[:-1]) / m    # lands in a new cell
        dist = new
    return float((dist * (idx / m) ** k).sum())

def bloom_classic(m, n, k):
    return (1 - exp(-k * n / m)) ** k

print(bloom_fp(1000, 100, 7), bloom_classic(1000, 100, 7))   # 0.00827 0.00819
print(bloom_fp(64, 8, 4), bloom_classic(64, 8, 4))           # 0.0254 0.0240

The Big Picture at a Glance

| Situation | Tool from the main text | Result in this section |

| Majority-vote ensemble | The tail of B(n,p), Hoeffding | If p > ½ it improves exponentially, and if p < ½ it worsens exponentially. The common-mistake rate ρ creates the ceiling ρp + (1−ρ) |

| Cross-entropy and perplexity | nH(q), multinomial distribution | Loss = the mean of the −log of the probability the model gave. The same as maximum likelihood. A 1-bit decrease halves the perplexity |

| One score | Margin of error, Wilson | 85% on 1000 questions is ±2.2 pp |

| Two scores | Comparing two proportions, binomial test | For the same test, pair the comparison to be sharp (p 0.0496 → 0.0021) |

| Building many and picking | 1 − 0.95ᵏ | The best of 100 equally skilled models is inflated by 3 pp on average |

| Mini-batch | Variance σ²/B | Noise shrinks only as √B |

| Hashing, Bloom filters | Poisson, (1 − λ/n)ⁿ → e^(−λ) | Collisions start at the √ scale of the space; optimal k = 0.693·m/n |

Additional things to remember are the following.

  • Read a single score with the Wilson interval. It can be used even when the questions are few or the score is near 100%.

  • Two models that solved the same test are compared with the McNemar test (the binomial test on discordant questions). The information content is not the total number of questions but the number of discordant questions.

  • The inflation from picking the best is bounded by s·√(2 ln k), and the criterion when comparing k times is α/k.

  • The number needed for a majority vote is proportional to pq/(p − ½)².

  • The classical expression for Bloom filters is an approximation and underestimates the actual value. The optimal k is log₂(1/ε), and the bits per item are 1.44·log₂(1/ε).

The one idea that ran through the whole main text, “count the same cases once all together and once by type,” keeps working in these chapters as well. Writing a model’s probability as a product (Chapter 4), taking the logarithm to turn it into a sum (Chapter 13), and reading the mean and spread of the sum with the normal distribution (Chapters 6 and 8) is the thread connecting every part of this section.

Proof Notes

Proof A-1. The ensemble ceiling and the variance of a correlated average

Claim 1: If for each problem, with probability ρ all models give the same result (with probability p > 1/2 of being right), and with probability 1−ρ they are mutually independent, then as n → ∞ the accuracy of the majority vote is ρp + (1−ρ).

Proof

  1. On a single problem, if the “common mode” occurs (probability ρ), all models give the same answer, so the majority vote is also that answer. The probability that this answer is correct is p, so the accuracy in this case is p.

  2. In the “independent mode” (probability 1−ρ), the binomial calculation of A-1 applies, and if p > 1/2, by the Hoeffding bound (Claim 3 below) the error rate is e^(−2n(p−1/2)²) → 0. The accuracy goes to 1.

  3. The two cases do not overlap and leave nothing out (T2), so the accuracy is ρ·p + (1−ρ)·(the accuracy of the independent mode) → ρp + (1−ρ). ∎

(This bound extends the p = 1/2 case of Proof 13-5 in the main text to general p, and is proved in Claim 3 below.)

Checking with numbers: With ρ = 0.5, p = 0.6, 0.5·0.6 + 0.5 = 0.8 (the limit 80% in the table). With ρ = 0.25, 0.15 + 0.75 = 0.90, and with ρ = 0.75, 0.45 + 0.25 = 0.70 ✓.

Claim 2: If X₁, …, Xₙ all have variance σ² and mutual correlation coefficient ρ, then the variance of the mean X̄ is σ²(ρ + (1−ρ)/n).

Proof: Var(ΣXᵢ) = Σ Var(Xᵢ) + Σ_{i≠j} Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) = nσ² + n(n−1)ρσ². (This is the same calculation as adding the covariances in Proof 11-4.) Dividing by n², σ²[1/n + (n−1)ρ/n] = σ²[ρ + (1−ρ)/n]. ∎

As n → ∞, ρσ² remains, and with ρ = 0 it is σ²/n (Proof 8-2).

Claim 3 (Hoeffding bound, general p): If X₁, …, Xₙ are independent, each 1 (right) with probability p and 0 with probability 1−p, and p > 1/2, then P(majority wrong) = P(ΣXᵢ ≤ (n−1)/2) ≤ e^(−2n(p−1/2)²).

Proof

  1. The event of being wrong, {ΣXᵢ ≤ (n−1)/2}, is contained in {ΣXᵢ ≤ n/2}. Setting a = p − 1/2 > 0, since Σ(p − Xᵢ) = np − ΣXᵢ, this event is the same as Σ(p − Xᵢ) ≥ na.

  2. For s > 0, apply Markov’s inequality (for non-negative W, P(W ≥ w) ≤ E[W]/w) to W = e^(sΣ(p−Xᵢ)). P(Σ(p − Xᵢ) ≥ na) ≤ e^(−sna)·E[e^(sΣ(p−Xᵢ))].

  3. Since the Xᵢ are independent, the expectation splits into a product. E[e^(sΣ(p−Xᵢ))] = (E[e^(s(p−X₁))])ⁿ.

  4. Lemma (the Bernoulli version of Hoeffding): E[e^(s(p−X))] ≤ e^(s²/8). Proof: Put t = −s and let ψ(t) = ln E[e^(t(X−p))] = −pt + ln(1 − p + pe^t). Then ψ(0) = 0 and ψ′(t) = −p + pe^t/(1 − p + pe^t), so ψ′(0) = 0. Letting u = pe^t/(1 − p + pe^t), we have 0 < u < 1 and ψ″(t) = u(1−u) ≤ 1/4 (the maximum of u(1−u) is 1/4 at u = 1/2). The Taylor expansion with the Lagrange remainder, ψ(t) = ψ(0) + ψ′(0)t + ψ″(ξ)t²/2 ≤ t²/8, gives the lemma.

  5. Putting 3 and 4 into 2, P ≤ exp(−sna + ns²/8). The exponent is quadratic in s, and from the derivative −na + ns/4 = 0 it is minimized at s = 4a, with value −4na² + 2na² = −2na². Therefore P ≤ e^(−2na²) = e^(−2n(p−1/2)²). ∎

Checking with numbers: With p = 0.6, n = 101, e^(−2·101·0.01) = e^(−2.02) = 13.3%, the same as the table in the main text.

Claim 4 (estimate of the number needed): For p > 1/2, to bring the probability that the majority vote is wrong to ε or less, by the normal approximation n ≳ z²·pq/(p−1/2)² (z is the (1−ε) quantile of the standard normal).

Proof

  1. The number correct X is B(n, p), and by the normal approximation of Chapter 6, X ≈ N(np, npq). Being wrong means X < n/2, so the probability is Φ((n/2 − np)/√(npq)) = Φ(−√n(p − 1/2)/√(pq)).

  2. For this to be at most ε we need √n(p − 1/2)/√(pq) ≥ z, that is, n ≥ z²pq/(p − 1/2)². ∎

Checking with numbers: With ε = 1% (z = 2.326), p = 0.6, we get 129.9 (the exact odd value is 133). With ε = 10% (z = 1.2816), p = 0.51, we get 4,104.6, nearly the same as the exact value 4,105.

Proof A-2. Properties of cross-entropy

(1) Maximum likelihood: CE(p,q) is minimal at q = p

Differentiating CE(p,q) = −p log q − (1−p) log(1−q) with respect to q gives −p/q + (1−p)/(1−q). Setting this to 0 gives (1−p)q = p(1−q), that is, q = p. The second derivative p/q² + (1−p)/(1−q)² > 0, so it is a minimum. ∎

(2) Gibbs’ inequality: D(p‖q) ≥ 0

Convention: terms with pᵢ = 0 are treated as 0·log 0 = 0 and dropped from the sum. If qᵢ = 0 while pᵢ > 0, D is taken to be ∞.

  1. Write it with the natural logarithm (changing the base only multiplies by a positive constant). D(p‖q) = Σ_{pᵢ>0} pᵢ ln(pᵢ/qᵢ).

  2. Lemma: ln x ≤ x − 1 (x > 0), with equality only at x = 1. The derivative f′(x) = 1 − 1/x of f(x) = x − 1 − ln x is negative for x < 1 and positive for x > 1, so f has its minimum f(1) = 0 at x = 1.

  3. Putting in x = qᵢ/pᵢ gives ln(qᵢ/pᵢ) ≤ qᵢ/pᵢ − 1, that is, −ln(qᵢ/pᵢ) ≥ 1 − qᵢ/pᵢ.

  4. Multiplying by pᵢ > 0 and summing, D = Σ pᵢ(−ln(qᵢ/pᵢ)) ≥ Σ_{pᵢ>0}(pᵢ − qᵢ) = 1 − Σ_{pᵢ>0} qᵢ ≥ 1 − 1 = 0.

  5. Equality holds only when qᵢ = pᵢ for all i with pᵢ > 0 and Σ_{pᵢ>0} qᵢ = 1, so qᵢ is also 0 where pᵢ = 0. That is, only when q = p.

  6. CE = H + D: CE(p, q) = −Σ pᵢ log qᵢ = −Σ pᵢ log pᵢ + Σ pᵢ(log pᵢ − log qᵢ) = H(p) + D(p‖q). ∎ This gives CE ≥ H, which means that no model can encode more shortly than the entropy.

(3) The gradient of the softmax

The loss is L = −ln p_y = −z_y + ln Σⱼ e^(zⱼ). Differentiating with respect to zᵢ gives −1[i = y] + e^(zᵢ)/Σⱼ e^(zⱼ) = pᵢ − 1[i = y]. ∎ (If the logits are (2, 1, 0) and the correct answer is the first, the gradient is (0.665 − 1, 0.245, 0.090) = (−0.335, 0.245, 0.090), which sums to 0.)

(4) The code length of a string: Section 3 of A-2 is the property of the logarithm log(ab) = log a + log b applied to the product qᵏ(1−q)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. ∎

(5) The temperature of the softmax

  1. Dividing the numerator and denominator of pᵢ(T) = e^(zᵢ/T)/Σⱼ e^(zⱼ/T) by e^(z_max/T) gives pᵢ = e^((zᵢ−z_max)/T)/Σⱼ e^((zⱼ−z_max)/T).

  2. As T → 0⁺, the exponents of terms with zⱼ < z_max go to −∞ and become 0, while the term with z_max remains 1. If the maximum is unique, p_max → 1 and the rest → 0. If the maximum is shared by r entries, those r share 1/r each.

  3. As T → ∞, all exponents go to 0 and e⁰ = 1, so pᵢ → 1/K.

  4. Gradient: Differentiating L = −ln p_y = −z_y/T + ln Σⱼ e^(zⱼ/T) with respect to zᵢ gives −1[i=y]/T + e^(zᵢ/T)/(T·Σⱼ e^(zⱼ/T)) = (pᵢ(T) − 1[i=y])/T. ∎ (For z = (2, 1, 0), T = 2, p = (0.506, 0.307, 0.186), and when the correct answer is the first, the gradient is (−0.247, 0.154, 0.093).)

(6) Multi-branch maximum likelihood

  1. If class i appeared nᵢ times (Σnᵢ = n) with proportion p̂ᵢ = nᵢ/n, the mean negative log-likelihood is −(1/n) ln Πqᵢ^(nᵢ) = −Σ p̂ᵢ ln qᵢ = CE(p̂, q) (the multinomial coefficient is independent of q and does not affect the optimization).

  2. From (2), CE(p̂, q) = H(p̂) + D(p̂‖q) ≥ H(p̂), with equality only when q = p̂. Therefore if q can be chosen freely, the maximum-likelihood answer is q = p̂. ∎

Checking with numbers: CE(0.1, 0.2) = −0.1·log₂ 0.2 − 0.9·log₂ 0.8 = 0.1·2.3219 + 0.9·0.3219 = 0.2322 + 0.2897 = 0.5219 ✓. The waste 0.5219 − 0.4690 = 0.0529 ✓.

Proof A-3. Why the paired comparison is a binomial test

Setup: For question i = 1, …, n, let the results of models A and B be Aᵢ, Bᵢ ∈ {0, 1} (right = 1), and assume that (Aᵢ, Bᵢ) are independent across questions. There are a questions both got right, b questions only A got right, c questions only B got right, and d questions both got wrong.

(1) On discordant questions, a fair coin

  1. The null hypothesis “the two models have the same accuracy” is P(Aᵢ=1) = P(Bᵢ=1). Subtracting the probability of both being right from both sides gives P(only A right) = P(only B right) =: θ.

  2. Given that a question is discordant, the probability that it is “A only” is θ/(θ + θ) = 1/2.

  3. Since the questions are independent, when there are m = b + c discordant questions, c (the number of questions only B got right) follows B(m, 1/2).

  4. Adding both tails, the p-value = min(1, 2·P(X ≤ min(b, c))). For (30, 60): m = 90, 2·P(X ≤ 30) = 0.00206. ∎

(2) The normal approximation and the McNemar statistic

  1. c ~ B(m, 1/2) has mean m/2 and variance m/4, so z = (c − m/2)/√(m/4) = (2c − m)/√m.

  2. Since 2c − m = c − b, z = (c − b)/√(b + c), and squaring gives z² = (b − c)²/(b + c) = χ² (the chi-square with 1 degree of freedom is the square of a standard normal).

  3. Since the binomial distribution takes only integer values, a continuity correction that replaces |b − c| with |b − c| − 1 is also used.

  4. Numbers: (30, 60) has χ² = 10.0 (p = 0.0016), the corrected version 9.34 (p = 0.0022), the exact value 0.0021, and mid-p 0.0015 (the exact p-value minus half the probability of the observed value). (12, 4) has exact value 0.077, χ² = 4.0 (p = 0.046), and the corrected version 3.06 (p = 0.080), so when the discordant questions are few, the uncorrected version gives an overly small p-value. ∎

(3) Why it is sharper than the independent comparison

  1. Letting the per-question difference be Dᵢ = Aᵢ − Bᵢ ∈ {−1, 0, 1}, the score difference is D̄ = (1/n)ΣDᵢ.

  2. Var(D̄) = Var(D₁)/n, and Var(D₁) = E[D₁²] − (E[D₁])² is estimated as (b + c)/n − ((b − c)/n)².

  3. Under the null hypothesis (E[D₁] = 0), Var(D̄) ≈ (b + c)/n², so the standard error is √(b + c)/n. For (30, 60), √90/1000 = 0.95 pp.

  4. The standard error of the independent comparison, √(p̂_A q̂_A/n + p̂_B q̂_B/n), is what remains from Var(D̄) = [Var(A) + Var(B) − 2Cov(A, B)]/n when the covariance term is discarded. Two models that solved the same questions have Cov(A, B) > 0 (both get the easy ones right), so the discarded term is positive and the actual variance is smaller.

  5. Numbers: the standard error of the independent comparison is √(0.85·0.15/1000 + 0.88·0.12/1000) = 1.53 pp and that of the paired comparison is 0.95 pp, so the z for the same 3 pp difference grows from 1.96 to 3.16. ∎

(4) Conditions for use

  • The paired test requires the two models’ individual results on the same questions. From the scores alone, b and c cannot be known.

  • Independence between questions is required. If there is clustering, such as several questions from the same passage, the p-value becomes overly small.

Proof A-4. The size of selection bias and the Bonferroni correction

Claim 1: If Z₁, …, Z_k are each standard normal (they need not be independent of each other), then E[max Zᵢ] ≤ √(2 ln k).

Proof

  1. Let M = max Zᵢ and λ > 0. Since exp is convex, Jensen’s inequality gives e^(λE[M]) ≤ E[e^(λM)].

  2. e^(λM) = max e^(λZᵢ) ≤ Σ e^(λZᵢ) (the maximum of non-negative numbers is at most their sum), so E[e^(λM)] ≤ Σ E[e^(λZᵢ)].

  3. For a standard normal, E[e^(λZ)] = e^(λ²/2). Completing the square in the exponent, λz − z²/2 = −(z − λ)²/2 + λ²/2, the integral of the whole density becomes 1 and what remains is e^(λ²/2).

  4. Therefore e^(λE[M]) ≤ k·e^(λ²/2), that is, E[M] ≤ (ln k)/λ + λ/2.

  5. Differentiating the right side with respect to λ, −(ln k)/λ² + 1/2 = 0 gives λ = √(2 ln k), and the value is then √(2 ln k)/2 + √(2 ln k)/2 = √(2 ln k). ∎

Checking with numbers: If the standard deviation of a score is s = 1.26 pp, the inflation bound s·√(2 ln k) is 2.3, 3.1, 3.8, 4.7 pp for k = 5, 20, 100, 1000. Directly simulating the mean of the standard normal maximum gives 1.16, 1.87, 2.51, 3.24, and multiplying by 1.26 pp gives 1.5, 2.4, 3.2, 4.1 pp, which agree with the main text’s table values 1.5, 2.3, 3.1, 4.0 pp to within 0.1 pp, and all lie below the bound. That the maximum approaches √(2 ln k) when independent is known, but it is not proved here.

Claim 2 (Bonferroni): If each of k tests is run at criterion α/k, then when all the null hypotheses are true, the probability that at least one comes out significant is at most α.

Proof: Let Aᵢ be “the i-th test comes out significant,” so P(Aᵢ) ≤ α/k. The probability of a union is at most the sum of the probabilities (Boole’s inequality), so P(A₁ ∪ … ∪ A_k) ≤ ΣP(Aᵢ) ≤ k·(α/k) = α. The assumption that the tests are independent is not needed. ∎ (If independent, the exact value is 1 − (1 − α/k)^k, which is 4.88% for α = 0.05, k = 20. Without lowering the criterion it was 1 − 0.95²⁰ = 64.2%.)

Proof A-5. The optimal k of a Bloom filter

  1. The probability that a bit remains 0 is (1 − 1/m)^(kn) → e^(−kn/m). This is the same limit as (1 − λ/N)^N → e^(−λ) in Proof 7-1 of Chapter 7. Multiplying the probability 1 − e^(−kn/m) that a bit is 1 over k positions is an approximation that uses the assumption that the bits are independent (Proof A-9).

  2. Letting u = e^(−kn/m), the false positive probability is (1 − u)^k, and since k = −(m/n)ln u, ln(false positive) = −(m/n)·ln u·ln(1 − u).

  3. Let g(u) = ln u·ln(1 − u) (0 < u < 1). Then ln(false positive) = −(m/n)g(u), and since both logarithms are negative, g > 0. Minimizing the false positives is maximizing g.

  4. g′(u) = ln(1−u)/u − ln u/(1−u) = N(u)/(u(1−u)), where N(u) = (1−u)ln(1−u) − u ln u.

  5. Uniqueness: N(0⁺) = 0 and N(1/2) = 0. N′(u) = −ln(u(1−u)) − 2 and N″(u) = −1/u + 1/(1−u) = −(1 − 2u)/(u(1−u)) < 0 (for 0 < u < 1/2), so N is strictly concave on (0, 1/2), and since it is 0 at both ends, N > 0 in the interior. That is, g′ > 0. Since N(1−u) = −N(u), on (1/2, 1) we have N < 0 and g′ < 0. Therefore g increases on (0, 1/2) and decreases on (1/2, 1), and has a unique maximum at u = 1/2.

  6. If u = 1/2, then kn/m = ln 2, that is, k = (m/n)ln 2. The false positive is then (1/2)^k = 2^(−(m/n)ln 2) = (2^(−ln 2))^(m/n) = 0.6185^(m/n).

  7. Finding m/n from ε: If the false positive is ε, then 2^(−(m/n)ln 2) = ε, so (m/n)ln 2 = log₂(1/ε), that is, m/n = log₂(1/ε)/ln 2 ≈ 1.44·log₂(1/ε), and the optimal k = (m/n)ln 2 = log₂(1/ε). ∎

Checking with numbers: For m/n = 10, k = 6.93 and the false positive is 0.6185¹⁰ = 0.82%. Taking k = 7 as an integer, the e approximation gives 0.821% (independence assumed), and taking into account the distribution of the number of 1 bits gives 0.827% ✓. For ε = 1% it is 9.59 bits (k = 6.64), for 0.1% it is 14.4 bits (k = 9.97), for 10⁻⁶ it is 28.8 bits (k = 19.9), and reducing the false positives to a tenth costs 1.44·log₂10 ≈ 4.79 bits.

Proof A-6. Derivation of the Wilson interval

  1. By the central limit theorem (Chapter 6), the proportion correct p̂ satisfies (p̂ − p)/√(p(1−p)/n) ≈ N(0, 1) under the true p. Therefore |p̂ − p| ≤ z·√(p(1−p)/n) holds with probability about 95% (z = 1.96).

  2. The Wald interval replaces the p on the right with p̂ to get p̂ ± z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n). The Wilson interval does not replace it and instead solves this inequality for p.

  3. Squaring both sides and rearranging gives (1 + z²/n)p² − (2p̂ + z²/n)p + p̂² ≤ 0.

  4. The range where an upward-opening quadratic is at most 0 lies between its two roots. The discriminant is (2p̂ + z²/n)² − 4(1 + z²/n)p̂² = 4p̂(1−p̂)z²/n + z⁴/n².

  5. By the quadratic formula, p = [p̂ + z²/(2n) ± z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²))]/(1 + z²/n). ∎

  6. Properties: (i) For the quadratic f(p) = (1 + z²/n)p² − (2p̂ + z²/n)p + p̂², f(0) = p̂² ≥ 0, f(1) = (1 − p̂)² ≥ 0, and f(p̂) = −z²p̂(1−p̂)/n ≤ 0, so the two roots lie between 0 and 1. (ii) The center (p̂ + z²/(2n))/(1 + z²/n) = n/(n+z²)·p̂ + z²/(n+z²)·1/2. (iii) If p̂ = 0 it is [0, z²/(n + z²)], and if p̂ = 1 it is [n/(n + z²), 1], and for n = 20, z = 1.96, z²/(n + z²) = 3.84/23.84 = 16.1%. (iv) As n → ∞, z²/n → 0, so it approaches Wald.

Checking with numbers: n = 100, p̂ = 0.85. 1 + z²/n = 1.0384, the center is (0.85 + 0.0192)/1.0384 = 0.8370, and the half-width is 1.96·√(0.001275 + 0.000096)/1.0384 = 0.0699, so the interval is [76.7%, 90.7%] ✓.

Proof A-7. The number of questions needed

(1) Independent comparison

  1. Let the true accuracies of the two models be p₁, p₂ (q = 1 − p), the difference δ = p₂ − p₁ > 0, and suppose each model independently solves n questions. The estimated difference D̂ = p̂₂ − p̂₁ is approximately N(δ, σ²), with σ² = (p₁q₁ + p₂q₂)/n.

  2. A test at significance level α (two-sided) rejects when |D̂| > z_α/2·σ₀. σ₀ is the standard error under the null hypothesis, and when p₁ and p₂ are close it is nearly the same as σ, so we set σ₀ ≈ σ (for 85% vs 86%, the variances are 0.2480/n and 0.2479/n).

  3. The probability of rejecting under the alternative hypothesis (the power) is P(D̂ > z_α/2·σ) = Φ((δ − z_α/2·σ)/σ) (ignoring the opposite tail). For this to be at least 1 − β, we need (δ − z_α/2·σ)/σ ≥ z_β, that is, δ ≥ (z_α/2 + z_β)·σ.

  4. Putting in the expression for σ and squaring gives n ≥ (z_α/2 + z_β)²(p₁q₁ + p₂q₂)/δ². ∎

Checking with numbers: (1.959964 + 0.841621)² = 7.849, p₁q₁ + p₂q₂ = 0.1275 + 0.1204 = 0.2479, δ² = 0.0001, so 7.849 × 0.2479/0.0001 = 19,457.4 → 19,458. Using the rounded 2.80 gives 19,435.

(2) Paired comparison

  1. For the per-question difference Dᵢ ∈ {−1, 0, 1}, P(Dᵢ ≠ 0) = π_d (the discordance rate), E[Dᵢ] = δ, and E[Dᵢ²] = π_d, so Var(Dᵢ) = π_d − δ².

  2. Under the null hypothesis (δ = 0), Var(Dᵢ) = π_d, so the rejection condition is |D̄| > z_α/2·√(π_d/n).

  3. Under the alternative hypothesis, D̄ ≈ N(δ, (π_d − δ²)/n). For power 1 − β we need δ − z_α/2·√(π_d/n) ≥ z_β·√((π_d − δ²)/n).

  4. Multiplying both sides by √n and rearranging gives √n·δ ≥ z_α/2·√π_d + z_β·√(π_d − δ²), that is, n ≥ (z_α/2·√π_d + z_β·√(π_d − δ²))²/δ². ∎

  5. If π_d ≫ δ², then n ≈ (z_α/2 + z_β)²·π_d/δ², so the number of questions needed is nearly proportional to the discordance rate.

Checking with numbers: With π_d = 0.09, δ = 0.03, (1.96 × 0.3 + 0.8416 × 0.2985)²/0.0009 = 0.8392²/0.0009 = 782.5 ≈ 783. The estimate 7.849 × 0.09/0.0009 = 785 is also close. The independent comparison is 7.849 × (0.1275 + 0.1056)/0.0009 = 2,033.

Proof A-8. The floor of mini-batch noise

  1. If the sample gradients gᵢ have variance σ² and mutual correlation coefficient ρ, the variance of the mean ḡ = (1/B)Σgᵢ is (1/B²)[Bσ² + B(B−1)ρσ²] = σ²[1/B + (B−1)ρ/B] = σ²[ρ + (1−ρ)/B] (the same calculation as Proof A-1, Claim 2).

  2. If ρ = 0, it is σ²/B (Proof 8-2) and the noise is σ/√B.

  3. As B → ∞, ρσ² remains, so the floor of the noise is √ρ·σ. The point B* = (1−ρ)/ρ, where the two terms ρ and (1−ρ)/B become equal, is where the gain bends. ∎

Checking with numbers: With ρ = 0.1, √(ρ + (1−ρ)/B) at B = 1, 9, 64, 1024, ∞ is 1, 0.447, 0.338, 0.318, 0.316.

Proof A-9. The one-sided inequality for hash collisions and the independence assumption of Bloom filters

(1) Probability of no collision ≤ e^(−λ)

  1. When inserting items one at a time, the probability that the (i + 1)-th item lands in a slot different from the previous i is (m − i)/m, so the probability of no collision is Π_{i=1}^{n−1}(1 − i/m).

  2. Lemma: 1 − x ≤ e^(−x). The derivative f′(x) = 1 − e^(−x) of f(x) = e^(−x) − (1 − x) is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0, so f has its minimum 0 at x = 0.

  3. Applying this to each factor and multiplying, Π ≤ exp(−Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} i/m) = exp(−n(n−1)/(2m)) = e^(−λ). ∎ Therefore the collision probability is at least 1 − e^(−λ).

(2) The classical Bloom filter expression underestimates the false positives

  1. Inserting n items into the filter is throwing kn balls into m cells (bits). If X denotes the fraction of bits that are 1, X is a random variable.

  2. If the k positions of an item not in the filter are determined uniformly and independently of the filter, then given the filter, the probability that all those positions are 1 is Xᵏ. Taking the expectation, the false positive probability is E[Xᵏ].

  3. The classical expression is (E[X])ᵏ = (1 − (1 − 1/m)^(kn))ᵏ.

  4. Since x ↦ xᵏ (k ≥ 2) is convex and X is not a constant, Jensen’s inequality gives E[Xᵏ] > (E[X])ᵏ. That is, the classical expression is smaller than the actual value. ∎

  5. Concentration: one ball changes the number of 1 bits Z = mX by at most 1, so by the Azuma–Hoeffding (McDiarmid) inequality, P(|Z − E[Z]| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−2t²/(kn)) (a method presented as a result of Mitzenmacher & Upfal). Because Z concentrates around its mean, in large filters the difference between E[Xᵏ] and (E[X])ᵏ is small.

Checking with numbers: For m = 1000, n = 100, E[Xᵏ] at k = 3, 7, 10 is 1.745%, 0.827%, 1.033%, and the classical expression gives 1.741%, 0.819%, 1.019%. For m = 64, n = 8, k = 4 they are 2.54% and 2.40% (computed with the code in the main text).

Glossary for the Further Reading

  • Ensemble: A method of combining the outputs of several models into one result. Majority voting is the simplest example

  • Diversity: The degree to which models are wrong on different problems. The smaller the correlation ρ, the more diverse

  • Cross-entropy: The average number of bits when data from the true distribution p is encoded with a model q. −Σ pᵢ log qᵢ

  • Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence): Cross-entropy minus entropy. The number of bits wasted because the model is wrong, and it is at least 0

  • Perplexity: 2^(cross-entropy in bits) = e^(cross-entropy in nats). The “number of candidates” the model wavers among

  • Maximum likelihood: A method of choosing the model that makes the probability of the data largest

  • Softmax: A function that converts scores z into probabilities e^(zᵢ)/Σe^(zⱼ). The probability vector of the multinomial distribution of Chapter 11

  • Logit: The score before it enters the softmax

  • Sign test: A binomial test that compares, among discordant pairs, which side won against a fair coin

  • Selection bias: The phenomenon whereby, when the best result among several candidates is picked and reported, it is on average inflated

  • Bonferroni correction: A conservative method of lowering the criterion to α/k when testing k times

  • Minibatch: The unit of B items drawn from the training data to estimate the gradient

  • Bloom filter: A structure that answers “have we seen it before?” with bits at hash positions. It has false positives but no false negatives

  • Wilson interval: A confidence interval obtained by solving |p̂ − p| ≤ z√(p(1−p)/n) for p. Its center is pulled toward 1/2, and it can be used with small n and extreme p̂

  • McNemar test: A test that compares two models that solved the same questions using only the discordant questions. The exact form is the binomial test of B(b + c, 1/2), and the approximation is (b − c)²/(b + c)

  • Jensen’s inequality: For a convex function φ, E[φ(X)] ≥ φ(E[X])

  • Union bound (Boole’s inequality): The probability of a union of events is at most the sum of the probabilities. The basis of the Bonferroni correction

  • Hoeffding’s inequality: An exponential upper bound on the probability that a sum of independent bounded variables deviates greatly from its expectation

Notes on the Further Reading

  • The hypothetical examples (accuracies, numbers of questions, numbers of models, hash sizes, and so on) are values chosen for explanation, and are not values of real systems.

  • The independence assumption of the ensemble and the common-mistake model (the ρ model) are toy models for understanding. The correlation structure of real models is far more complicated.

  • What this section states without proof is how accurate the normal approximation and the chi-square approximation are (the size of the error), and the fact that the maximum of independent models approaches √(2 ln k). For the former we simply assume that the approximation is good; for the latter only the upper bound was proved.

  • The statements about the Wilson interval, the McNemar test, and the independence assumption of Bloom filters follow the references listed below.

Appendix. Glossary and Sources (Common to Parts 1 and 2)

Glossary

  • Binomial coefficient: The number of ways to choose k out of n, C(n,k)

  • Binomial distribution: The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials with success probability p

  • Bernoulli trial: A single trial with only two outcomes, success or failure. A single coin toss is the typical example

  • Independence: That the outcome of one trial does not affect the probabilities of other trials

  • Expected value (mean): The average of the outcomes when the trial is repeated indefinitely. For the binomial distribution it is np

  • Variance and standard deviation: A measure of how widely the outcomes scatter around the mean. The variance of the binomial distribution is np(1−p) and the standard deviation is its square root

  • Normal distribution: A bell-shaped distribution symmetric about its mean

  • de Moivre–Laplace theorem: The theorem that approximates the binomial distribution by a normal distribution for large n

  • Continuity correction: A correction that widens both ends of an interval by 0.5 when approximating discrete values by a continuous curve

  • Poisson distribution: A distribution for the number of occurrences of a rare event. The mean and variance are equal

  • Central limit theorem: The theorem that a sum of independent values approaches a normal distribution

  • Law of large numbers: The law that the larger the sample, the more the mean gathers around the true value

  • Confidence interval: An interval estimate constructed to contain the true value

  • Margin of error: The half-width of a confidence interval

  • p-value: The probability, when the assumption is correct, of obtaining a result as extreme as the observation

  • Catalan number: The number of correctly matched sets of n pairs of parentheses. C(2n,n)/(n+1)

  • Sierpiński triangle: The fractal pattern that appears when only the odd cells of Pascal’s triangle are colored

  • Factorial: n! = 1×2×…×n, with the convention 0! = 1

  • Skewness: The degree to which a distribution leans to one side. For the binomial distribution it is (1−2p)/√(np(1−p)), and if 0 the distribution is symmetric

  • Multinomial coefficient: n!/(a!b!c!). The number of ways to divide or arrange n items into three groups without distinguishing identical ones

  • Multinomial distribution: The distribution of the number of times each branch occurs in independent trials with three or more branches

  • Pascal’s pyramid: The structure obtained by stacking, layer by layer, the coefficients of (x+y+z)ⁿ as triangles

  • Chi-square statistic: ∑(O−E)²/E. A measure of how different the observed counts are from the expected counts

  • Generating function: An expression that holds a sequence as the coefficients of a polynomial or power series

  • Probability generating function: G(x) = ∑P(X=k)xᵏ. A sum of independent variables becomes a product, and the mean is G′(1)

  • Characteristic function: The generating function with x = e^(it) substituted

  • Stirling’s formula: n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ

  • Binary entropy: H(q) = −q log₂q − (1−q) log₂(1−q). The uncertainty (in bits) of a single toss of a coin with heads probability q
